title: 22.7 Zariski Decomposition
text:
Theorem 1 (Zariski Decomposition on Surfaces) Let \(X\) be a smooth projective surface and let \(D\) be a pseudoeffective integral Cartier divisor on \(X\). Then there exists a unique decomposition into \(\mathbb{Q}\)-divisors: \[
D = P + N
\] satisfying the following properties:

\(P\) is nef;
\(N = \sum_{i=1}^r a_i E_i\) is effective (\(a_i > 0\)), and if \(N \neq 0\), the intersection matrix \((E_i \cdot E_j)_{1 \le i, j \le r}\) is negative definite;
\(P \cdot E_i = 0\) for every irreducible component \(E_i\) of \(N\). (In particular, if \(N \neq 0\), \(P \in \partial \operatorname{Nef}(X)\)).

Moreover, the natural inclusion induces an isomorphism on global sections: \[
H^0\big(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD - \lceil m N \rceil)\big) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} H^0\big(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD)\big) \quad \text{for all } m \ge 1.
\] In particular, \(\operatorname{vol}(D) = \operatorname{vol}(P) = (P^2)\).


Proof. We prove the isomorphism on global sections. It suffices to show that for every effective divisor \(D' \sim m D\), we have \(D' \ge m N\). Clearing denominators, we may assume \(m = 1\) and \(P, N\) are integral.
Let \(D' \sim D\) be an effective divisor. Write \(D' = N_1 + M_1\), where \(N_1 = \sum c_i E_i \in \bigoplus \mathbb{Z} E_i\) and \(M_1\) shares no components with \(N\). Because \(P \cdot E_i = 0\), we have: \[
(D' - N) \cdot E_i = (D' - D) \cdot E_i + (D - N) \cdot E_i = 0 + P \cdot E_i = 0.
\] Since \(D' = N_1 + M_1\) and \(M_1 \cdot E_i \ge 0\), this implies: \[
(N_1 - N) \cdot E_i = (D' - N) \cdot E_i - M_1 \cdot E_i \le 0 \quad \text{for all } i.
\] Write \(N_1 - N = N' - N''\), where \(N', N'' \in \bigoplus \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0} E_i\) have no common components. We must show \(N'' = 0\). If \(N'' \neq 0\), then \((N''^2) < 0\) by the negative definiteness of \((E_i \cdot E_j)\). Hence: \[
(N_1 - N) \cdot N'' = N' \cdot N'' - (N''^2) > 0,
\] since \(N' \cdot N'' \ge 0\). On the other hand, \((N_1 - N) \cdot E_i \le 0\) for all \(i\) implies that \((N_1 - N) \cdot N'' \le 0\), a contradiction. Thus \(N'' = 0\), which proves \(N_1 \ge N\).


Corollary 1 (Finite Generation via the Positive Part) Let \(D\) be a big divisor on a smooth projective surface \(X\), with Zariski decomposition \(D = P + N\). Then the section ring \(R(X, D)\) is finitely generated if and only if \(P\) is semiample.


Proof. By Theorem 1, \(R(X, D) \cong R(X, P)\). Since \(\operatorname{vol}(P) = \operatorname{vol}(D) > 0\) and \(P\) is nef, \(P\) is big and nef. The result follows immediately from ?@thm-criterion-fg-nef-big.



Definition 1 (Extremal Ray) Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space and \(K \subseteq V\) a closed convex cone. A 1-dimensional subcone \(R = \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0} \cdot v \subseteq K\) is called an extremal ray of \(K\) if whenever \(x, y \in K\) satisfy: \[
x + y \in R,
\] then both \(x, y \in R\).


Example 1 (Curves on a Surface and Extremal Rays) Let \(X\) be a smooth projective surface. Poincaré duality identifies 1-cycles with divisors, so \(N^1(X)_{\mathbb{R}} \cong N_1(X)_{\mathbb{R}}\).

\(\operatorname{Nef}(X) \subseteq \overline{\operatorname{NE}}(X)\). If \((C^2) \ge 0\) for every irreducible curve \(C \subseteq X\), then \(\operatorname{Nef}(X) = \overline{\operatorname{NE}}(X)\).
If \(C \subseteq X\) is an irreducible curve with \((C^2) < 0\), then: \[
\overline{\operatorname{NE}}(X) = \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0} [C] + \overline{\operatorname{NE}}(X)_{C_{\ge 0}}, \quad \text{where } \overline{\operatorname{NE}}(X)_{C_{\ge 0}} := \{ \gamma \in \overline{\operatorname{NE}}(X) \mid \gamma \cdot C \ge 0 \}.
\]
If \(C\) is an irreducible curve with \((C^2) < 0\), then \([C]\) spans an extremal ray in \(\overline{\operatorname{NE}}(X)\).



Proof. Proof of (2) and (3): For any irreducible curve \(C' \neq C\), \((C' \cdot C) \ge 0\), so \([C'] \in \overline{\operatorname{NE}}(X)_{C_{\ge 0}}\). Any effective 1-cycle decomposes as \(E = a C + E'\) where \(C \not\subseteq \operatorname{Supp}(E')\), proving the sum formula.
Since \((C^2) < 0\), \([C] \notin \overline{\operatorname{NE}}(X)_{C_{\ge 0}}\). Suppose \(v, w \in \overline{\operatorname{NE}}(X)\) satisfy \(v + w = \lambda [C] \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0} [C]\). Decomposing \(v = v_1 + v_2\) and \(w = w_1 + w_2\) with \(v_1, w_1 \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0} [C]\) and \(v_2, w_2 \in \overline{\operatorname{NE}}(X)_{C_{\ge 0}}\), we obtain \(v_2 + w_2 = 0\). Because \(\overline{\operatorname{NE}}(X)\) contains no straight lines (as \((H \cdot \gamma) > 0\) for ample \(H\)), this forces \(v_2 = w_2 = 0\), so \(v, w \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0} [C]\).


Example 2 (Kollár’s Example: Unboundedness of Very Ample Multiples) On a curve \(Y\) of genus \(g\), every ample line bundle \(D\) satisfies that \(m D\) is very ample for \(m \ge 2g + 1\). Kollár showed that in dimension \(\ge 2\), there is no uniform bound \(m(Y)\) such that \(m D\) is very ample for all ample divisors \(D\).
Construction: Let \(X = E \times E\) for an elliptic curve \(E\). For \(n \ge 2\), define the divisor: \[
A_n := n F_1 + (n^2 - n + 1) F_2 - (n-1)\Delta.
\] Computing intersection numbers yields \((A_n^2) = 2\) and \(A_n \cdot (F_1 + F_2) = n^2 - 2n + 3 > 0\), so \(A_n\) is ample. Set \(R = F_1 + F_2\). Choose a smooth curve \(B \in |2 R|\) and let \(\pi: Y \to X\) be the double cover branched along \(B\).
Pulling back gives an ample divisor \(D_n := \pi^* A_n\) on \(Y\). We compute: \[
\pi_* \mathcal{O}_Y(n D_n) = \mathcal{O}_X(n A_n) \oplus \mathcal{O}_X(n A_n - R).
\] The self-intersection of \(n A_n - R\) is: \[
(n A_n - R)^2 = 2n^2 - 2n(n^2 - 2n + 3) + 2 = -2(n-1)^3 < 0.
\] If \(H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(n A_n - R)) \neq 0\), the effective divisor would lie in \(\overline{\operatorname{NE}}(X) = \operatorname{Nef}(X)\), forcing its self-intersection to be non-negative, a contradiction. Thus: \[
H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(n A_n)) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} H^0(Y, \mathcal{O}_Y(n D_n)).
\] Because the global sections of \(n D_n\) all factor through \(X\), they cannot separate the two sheets of the double cover \(\pi: Y \to X\). Hence \(n D_n\) is not very ample, which forces the very ample threshold \(m(D_n) > n\) to grow arbitrarily large.



Definition 2 (The Null Cone) Let \(X\) be an irreducible projective variety of dimension \(n\), and let \(V \subseteq X\) be a subvariety of dimension \(d\).

The polynomial map associated with \(V\) is: \[
q_V: N^1(X)_{\mathbb{R}} \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}, \quad q_V(\xi) := (\xi^d \cdot V).
\]
The null cone of \(V\) is the algebraic variety: \[
\mathcal{N}_V := \big\{ \xi \in N^1(X)_{\mathbb{R}} \;\big|\; q_V(\xi) = 0 \big\}.
\]



Definition 3 (The Nef Boundary) The nef boundary of \(X\) is the boundary of the nef cone: \[
\mathcal{B}_X := \partial \operatorname{Nef}(X) \subseteq N^1(X)_{\mathbb{R}}.
\]


Proposition 1 (Boundary Covered by Null Cones) For every \(\xi \in \mathcal{B}_X\), there exists an irreducible subvariety \(V \subseteq X\) such that \(q_V(\xi) = 0\). That is: \[
\mathcal{B}_X \subseteq \bigcup_{V \subseteq X} \mathcal{N}_V.
\]


Proof. By definition of the nef cone, \(q_V(\xi) \ge 0\) for all subvarieties \(V \subseteq X\). If \(q_V(\xi) > 0\) for all \(V\), the Nakai-Moishezon criterion (?@thm-nakai-r-divisors) implies that \(\xi\) is ample, which means \(\xi \in \operatorname{int}(\operatorname{Nef}(X))\), contradicting \(\xi \in \mathcal{B}_X\).


Theorem 2 (Campana-Peternell Theorem) Let \(X\) be an irreducible projective variety. There exists an open dense subset \(\mathcal{CP}(X) \subseteq \mathcal{B}_X\) such that for every \(\xi \in \mathcal{CP}(X)\), there exists an open neighborhood \(U = U(\xi) \subseteq N^1(X)_{\mathbb{R}}\) and an irreducible subvariety \(V \subseteq X\) such that: \[
\mathcal{B}_X \cap U = \mathcal{N}_V \cap U.
\] In other words, the nef boundary is generically real-analytic, cut out locally by the polynomials \(q_V\).


Proof. For each subvariety \(V \subseteq X\), define the open subset of the boundary: \[
\mathcal{O}_V := \big\{ \xi \in \mathcal{B}_X \;\big|\; \exists U(\xi) \text{ s.t. } U(\xi) \cap \mathcal{B}_X \subseteq \mathcal{N}_V \big\}, \qquad \mathcal{O} := \bigcup_{V \subseteq X} \mathcal{O}_V.
\]
Claim: \(\mathcal{O}\) is dense in \(\mathcal{B}_X\). Suppose it is not. Then there exists an open set \(U \subseteq N^1(X)_{\mathbb{R}}\) intersecting \(\mathcal{B}_X\) such that \(U \cap \mathcal{O} = \emptyset\), so \(U \cap \mathcal{O}_V = \emptyset\) for all \(V\). Thus \(\overline{U} \setminus \mathcal{N}_V\) is dense in \(\overline{U}\) for each \(V\). Since the topological cycle class \([V] \in H_{2d}(X, \mathbb{Z})\) belongs to a finitely generated abelian group, there are at most countably many distinct null cones \(\mathcal{N}_V\). By the Baire Category Theorem, the countable intersection: \[
\bigcap_V (\overline{U} \setminus \mathcal{N}_V) = \overline{U} \setminus \bigcup_V \mathcal{N}_V
\] is dense in \(\overline{U}\). But this contradicts Proposition 1, which states that \(\mathcal{B}_X \subseteq \bigcup_V \mathcal{N}_V\).
Now, let \(\mathcal{P} \subseteq \mathcal{B}_X\) be the set of points satisfying the local equality of the theorem. Fix \(\xi_1 \in \mathcal{O}_V\) with \(\dim V\) minimal. Choose a general very ample divisor \(H\) such that \(H \cap V\) is proper. By the minimality of \(\dim V\), \(\xi_1 \notin \mathcal{O}_{H \cap V}\). Hence there exists a sequence \(\eta_n \to \xi_1\) with \(q_{H \cap V}(\eta_n) > 0\). The directional derivative satisfies: \[
\lim_{t \to 0} \frac{q_V(\eta_n + t [H]) - q_V(\eta_n)}{t} = \dim V \cdot (\eta_n^{\dim V - 1} \cdot H \cdot V) = \dim V \cdot q_{H \cap V}(\eta_n) > 0.
\] Thus the differential \(D q_V(\eta_n) \neq 0\), so \(\mathcal{N}_V\) is a smooth manifold near \(\eta_n\). Projecting locally onto the tangent space \(T_{\eta_n} \mathcal{N}_V\), topological invariance of domain implies that \(\mathcal{B}_X\) and \(\mathcal{N}_V\) must coincide in a small neighborhood of \(\eta_n\).


Corollary 2 (Dual Campana-Peternell Theorem) By cone duality between \(N^1(X)_{\mathbb{R}}\) and \(N_1(X)_{\mathbb{R}}\), there exists an open dense subset \(\mathcal{CP}(X)^* \subseteq \partial \overline{\operatorname{NE}}(X)\) that is locally cut out by linear hyperplanes associated with subvarieties of \(X\).



Theorem 3 (Mori’s Cone Theorem) Let \(X\) be a smooth projective variety of dimension \(n\).

There exists a countable family of rational curves \(\{C_i\}_{i \in I}\) on \(X\) satisfying \(0 < -(K_X \cdot C_i) \le n + 1\) such that: \[
\overline{\operatorname{NE}}(X) = \overline{\operatorname{NE}}(X)_{K_X \ge 0} + \sum_{i \in I} \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0} [C_i].
\]
For any ample divisor \(H\) and any \(\varepsilon > 0\), there are only finitely many curves \(C_1, \dots, C_t\) spanning extremal rays in the half-space \((K_X + \varepsilon H)_{\le 0}\), so that: \[
\overline{\operatorname{NE}}(X) = \overline{\operatorname{NE}}(X)_{K_X + \varepsilon H \ge 0} + \sum_{i=1}^t \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0} [C_i].
\]



Corollary 3 (Cone of Fano Varieties) If \(X\) is a Fano variety (that is, \(-K_X\) is ample), then the cone of curves \(\overline{\operatorname{NE}}(X) = \operatorname{NE}(X)\) is a rational polyhedral cone generated by finitely many classes of rational curves.


Corollary 4 (Numerical Ampleness Bounds) Let \(X\) be a smooth projective variety of dimension \(n\).

If \(D\) is an ample divisor such that \((D \cdot C) \ge n + 2\) for all rational curves \(C \subseteq X\), then \(K_X + D\) is ample.
If \(D\) is a nef divisor such that \((D \cdot C) \ge n + 1\) for all rational curves \(C \subseteq X\), then \(K_X + D\) is nef.



Proof. By the Cone Theorem (Theorem 3), any class \(\gamma \in \overline{\operatorname{NE}}(X)\) decomposes as \(\gamma = \gamma_0 + \sum a_i [C_i]\) with \(K_X \cdot \gamma_0 \ge 0\) and \(-(K_X \cdot C_i) \le n+1\). For (1): \[
(K_X + D) \cdot C_i = (K_X \cdot C_i) + (D \cdot C_i) \ge -(n+1) + (n+2) = 1 > 0,
\] and \((K_X + D) \cdot \gamma_0 \ge D \cdot \gamma_0 > 0\). By Kleiman’s criterion (?@thm-kleiman-cone-criterion), \(K_X + D\) is ample. Statement (2) follows similarly.


Example 3 (Extremal Rays on Blowups of \(\mathbb{P}^2\)) Let \(X = \operatorname{Bl}_{P_1, \dots, P_n}(\mathbb{P}^2)\) be the blow-up of \(\mathbb{P}^2\) at \(n\) points in general position. Let \(\ell\) be the pullback of the line class and \(e_1, \dots, e_n\) the exceptional divisors, so \(-K_X = 3\ell - \sum_{i=1}^n e_i\).

For \(1 \le n \le 8\), \(-K_X\) is ample (so \(X\) is a del Pezzo surface). By the adjunction formula: \[
(C^2) + (C \cdot K_X) = 2 g - 2.
\] Every \(K_X\)-negative extremal ray must have \(g = 0\) and \((C^2) = -1\), meaning it is spanned by a \((-1)\)-curve. Writing \(C = d \ell - \sum m_i e_i\), the conditions \(d^2 = \sum m_i^2 - 1\) and \(3d - 1 = \sum m_i\) combined with Cauchy-Schwarz give: \[
(9 - n) d^2 - 6d + (1 - n) \le 0.
\] Since \(9 - n > 0\), this inequality yields only finitely many integer solutions for \(d\), reflecting the finiteness of the cone.
For \(n \ge 10\), \(-K_X\) is no longer nef. There exist infinitely many \((-1)\)-curves with degrees \(d \to \infty\). Their normalized classes in the affine slice accumulate on the boundary of the cone of curves.



Example 4 (Variational Pathologies of the Iitaka Dimension) Let \(T\) be a smooth curve. There exists a family of smooth projective surfaces \(X \to T\) and a line bundle \(L\) on \(X\) such that: \[
\kappa(X_t, L_t) = -\infty \quad \text{for general } t \in T, \qquad \text{while} \qquad \kappa(X_0, L_0) = 2 \quad (\text{big})
\] at a special closed point \(0 \in T\).
Construction: Let \(S \subseteq \mathbb{P}^2\) be a set of 9 distinct points, and consider \(X_S = \operatorname{Bl}_S(\mathbb{P}^2)\) with divisor \(D_S = 2 H_S - E_S\). - If the 9 points lie on a smooth cubic \(B\), the strict transform \(C = 3H - E\) satisfies \((D_S \cdot C) = -3 < 0\). Slicing by multiples of \(C\) reveals that \(H^0(X_S, \mathcal{O}_{X_S}(m D_S)) = 0\) for all \(m \ge 1\). Hence \(\kappa(X_S, D_S) = -\infty\) for general configurations \(S\). - If the 9 points become collinear, \(D_S - H_S\) becomes effective, which implies \(D_S\) is big, so \(\kappa = 2\).

title: 22.9 Connectedness I
text:
Theorem 1 (Bertini’s Theorem on Irreducibility) Let \(X\) be a variety over \(\mathbb{C}\), and let \(f: X \to \mathbb{P}^r\) be a morphism. Fix an integer \(d < \dim \overline{f(X)}\). If \(L \subseteq \mathbb{P}^r\) is a general \((r - d)\)-plane (i.e., belonging to a dense open subset in the Grassmannian \(\mathbb{G}(r - d, r)\)), then the preimage: \[
f^{-1}(L)
\] is irreducible.


Lemma 1 (Irreducibility of Fibers Admitting a Section) Let \(p: V \to T\) be a dominant morphism of irreducible complex varieties. If \(p\) admits a section \(s: T \to V\) such that \(s(T) \nsubseteq \operatorname{Sing}(V)\), then the fiber: \[
V_t = p^{-1}(t)
\] is irreducible for general \(t \in T\).


Proof. Since \(s(T) \nsubseteq \operatorname{Sing}(V)\), the generic point \(\eta_T \notin s^{-1}(\operatorname{Sing} V)\). Define the open subset \(U := T \setminus s^{-1}(\operatorname{Sing} V)\). Shrinking \(T\) to \(U\) and \(V\) to \(p^{-1}(U)\), we may assume without loss of generality that \(T\) is smooth, \(s(T) \cap \operatorname{Sing}(V) = \varnothing\), and \(p\) is flat (hence every fiber has pure dimension).
Now consider \(V_t \cap \operatorname{Sing}(V)\). Since \(s(t) \notin \operatorname{Sing}(V)\), we have \(V_t \nsubseteq \operatorname{Sing}(V)\), so \(V_t \setminus \operatorname{Sing}(V)\) is dense in \(V_t\). Replacing \(V\) by \(V \setminus \operatorname{Sing}(V)\), we may assume that \(V\) is smooth. By generic smoothness, shrinking the target \(T\) further, we may assume that \(p\) is smooth.
It now suffices to show that the fibers of \(p\) are generally connected: 1. By [Stacks Project, Tag 055J], for a smooth morphism, the fibers are geometrically irreducible if and only if they are geometrically connected. Hence it suffices to show that the geometric generic fiber \(V_{\bar{\eta}}\) is irreducible. 2. By [Stacks Project, Tag 054Q], this is equivalent to showing that the function field \(k(T)\) is separably closed in \(k(V)\).
Consider the Stein factorization: let \(\widetilde{k(T)}\) be the separable closure of \(k(T)\) in \(k(V)\), and let \(\widetilde{T}\) be the normalization of \(T\) with respect to \(\widetilde{k(T)}\). This yields the factorization: \[
\begin{CD}
V @>{\tilde{p}}>> \widetilde{T} \\
@V{p}VV @VV{f}V \\
T @= T
\end{CD}
\] where \(\tilde{p}\) is induced by \(\mathcal{O}_T \hookrightarrow \widetilde{\mathcal{O}}_T \hookrightarrow p_* \mathcal{O}_V\) (using that \(V\) is normal).
Then \(f: \widetilde{T} \to T\) is finite, and \(\tilde{p}: V \to \widetilde{T}\) has geometrically connected fibers. Because \(p \circ s = \operatorname{id}_T\), we have: \[
f \circ (\tilde{p} \circ s) = \operatorname{id}_T,
\] so \(\tilde{p} \circ s\) is a section of \(f\). Since \(T\) is normal and \(f\) is a finite morphism admitting a section, \(f\) must be an isomorphism (\(\widetilde{T} \cong T\)). Hence \(\widetilde{k(T)} = k(T)\), which proves that the fibers of \(p\) are irreducible for general \(t \in T\).


Proof. (Proof of Theorem 1) Let \(n := \dim \overline{f(X)}\). It suffices to prove the theorem for \(d = n - 1\).
Indeed, suppose the result holds for \(d = n - 1\). For any other \(d < n - 1\), let \(L \subseteq \mathbb{P}^r\) be an \((r - d)\)-plane. If \(f^{-1}(L)\) were reducible for general \(L\), we could choose an \((r - n + 1)\)-plane \(L' \subseteq L\) such that \(L'\) is “general” (i.e., \(f^{-1}(L')\) is irreducible).
Writing \(f^{-1}(L) = Y_1 \cup Y_2\) with \(Y_1, Y_2\) irreducible, each component has dimension \(\dim Y_i \ge n - d\). Setting \(k := n - 1 - d \ge 1\), we have \(\dim Y_i \ge k + 1\). Then: \[
f^{-1}(L') = \big(f^{-1}(L') \cap Y_1\big) \cup \big(f^{-1}(L') \cap Y_2\big).
\] Adjust \(L'\) so that \(\dim\big(f^{-1}(L') \cap Y_1 \cap Y_2\big) = \dim(Y_1 \cap Y_2) - k\). If \(f^{-1}(L') \cap Y_1 \subseteq f^{-1}(L') \cap Y_2\), then \(f^{-1}(L') \cap Y_1 \subseteq f^{-1}(L') \cap Y_1 \cap Y_2\), which yields: \[
\dim\big(f^{-1}(L') \cap Y_1\big) \ge \dim Y_1 - 1, \quad \text{while} \quad \dim\big(f^{-1}(L') \cap Y_1 \cap Y_2\big) \le \dim Y_1 - 1 - k,
\] a contradiction! The same argument applies to \(Y_2\), which would imply that \(f^{-1}(L')\) is reducible, contradicting the choice of \(L'\). Therefore, \(f^{-1}(L)\) must be irreducible.
Now assume \(d = n - 1\). Fix a general \((r - n)\)-plane \(\Lambda \subseteq \mathbb{P}^r\). The set of all \((r - n + 1)\)-planes \(L \subseteq \mathbb{P}^r\) passing through \(\Lambda\) is parametrized by \(T = \mathbb{P}^{n-1}\). Consider the incidence family: \[
V := \big\{ (x, t) \in X \times T \;\big|\; f(x) \in L_t \big\} \subseteq X \times T,
\] equipped with the projection \(p: V \to T\). It suffices to show that the general fiber of \(p\) is irreducible.
Observe the projection \(V \to X\). For any \(x \in X \setminus f^{-1}(\Lambda)\), the point \(f(x)\) and \(\Lambda\) span a unique \((r - n + 1)\)-plane \(L_t\), which defines a unique \(t \in T\). Thus: \[
V \setminus \big(f^{-1}(\Lambda) \times T\big) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} X \setminus f^{-1}(\Lambda).
\] Since \(X \setminus f^{-1}(\Lambda)\) is irreducible, \(V \setminus (f^{-1}(\Lambda) \times T)\) is irreducible and dense in \(V\), so \(V\) is irreducible.
Note that the blow-up \(\mathrm{Bl}_\Lambda \mathbb{P}^r \hookrightarrow \mathbb{P}^r \times T\) has image \(\big\{ (x, L_t) \mid x \in L_t \big\}\). We obtain a commutative diagram with strict transforms: \[
\begin{CD}
\mathrm{Bl}_{f^{-1}(\Lambda)} X @>>> X \times T @>>> X \\
@VV{\text{strict transf.}}V @VVV @VVV \\
\mathrm{Bl}_\Lambda \mathbb{P}^r @>>> \mathbb{P}^r \times T @>>> \mathbb{P}^r
\end{CD}
\] Choosing \(\Lambda\) such that \(f^{-1}(\Lambda)\) is cut out by a regular sequence (i.e., intersects properly), we have \(V = \mathrm{Bl}_{f^{-1}(\Lambda)} X\). In particular, for any \(x \in f^{-1}(\Lambda) \cap X^{\mathrm{reg}}\), \(V\) is smooth near \(x\).
Since \(X \to \overline{f(X)}\) is generically smooth on the source, there exist open dense subsets \(U \subseteq X^{\mathrm{reg}}\) and \(W \subseteq \overline{f(X)}\) such that \(U \to W\) is smooth. Choosing \(\Lambda\) such that \(\Lambda \cap W \neq \varnothing\), there exists a point: \[
x_0 \in f^{-1}(\Lambda) \cap X^{\mathrm{reg}} \cap f^{-1}(W)^{\mathrm{reg}}.
\] Then the map: \[
s: T \longrightarrow V, \quad t \longmapsto (x_0, t)
\] defines a section of \(p: V \to T\) with \(s(T) \subseteq V^{\mathrm{reg}}\). By Lemma 1, the general fiber of \(p\) is irreducible.



Theorem 2 (Bertini’s Theorem for Connectedness (Proper Version)) Let \(X\) be an irreducible proper variety over \(\mathbb{C}\), and let \(f: X \to \mathbb{P}^r\) be a morphism. Let \(L \subseteq \mathbb{P}^r\) be a linear subspace of codimension \(d < \dim \overline{f(X)}\). Then the preimage: \[
f^{-1}(L)
\] is connected for all \(L\). (More generally, this holds whenever \(f^{-1}(L)\) is proper).


Proof. Let \(G = \mathbb{G}(r - d, r)\) be the Grassmannian parametrizing all codimension \(d\) linear spaces in \(\mathbb{P}^r\). Consider the closed incidence variety: \[
Z := \big\{ (x, L) \in X \times G \;\big|\; x \in f^{-1}(L) \big\} \subseteq X \times G.
\] The projection \(Z \to X\) realizes \(Z\) as a Grassmannian bundle over \(X\). Since \(Z \to X\) is an irreducible smooth bundle with irreducible fibers and \(X\) is irreducible, \(Z\) is irreducible.
Let \(p: Z \to G\) be the projection onto the second factor. Because \(X\) is proper, \(p\) is proper. Consider its Stein factorization: \[
Z \xrightarrow{\;\tilde{p}\;} W \xrightarrow{\;r\;} G.
\] The general fiber of \(p\) is irreducible by Theorem 1, so \(r: W \to G\) is generically bijective. Since \(G\) is smooth, it is normal. By Zariski’s Main Theorem, \([K(W) : K(G)] = 1\) implies \(W \cong G\). Therefore, every fiber of \(p\) is connected, which shows that \(f^{-1}(L)\) is connected for all \(L\).


Corollary 1 (Curves Connecting Two Points) Let \(X\) be an irreducible quasi-projective variety over \(\mathbb{C}\). Any two distinct points \(x_1, x_2 \in X\) can be joined by an irreducible curve \(C \subseteq X\) (which may not be smooth).


Proof. Let \(X' := \mathrm{Bl}_{\{x_1, x_2\}} X\), and let \(E_1, E_2 \subseteq X'\) be the exceptional divisors. Choose a quasi-finite morphism \(f: X' \to \mathbb{P}^r\). Let \(L \subseteq \mathbb{P}^r\) be a linear subspace of codimension \(\dim X - 1\) such that \(f(E_i) \cap L \neq \varnothing\). For a general choice of \(L\), the restriction \(f|_{E_i}\) is finite.
By Theorem 1, \(f^{-1}(L)\) is irreducible of dimension \(1\). Setting \(\widetilde{C} := f^{-1}(L)\) and taking its image \(C := \pi\big(f^{-1}(L)\big) \subseteq X\) under the blow-down morphism \(\pi: X' \to X\), we obtain an irreducible curve \(C\) joining \(x_1\) and \(x_2\).



Theorem 3 (Fulton–Hansen Connectedness Theorem) Let \(X\) be an irreducible proper variety over \(\mathbb{C}\), and let \(f: X \to \mathbb{P}^r \times \mathbb{P}^r\) be a morphism such that \(\dim \overline{f(X)} > r\). Then: \[
f^{-1}(\Delta) \subseteq X
\] is connected, where \(\Delta \subseteq \mathbb{P}^r \times \mathbb{P}^r\) is the diagonal projective subspace.


Proof. Observation: Consider the open subvariety \(V \subseteq \mathbb{P}^{2r+1}\) defined by \(V := \mathbb{P}^{2r+1} \setminus (L_1 \cup L_2)\), where: \[
L_1 = \big\{ [0, \dots, 0, y_0, \dots, y_r] \big\}, \qquad L_2 = \big\{ [x_0, \dots, x_r, 0, \dots, 0] \big\}.
\] The morphism \(p: V \to \mathbb{P}^r \times \mathbb{P}^r\) is defined by: \[
[x_0, \dots, x_r, y_0, \dots, y_r] \longmapsto \big([x_0, \dots, x_r], [y_0, \dots, y_r]\big).
\] Locally on \(\mathbb{P}^r \times D(y_i)\), we have \(V|_{\mathbb{P}^r \times D(y_i)} \cong (\mathbb{A}^{r+1} \setminus \{0\}) \times \mathbb{A}^r\), fitting into the Cartesian diagram: \[
\begin{CD}
V|_{\mathbb{P}^r \times D(y_i)} @>{\sim}>> (\mathbb{A}^{r+1} \setminus \{0\}) \times \mathbb{A}^r \\
@VVV @VVV \\
\mathbb{P}^r \times D(y_i) @>{\sim}>> \mathbb{P}^r \times \mathbb{A}^r
\end{CD}
\] where \(\mathbb{A}^{r+1} \setminus \{0\} \to \mathbb{P}^r\) is the natural projection. Hence \(V \to \mathbb{P}^r \times \mathbb{P}^r\) is a principal \(\mathbb{G}_m\)-bundle.
Define the projective subspace: \[
\mathcal{L} := \big\{ [x_0, \dots, x_r, y_0, \dots, y_r] \in V \;\big|\; x_i = y_i \text{ for all } i \big\} \subseteq V.
\] Then \(\mathcal{L} \xrightarrow{\sim} \Delta\) under \(p\).
Now, given \(f: X \to \mathbb{P}^r \times \mathbb{P}^r\), form the fiber product: \[
\begin{CD}
V_X @>{f_V}>> V \\
@V{p}VV @VV{p}V \\
X @>{f}>> \mathbb{P}^r \times \mathbb{P}^r
\end{CD}
\] Since \(X\) is irreducible and \(V_X \to X\) is smooth with irreducible fibers (hence an open map), \(V_X\) is irreducible. Moreover, \(f\) proper implies \(f_V\) is proper.
Consider the factorization through the image: \[
\begin{CD}
V_X @>>> V_{f(X)} @>>> V \\
@VVV @VVV @VV{p}V \\
X @>>> f(X) @>>> \mathbb{P}^r \times \mathbb{P}^r
\end{CD}
\] where \(V_{f(X)} := \operatorname{Im}(f_V)\) is a \(\mathbb{G}_m\)-bundle over \(f(X)\). By flatness, \(\dim V_{f(X)} = \dim \overline{f(X)} + 1\). Thus: \[
\dim \overline{f_V(V_X)} = \dim \overline{f(X)} + 1 > r + 1 = \operatorname{codim}_{\mathbb{P}^{2r+1}}(\mathcal{L}).
\] By Theorem 2, \(f_V^{-1}(\mathcal{L})\) is connected.
Set-theoretically, we have \(p\big(f_V^{-1}(\mathcal{L})\big) = f^{-1}(\Delta)\): - First, \(p\big(f_V^{-1}(\mathcal{L})\big) \subseteq f^{-1}(\Delta)\) is clear because \(p(\mathcal{L}) = \Delta\). - Conversely, for any \(x \in f^{-1}(\Delta)\), lift \(f(x)\) to the unique point \(y \in \mathcal{L}\). Then there exists a unique \((x, y) \in V_X\) such that \(f_V(x, y) = y \in \mathcal{L}\) and \(p(x, y) = x\). Thus \((x, y) \in f_V^{-1}(\mathcal{L})\), which gives \(x \in p\big(f_V^{-1}(\mathcal{L})\big)\).
Since \(p\) is continuous, \(f^{-1}(\Delta) = p\big(f_V^{-1}(\mathcal{L})\big)\) is connected.


Example 1 (Intersection of Subvarieties in Projective Space) Let \(X, Y \subseteq \mathbb{P}^r\) be irreducible subvarieties over an algebraically closed field. If \(\dim X + \dim Y > r\), then: \[
X \cap Y
\] is connected.
Proof: Notice that \(X \cap Y\) is the preimage of \(\Delta\) under the inclusion \(X \times Y \hookrightarrow \mathbb{P}^r \times \mathbb{P}^r\). Since \(\dim(X \times Y) = \dim X + \dim Y > r\), the connectedness follows directly from Theorem 3.


Example 2 (Generalization to Multi-Projective Spaces) Let \(f: X \to \prod_{i=1}^k \mathbb{P}^r\) be a morphism from an irreducible projective variety \(X\). If: \[
\dim \overline{f(X)} > (k - 1)r,
\] then \(f^{-1}(\Delta)\) is connected, where \(\Delta \cong \mathbb{P}^r\) is the diagonal (using the embedding \(V \hookrightarrow \mathbb{P}^{kr + k - 1}\)).



Definition 1 (Connectedness in Dimension \(k\)) A Noetherian scheme \(X\) is said to be connected in dimension \(k\) (or \(k\)-connected) if \(\dim X > k\) and for every closed subset \(T \subseteq X\) with \(\dim T < k\), the complement: \[
X \setminus T
\] is connected.


Example 3 (Basic Properties of \(k\)-Connectedness)  

\(X\) is connected if and only if \(X\) is \(0\)-connected (since \(\dim \varnothing = -1\)).
If \(X\) is \(d\)-connected and \(d' \le d\), then \(X\) is \(d'\)-connected.
If \(X\) is irreducible of dimension \(n\), then \(X\) is \((n - 1)\)-connected (in fact, \(X\) is irreducible if and only if \(X\) is “\(\dim X\)-connected”).



Proposition 1 (Characterization via Chains of Irreducible Components) For any \(k < \dim X\), a Noetherian scheme \(X\) is \(k\)-connected if and only if for every pair of irreducible components \(X \neq X'\), there exists a sequence of components: \[
X_0 = X, \; X_1, \; \dots, \; X_p = X' \quad (X_i \neq X_j)
\] such that for all \(1 \le i \le p\): \[
\dim(X_{i-1} \cap X_i) \ge k.
\]


Remark 1 (Restriction on the Dimension of \(T\)). Why do we require \(\dim T < k \le \dim X\), and what happens if \(\dim T = \dim X - 1\)?
If \(X = X_1 \cup \dots \cup X_m\) is the decomposition into irreducible components with \(\dim X_1 \ge \dots \ge \dim X_m\), then: \[
\dim(X_1 \cap X_i) \le \dim X_1 - 1 = \dim X - 1.
\] Since \(\big(X_1 \setminus \bigcup_{i \ge 2} X_i\big) \cap \big(\bigcup_{i \ge 2} X_i \setminus X_1\big) = \varnothing\), removing the closed subset: \[
T := \bigcup_{i \ge 2} (X_1 \cap X_i)
\] of codimension \(\ge 1\) disconnects \(X\). Thus, to have a non-trivial notion of connectedness, one must test against closed subsets \(T\) with \(\dim T \le \dim X - 2\).


Theorem 4 (Grothendieck’s Connectedness Theorem) Let \((A, \mathfrak{m})\) be a complete local Noetherian ring, and let \(k \ge 1\). If \(X = \operatorname{Spec} A\) is \(k\)-connected, then for any \(f \in \mathfrak{m}\), the scheme: \[
\operatorname{Spec}(A / fA)
\] is \((k - 1)\)-connected.


Corollary 2 (Complete Local Noetherian Domains) Let \((A, \mathfrak{m})\) be a complete local Noetherian domain of dimension \(n\). Fix \(d \le n - 1\). For any \(f_1, \dots, f_d \in \mathfrak{m}\), the scheme: \[
\operatorname{Spec}\big(A / (f_1, \dots, f_d)\big)
\] is \((n - d - 1)\)-connected.


Corollary 3 (Stronger Bertini for Connectedness) Let \(X \subseteq \mathbb{P}^r\) be a closed algebraic subset that is \(k\)-connected, and let \(L \subseteq \mathbb{P}^r\) be a linear subspace of codimension \(d\). Then: \[
X \cap L
\] is connected in dimension \(k - d\).
In particular, if \(X\) is irreducible of dimension \(n\), it is \((n - 1)\)-connected. If \(d < n\), then \(k - d = n - 1 - d \ge 0\), so \(X \cap L\) is \(0\)-connected (i.e., connected).


Example 4 (Verification of Set-Theoretic Complete Intersections) Let \(X \subseteq \mathbb{A}^6_{\mathbb{C}}\) be the union of two \(3\)-planes meeting only at the origin: \[
X = V(x_1, x_2, x_3) \cup V(x_4, x_5, x_6) = V\big(\{x_i x_j \mid 1 \le i \le 3, \; 4 \le j \le 6\}\big) \subseteq \mathbb{A}^6, \quad \dim X = 3.
\]
Question: Is \(X\) a set-theoretic local complete intersection (LCI) defined by \(3\) functions at the origin? (Check on stalk/completion).
Analysis: Since \(V(x_1, x_2, x_3) \cap V(x_4, x_5, x_6) = \{0\}\), the scheme \(X\) is \(0\)-connected, but not \(1\)-connected.
For any affine open neighborhood \(U = \operatorname{Spec} A \ni 0\) with \(A\) regular of dimension \(6\), if \(U \cap X = \operatorname{Spec}\big(A / (f_1, f_2, f_3)\big)\), then by Corollary 2: \[
U \cap X \quad \text{would be } (6 - 1 - 3 = 2)\text{-connected},
\] which is a contradiction. The claim is even false for \(4\) functions (which would force \(U \cap X\) to be \(1\)-connected). What about \(5\) functions?
Answer: \(X\) is a set-theoretic complete intersection of \(5\) functions. Consider the polynomials in the indeterminate \(T\): \[
f_1(T) = x_1 + x_2 T + x_3 T^2, \qquad f_2(T) = x_4 + x_5 T + x_6 T^2.
\] Then \(f_1(T) f_2(T) \equiv 0\) if and only if \(f_1 \equiv 0\) or \(f_2 \equiv 0\), which is equivalent to \(x \in X\). Expanding the product: \[
f_1 f_2 = x_1 x_4 + (x_1 x_5 + x_2 x_4) T + (x_1 x_6 + x_2 x_5 + x_3 x_4) T^2 + (x_2 x_6 + x_3 x_5) T^3 + x_3 x_6 T^4.
\] The vanishing of these \(5\) coefficients cuts out \(X\) set-theoretically.



Theorem 5 (Unramified Morphisms into Projective Space) Let \(X\) be a complete irreducible variety of dimension \(n\), and let \(f: X \to \mathbb{P}^r\) be an unramified morphism. If: \[
2n > r,
\] then \(f\) is a closed embedding.


Proof. Fact: A morphism from a complete variety that is injective on closed points and unramified is a closed immersion.
Consider the product morphism \(F = f \times f: X \times X \to \mathbb{P}^r \times \mathbb{P}^r\). Then: \[
F^{-1}(\Delta_{\mathbb{P}^r}) = X \times_{\mathbb{P}^r} X = \big\{ (x, y) \in X \times X \;\big|\; f(x) = f(y) \big\}.
\] The morphism \(f\) is injective on closed points if and only if \(F^{-1}(\Delta_{\mathbb{P}^r}) = \Delta_X\).
Because \(\dim \overline{\operatorname{Im} F} = \dim(X \times X) = 2n > r\), Theorem 3 implies that: \[
X \times_{\mathbb{P}^r} X
\] is connected.
Since \(f: X \to \mathbb{P}^r\) is separated and unramified, the diagonal morphism: \[
\Delta_{X / \mathbb{P}^r}: X \longrightarrow X \times_{\mathbb{P}^r} X
\] is an open and closed immersion (unramified and proper implies finite, hence clopen). Since \(X \times_{\mathbb{P}^r} X\) is connected, the clopen subset \(\Delta_X\) must be the entire space: \[
\Delta_X = X \times_{\mathbb{P}^r} X.
\] Therefore, \(f\) is injective, which implies that \(f\) is a closed embedding.


Remark 2 (Sharpness and Geometric Intuition). The inequality \(2n > r\) is sharp: for \(n = 1\) and \(r = 2\), let \(C \subseteq \mathbb{P}^2\) be a nodal curve and let \(X = \widetilde{C} \cong \mathbb{P}^1\) be its normalization. Then \(X \to C \hookrightarrow \mathbb{P}^2\) is unramified, but not an embedding.
Geometrically, one has to fold something to map \(X\) into \(\mathbb{P}^r\) when \(2n > r\).


Example 5 (Nonexistence of Hypersurfaces with Normal Crossing Singularities) If \(r \ge 3\), there are no irreducible singular hypersurfaces \(X \subseteq \mathbb{P}^r\) having only normal crossing singularities.


Proof. A hypersurface \(X\) has a normal crossing singularity at \(p\) if and only if: - Formally: \(\widehat{\mathcal{O}}_{X, p} \cong k[[x_1, \dots, x_r]] / (x_1 \cdots x_k)\) for some \(k \ge 2\); - Étale-locally: there exists an étale neighborhood \((V, v) \to (X, p)\) and \((V, v) \to (U, 0)\), where \(U = \operatorname{Spec}\big(k[x_1, \dots, x_r]/(x_1 \cdots x_k)\big)\) (by Artin approximation [Alper, Theorem B.5.2]); - Analytically: there exists a neighborhood \(U \ni p\) with \(U \cong V \cap V(z_1 \cdots z_k) \subseteq \mathbb{C}^n\) for \(V \subseteq \mathbb{C}^n\) open (Grothendieck–Riemann extension).
If \(X\) has only normal crossing singularities, then at each singular point \(x\): \[
\widehat{\mathcal{O}}_{X, x} \cong k[[x_1, \dots, x_r]] / (x_1 \cdots x_k).
\] The normalization \(\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}_{X, x}\) satisfies: \[
\widetilde{\widehat{\mathcal{O}}_{X, x}} \cong \prod_{i=1}^k k[[x_1, \dots, x_r]] / (x_i).
\] Checking the tangent space: \[
T_x X^\vee = T(\mathcal{O}_{X, x})^\vee = T(\widehat{\mathcal{O}}_{X, x})^\vee = (x_1, \dots, x_r) / \big((x_1 \cdots x_k) + (x_i x_j)\big).
\] For \(r \ge 2\), this equals \((x_1, \dots, x_r) / (x_i x_j) = \big\{ \sum_{i=1}^r a_i x_i \mid a_i \in k \big\}\).
Because normalization commutes with localization, we have the Cartesian diagram: \[
\begin{CD}
\prod_{i=1}^k \mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{X}, y_i} @>>> \widetilde{X} \\
@VVV @VV{\nu}V \\
\mathcal{O}_{X, x} @>>> X
\end{CD}
\] Analytically, \(\widehat{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{X}, y_i} \cong k[[x_1, \dots, x_{r-1}]]\), which has cotangent space \(k^{r-1}\). The differential map on cotangent spaces: \[
T_x X^\vee \twoheadrightarrow T_{y_i} \widetilde{X}^\vee, \quad \sum_{j=1}^r a_j x_j \longmapsto (a_1, \dots, \hat{a}_i, \dots, a_r)
\] is surjective. Hence the normalization map \(\widetilde{X} \to X\) is unramified, and \(\widetilde{X}\) is regular of dimension \(r - 1\).
Now consider the composition: \[
\widetilde{X} \xrightarrow{\;\nu\;} X \longhookrightarrow \mathbb{P}^r.
\] Then \(\widetilde{X} \to \mathbb{P}^r\) is an unramified morphism from a complete variety of dimension \(\dim \widetilde{X} = r - 1\). Since \(r \ge 3\): \[
2(r - 1) = 2r - 2 > r.
\] By Theorem 5, \(\widetilde{X} \hookrightarrow \mathbb{P}^r\) must be a closed embedding. But this implies that \(X \cong \widetilde{X}\) is smooth, contradicting the assumption that \(X\) is singular.


Example 6 (Étale Fundamental Group of Large Subvarieties) Let \(X \subseteq \mathbb{P}^r\) be an irreducible subvariety of dimension \(n\). If: \[
2n > r,
\] then the étale fundamental group of \(X\) is trivial: \[
\pi_1^{\text{ét}}(X) = \{e\}.
\]


Proof. Suppose \(p: Y \to X\) is a connected finite étale cover. Let \(Y' \subseteq Y\) be an irreducible component of \(Y\). The composite morphism: \[
Y' \longhookrightarrow Y \xrightarrow{\;p\;} X \longhookrightarrow \mathbb{P}^r
\] is unramified. Since \(\dim Y' = n\) and \(2n > r\), Theorem 5 implies that \(Y' \hookrightarrow \mathbb{P}^r\) is a closed embedding.
Therefore, \(p|_{Y'}: Y' \xrightarrow{\sim} X\) is an isomorphism. Because \(Y\) is connected and étale over \(X\), it follows that \(Y = Y' \cong X\), so \(X\) admits no nontrivial connected finite étale covers. Hence \(\pi_1^{\text{ét}}(X) = \{e\}\).

title: 22.4 Big Line Bundles
text:
Proposition 1 (Asymptotic Bounds for \(h^0(X, L^{\otimes m})\)) Let \(X\) be an irreducible normal projective variety over a field \(k\) of characteristic zero, and let \(L\) be a line bundle on \(X\) with Iitaka dimension \(\kappa = \kappa(X, L) \ge 1\). Then there exist positive constants \(a, A > 0\) such that: \[
a \cdot m^\kappa \le h^0(X, L^{\otimes m}) \le A \cdot m^\kappa
\] for all \(m \in N(X, L)\) sufficiently large.


Proof. Replacing \(L\) by \(L^{\otimes e(L)}\), we may assume without loss of generality that the exponent \(e(L) = 1\). Passing to the Iitaka fibration model \(X_\infty \to Y\), we may assume \(X = X_\infty\) and \(L = L_\infty\). By Hironaka’s resolution of singularities, there exists a projective birational morphism \(f: \widetilde{X} \to X\) with \(\widetilde{X}\) smooth. Because \(f\) is projective, birational, and surjective between normal varieties, \(f\) is an algebraic fiber space (?@prp-afs-function-fields). Hence \(h^0(X, L^{\otimes m}) = h^0(\widetilde{X}, f^* L^{\otimes m})\). Thus, we may assume \(X\) is smooth.
Lower Bound: By the construction of the Iitaka fibration (?@cor-iitaka-fibers), there exists an ample line bundle \(B\) on \(Y\) and an integer \(m_0 \gg 0\) such that \(L^{\otimes m_0} \otimes \phi^* B^\vee\) has a non-zero global section. For any \(\ell \ge 1\), multiplication by this section yields: \[
H^0(Y, B^{\otimes \ell}) \cong H^0(X, \phi^* B^{\otimes \ell}) \hookrightarrow H^0(X, L^{\otimes \ell m_0}).
\] By Asymptotic Riemann-Roch I (?@thm-asymptotic-rr-1) on \(Y\) (where \(\dim Y = \kappa\)), \[
h^0(X, L^{\otimes \ell m_0}) \ge h^0(Y, B^{\otimes \ell}) = \frac{(B^\kappa)}{\kappa!} \ell^\kappa + O(\ell^{\kappa-1}) \ge a' \cdot \ell^\kappa
\] for some \(a' > 0\) and all \(\ell \gg 0\). Choose a system of representatives \(k_1, \dots, k_{m_0} \in N(X, L)\) for the congruence classes modulo \(m_0\). For any \(m \in N(X, L)\) with \(m \gg 0\), write \(m = \ell m_0 + k_i\). Then: \[
h^0(X, L^{\otimes m}) \ge h^0(X, L^{\otimes \ell m_0}) \ge a' \left(\frac{m - k_i}{m_0}\right)^\kappa \ge a \cdot m^\kappa.
\]
Upper Bound: Fix \(u \in N(X, L)\) and choose an effective divisor \(D \in |L^{\otimes u}|\). Since \(X\) is smooth, \(\operatorname{CaCl}(X) = \operatorname{WDiv}(X)\). Write \(D = \sum a_i W_i\) and decompose \(D = D_v + D_h\) into vertical and horizontal components: \[
D_v := \sum_{\phi(W_i) \subsetneq Y} a_i W_i, \qquad D_h := \sum_{\phi(W_i) = Y} a_i W_i.
\]
Claim: \(H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(m D_v)) = H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(m D))\) for all \(m \ge 0\). Suppose toward a contradiction that there exists a sequence \(m_n \to \infty\) with sections \(s_n \in H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(m_n D)) \setminus H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(m_n D_v))\). Then \(C_n := \operatorname{div}(s_n) + m_n D \ge 0\), but \(C_n - m_n D_h \not\ge 0\). For a very general point \(y \in Y\), the fiber \(F = X_y\) is smooth, \(\dim F = \dim X - \kappa\), and \(F \cap \operatorname{Supp}(D_v) = \emptyset\). Thus \(L^{\otimes m u}|_F \cong \mathcal{O}_F(m D_h|_F)\). Restriction gives non-trivial sections \(s_n|_F \in H^0(F, \mathcal{O}_F(m_n D_h|_F))\) that are not constant multiples of the canonical section. This implies \(h^0(F, L^{\otimes m_n u}|_F) \ge 2\), contradicting ?@cor-iitaka-fibers (\(\kappa(F, L|_F) = 0\)).
Using the Claim, write \(D_v = \sum a_i E_i\) with \(\phi(E_i) \subsetneq Y\). Choose an ample effective divisor \(H\) on \(Y\) and \(b \gg 0\) such that \(B := b H\) satisfies \(\operatorname{Supp}(B) \supseteq \bigcup \phi(E_i)\). Then \(\phi^* B \ge D_v\) after scaling. Thus: \[
h^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(m D)) = h^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(m D_v)) \le h^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(m r \phi^* B)) = h^0(Y, \mathcal{O}_Y(m r B)) \le A' \cdot m^\kappa.
\] For general \(m \gg 0\), write \(m = u r - q\) with \(q \in N(X, L)\), which yields \(h^0(X, L^{\otimes m}) \le h^0(X, L^{\otimes u r}) \le A \cdot m^\kappa\).


Lemma 1 (Bigness by Growth of \(h^0\)) Let \(X\) be a projective variety of dimension \(n\). A Cartier divisor \(D\) on \(X\) is big if and only if there exists a constant \(C > 0\) such that: \[
h^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) \ge C \cdot m^n \quad \text{for all } m \in N(X, D), \; m \gg 0.
\]


Proof. If \(X\) is normal, this is immediate from Proposition 1 by setting \(\kappa(X, D) = n\). In general, let \(\nu: X^\nu \to X\) be the normalization and \(D^\nu = \nu^* D\). The exact sequence \(0 \to \mathcal{O}_X \to \nu_* \mathcal{O}_{X^\nu} \to \mathcal{C} \to 0\) has \(\dim \operatorname{Supp}(\mathcal{C}) \le n - 1\). Tensoring with \(\mathcal{O}_X(mD)\) yields: \[
h^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) \le h^0(X^\nu, \mathcal{O}_{X^\nu}(m D^\nu)) \le h^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) + O(m^{n-1}).
\] Hence the maximal growth rate \(m^n\) on \(X^\nu\) is equivalent to that on \(X\).


Proposition 2 (Kodaira’s Lemma) Let \(X\) be an irreducible projective variety of dimension \(n\). Let \(D\) be a big Cartier divisor and \(F\) an arbitrary effective Cartier divisor on \(X\). Then: \[
H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD - F)) \neq 0 \quad \text{for all } m \in N(X, D) \text{ with } m \gg 0.
\]


Proof. Consider the standard restriction sequence: \[
0 \longrightarrow \mathcal{O}_X(mD - F) \longrightarrow \mathcal{O}_X(mD) \longrightarrow \mathcal{O}_F(mD) \longrightarrow 0.
\] By Lemma 1, \(h^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) \ge C \cdot m^n\) for some \(C > 0\). Because \(\dim F = n - 1\), the growth of global sections on \(F\) is bounded by: \[
h^0(F, \mathcal{O}_F(mD)) \le C' \cdot m^{n-1}.
\] For \(m \gg 0\), \(C m^n > C' m^{n-1}\), forcing the restriction map to have a non-trivial kernel. Thus \(H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD - F)) \neq 0\).


Corollary 1 (Characterization of Bigness) Let \(D\) be a Cartier divisor on an irreducible projective variety \(X\). The following conditions are equivalent:

\(D\) is big;
For every ample Cartier divisor \(A\) on \(X\), there exists an integer \(m > 0\) and an effective divisor \(N\) such that \(m D \sim A + N\);
There exists an ample Cartier divisor \(A\), an integer \(m > 0\), and an effective divisor \(N\) such that \(m D \sim A + N\);
There exists an ample \(\mathbb{R}\)-divisor \(A\), an integer \(m > 0\), and an effective \(\mathbb{R}\)-divisor \(N\) such that \(m D \equiv_{\mathrm{num}} A + N\).



Proof. 

\((1) \implies (2)\): Fix \(r \gg 0\) such that \(r A \sim H_r\) and \((r+1)A \sim H_{r+1}\) are effective. By Kodaira’s Lemma (Proposition 2), \(H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD - H_{r+1})) \neq 0\) for \(m \gg 0\). Hence \(m D \sim H_{r+1} + N' \sim A + (H_r + N')\). Setting \(N = H_r + N'\) gives the result.
\((2) \implies (3) \implies (4)\): Trivial.
\((4) \implies (1)\): If \(m D \equiv_{\mathrm{num}} A + N\), then \(m D - N\) is ample. For \(k \gg 0\), \(k(m D - N)\) is very ample. Since \(k N \ge 0\), we have \(\kappa(X, D) = \kappa(X, k m D) \ge \kappa(X, k(m D - N)) = \dim X\), so \(D\) is big.



Corollary 2 (Numerical Nature and Exponent of Big Divisors)  

Bigness is a numerical property: if \(D_1 \equiv_{\mathrm{num}} D_2\), then \(D_1\) is big if and only if \(D_2\) is big.
If \(D\) is big, its exponent is \(e(D) = 1\).



Proposition 3 (Twisting Theorem for Bigness) A Cartier divisor \(D\) on an irreducible projective variety \(X\) is big if and only if for every coherent sheaf \(\mathcal{F} \in \operatorname{Coh}(X)\), there exists an integer \(m_0 = m(\mathcal{F})\) such that for all \(m \ge m_0\): \[
H^0(X, \mathcal{F} \otimes_{\mathcal{O}_X} \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) \otimes_k \mathcal{O}_X \longrightarrow \mathcal{F} \otimes_{\mathcal{O}_X} \mathcal{O}_X(mD)
\] is generically surjective.


Proof. \((\implies)\): Fix an ample divisor \(H\). By Serre generation, \(\mathcal{F}(m H)\) is globally generated for all \(m \ge m_0\). By Corollary 1, there exists \(n > 0\) such that \(n D \sim H + N\) with \(N \ge 0\). The canonical injection \(\mathcal{F}(m H) \hookrightarrow \mathcal{F}(m n D)\) induces a commutative evaluation diagram. Since \(\mathcal{O}_X(m n D) \to \mathcal{O}_X(m H)\) is an isomorphism away from \(\operatorname{Supp}(N)\), generic surjectivity follows.
\((\impliedby)\): Taking \(\mathcal{F} = \mathcal{O}_X(-H)\) for an ample divisor \(H\), generic surjectivity implies \(H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD - H)) \neq 0\) for \(m \gg 0\). Hence \(m D \sim H + N\) for some \(N \ge 0\), which implies \(D\) is big.


Proposition 4 (Restriction of Big Divisors to Subvarieties) Let \(L\) be a big line bundle on an irreducible projective variety \(X\). There exists a proper closed algebraic subset \(V \subsetneq X\) such that for every irreducible subvariety \(Y \not\subseteq V\), the restriction \(L|_Y\) is big on \(Y\). In particular, if \(H\) is a general hyperplane section, \(L|_H\) is big.


Proof. Write \(L \cong \mathcal{O}_X(D)\). By Corollary 1, \(m D \sim H + N\) with \(H\) very ample and \(N \ge 0\). Set \(V = \operatorname{Supp}(N)\). If \(Y \not\subseteq V\), then by Bertini’s Theorem we may choose \(H' \sim H\) such that \(Y \not\subseteq \operatorname{Supp}(H')\). The restriction gives \(m D|_Y \sim H|_Y + N|_Y\). Because \(H|_Y\) is ample and \(N|_Y \ge 0\), \(L|_Y\) is big by Corollary 1(3).



Definition 1 (Big \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Divisors)  

An integral divisor \(D\) is big if and only if \(m D\) is big for some \(m \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}\).
A \(\mathbb{Q}\)-divisor \(D \in \operatorname{Div}_{\mathbb{Q}}(X)\) is big if \(m D\) is an integral big Cartier divisor for some \(m \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}\).
Bigness is an open numerical condition on \(N^1(X)_{\mathbb{Q}}\).



Theorem 1 (Numerical Criterion for Bigness) Let \(X\) be an irreducible projective variety of dimension \(n\). Let \(D, E\) be nef \(\mathbb{Q}\)-divisors on \(X\). If: \[
(D^n) > n (D^{n-1} \cdot E),
\] then the difference \(D - E\) is big.


Proposition 5 (Bigness of Nef Divisors) Let \(D\) be a nef \(\mathbb{Q}\)-divisor on an irreducible projective variety \(X\) of dimension \(n\). Then: \[
D \text{ is big} \iff (D^n) > 0.
\]


Proof. If \(D\) is big, \(h^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) \sim \Theta(m^n)\). By Asymptotic Riemann-Roch III (?@prp-asymptotic-rr-3), \((D^n) = n! \lim_{m \to \infty} \frac{h^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD))}{m^n} > 0\). The converse follows from Theorem 1 by setting \(E = 0\).


Definition 2 (\(\mathbb{Q}\)-Effective and Big \(\mathbb{R}\)-Divisors)  

A \(\mathbb{Q}\)-divisor \(D\) is effective if \(m D\) is effective for some \(m \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}\).
A \(\mathbb{Q}\)-divisor \(D\) is big if and only if \(D \equiv_{\mathrm{num}} A + N\) for an ample \(\mathbb{Q}\)-divisor \(A\) and an effective \(\mathbb{Q}\)-divisor \(N\).
An \(\mathbb{R}\)-divisor \(D\) is effective if \(D = \sum a_i D_i\) with \(a_i \ge 0\) and \(D_i\) effective Cartier divisors.



Definition 3 (Big \(\mathbb{R}\)-Divisors) An \(\mathbb{R}\)-divisor \(D \in \operatorname{Div}_{\mathbb{R}}(X)\) is big if \(D = \sum a_i D_i\) where each \(D_i\) is an integral big Cartier divisor and \(a_i \in \mathbb{R}_{>0}\).


Proposition 6 (Properties of Big \(\mathbb{R}\)-Divisors) Let \(D, D' \in \operatorname{Div}_{\mathbb{R}}(X)\).

Numerical invariance: \(D \equiv_{\mathrm{num}} D' \implies (D \text{ big} \iff D' \text{ big})\).
Kodaira decomposition: \(D\) is big if and only if \(D \equiv_{\mathrm{num}} A + N\) for an ample \(\mathbb{R}\)-divisor \(A\) and an effective \(\mathbb{R}\)-divisor \(N\).
Openness: If \(D\) is big and \(E_1, \dots, E_r \in \operatorname{Div}_{\mathbb{R}}(X)\), then \(D + \sum_{i=1}^r \varepsilon_i E_i\) is big for all \(\sum |\varepsilon_i| \ll 1\).



Definition 4 (The Big Cone and Pseudoeffective Cone)  

The big cone \(\operatorname{Big}(X) \subseteq N^1(X)_{\mathbb{R}}\) is the convex cone of all big \(\mathbb{R}\)-divisor classes.
The effective cone \(\operatorname{Eff}(X) \subseteq N^1(X)_{\mathbb{R}}\) is the convex cone spanned by effective classes. Its closure: \[
\overline{\operatorname{Eff}}(X) = \operatorname{Pseff}(X)
\] is called the pseudoeffective cone.



Theorem 2 (The Interior of the Pseudoeffective Cone) Let \(X\) be an irreducible projective variety. Then: \[
\operatorname{Big}(X) = \operatorname{int}\big(\operatorname{Eff}(X)\big) = \operatorname{int}\big(\overline{\operatorname{Eff}}(X)\big), \qquad \overline{\operatorname{Big}(X)} = \overline{\operatorname{Eff}}(X).
\]


Proof. By Proposition 6, every big class has the form \([D] = [A] + [E]\) with \([A]\) ample and \([E]\) effective. Because the ample cone is open, \(\operatorname{Big}(X)\) is open, so \(\operatorname{Big}(X) \subseteq \operatorname{int}(\operatorname{Eff}(X)) \subseteq \operatorname{int}(\overline{\operatorname{Eff}}(X))\).
Conversely, let \(\eta \in \overline{\operatorname{Eff}}(X)\). There exists a sequence of effective classes \(\eta_k \in \operatorname{Eff}(X)\) converging to \(\eta\). Fixing an ample class \(\alpha \in \operatorname{Amp}(X)\), the perturbed classes \(\eta_k + \frac{1}{k} \alpha\) are big for all \(k \ge 1\). Since \(\lim_{k \to \infty} (\eta_k + \frac{1}{k} \alpha) = \eta\), we see that \(\eta \in \overline{\operatorname{Big}(X)}\). Hence \(\overline{\operatorname{Big}(X)} = \overline{\operatorname{Eff}}(X)\), and taking interiors yields \(\operatorname{Big}(X) = \operatorname{int}(\overline{\operatorname{Eff}}(X))\).


Corollary 3 (Inclusions of Cones)  

The following inclusions hold: \[
\operatorname{Amp}(X) \subseteq \operatorname{Big}(X) \subseteq \operatorname{Eff}(X) \subseteq \overline{\operatorname{Eff}}(X), \qquad \operatorname{Nef}(X) \subseteq \overline{\operatorname{Eff}}(X).
\]
Let \(\operatorname{SA}(X) := \{ \sum a_i [D_i] \mid D_i \text{ semiample}, a_i \ge 0 \}\) be the semiample cone. Then: \[
\operatorname{Amp}(X) \subseteq \operatorname{SA}(X) \subseteq \operatorname{Nef}(X).
\]



Theorem 3 (Nakai-Moishezon Criterion for \(\mathbb{R}\)-Divisors) Let \(X\) be a projective scheme. An \(\mathbb{R}\)-divisor class \(\delta \in N^1(X)_{\mathbb{R}}\) is ample if and only if for every irreducible subvariety \(V \subseteq X\) with \(\dim V \ge 1\): \[
(\delta^{\dim V} \cdot V) > 0.
\]


Proof. We reduce to the case where \(X\) is an irreducible and reduced variety of dimension \(n\). If \(n = 1\), the condition \((\delta \cdot X) > 0\) implies amplitude immediately. We proceed by induction on \(n\):
Assume the criterion holds in dimensions \(< n\). For every proper subvariety \(Y \subsetneq X\), \(\delta|_Y\) is ample, hence \(\delta\) is nef. Choose small ample classes \(\alpha, \alpha' \in N^1(X)_{\mathbb{R}}\) such that \(\delta + \alpha'\) is ample and \(\delta - \alpha\) is rational. For \(\alpha, \alpha'\) sufficiently small, continuity of intersection products ensures: \[
((\delta + \alpha')^n) > n \big((\delta + \alpha')^{n-1} \cdot (\alpha + \alpha')\big).
\] By Theorem 1, the rational class \((\delta + \alpha') - (\alpha + \alpha') = \delta - \alpha\) is big.
Write \(\delta - \alpha \equiv_{\mathrm{num}} E\) for an effective \(\mathbb{Q}\)-divisor \(E = \sum q_i Y_i\). For \(0 < \varepsilon \ll 1\), the restriction \((\delta - \varepsilon \alpha)|_{Y_i}\) is nef by induction. For any curve \(C \subseteq X\): - If \(C \subseteq Y_i\), then \(((\delta - \varepsilon \alpha) \cdot C) \ge 0\); - If \(C \not\subseteq \operatorname{Supp}(E)\), then \((E \cdot C) \ge 0\), which implies \(((\delta - \varepsilon \alpha) \cdot C) \ge 0\).
Thus \(\delta - \varepsilon \alpha\) is nef. Finally, decomposing: \[
\delta = (\delta - \varepsilon \alpha) + \varepsilon \alpha
\] as the sum of a nef class and an ample class, Kleiman’s perturbation theorem (?@cor-kleiman-perturbation) guarantees that \(\delta\) is ample.

title: 22.5 Volume
text:
Theorem 1 (Big Input: Fujita’s Vanishing Theorem) Let \(X\) be a projective scheme and \(H\) an ample Cartier divisor on \(X\). For every coherent sheaf \(\mathcal{F} \in \operatorname{Coh}(X)\), there exists an integer \(m(\mathcal{F}, H) > 0\) such that for all \(i > 0\), all \(m \ge m(\mathcal{F}, H)\), and every nef Cartier divisor \(D\): \[
H^i\big(X, \mathcal{F} \otimes_{\mathcal{O}_X} \mathcal{O}_X(m H + D)\big) = 0.
\]


Definition 1 (Volume of a Line Bundle) Let \(X\) be an irreducible projective variety of dimension \(n\), and let \(L \in \operatorname{Pic}(X)\). The volume of \(L\) is defined by: \[
\operatorname{vol}(L) = \operatorname{vol}_X(L) := \limsup_{m \to \infty} \frac{h^0(X, L^{\otimes m})}{m^n / n!}.
\] - \(\operatorname{vol}(L) = 0 \iff L\) is not big. - \(\operatorname{vol}(L) > 0 \iff L\) is big. - If \(L\) is nef, then by Asymptotic Riemann-Roch III (?@prp-asymptotic-rr-3), \(\operatorname{vol}(L) = (L^n)\).


Proposition 1 (Volume Lower Bound for Differences of Nef Divisors) Let \(X\) be an irreducible projective variety of dimension \(n\). If \(D, E\) are nef Cartier divisors on \(X\), then: \[
\operatorname{vol}(D - E) \ge (D^n) - n (D^{n-1} \cdot E).
\]


Proposition 2 (Extension of Volume to \(\mathbb{Q}\)-Divisors)  

Homogeneity: For any Cartier divisor \(D\) and any integer \(a \ge 0\), \[
\operatorname{vol}(a D) = a^n \operatorname{vol}(D).
\]
The volume function extends well-definedly to \(\mathbb{Q}\)-divisors: for \(D \in \operatorname{Div}_{\mathbb{Q}}(X)\) with \(a D \in \operatorname{Div}(X)\) (\(a \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}\)), \[
\operatorname{vol}(D) := \frac{1}{a^n} \operatorname{vol}(a D).
\]
Ray continuity: For any divisor \(N\) and any \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists \(p_0 \ge 1\) such that for all \(p \ge p_0\): \[
\left| \operatorname{vol}\left(D \pm \frac{1}{p} N\right) - \operatorname{vol}(D) \right| < \varepsilon.
\]



Proposition 3 (Numerical Invariance of Volume) If \(D \equiv_{\mathrm{num}} D'\) in \(\operatorname{Div}_{\mathbb{Q}}(X)\), then \(\operatorname{vol}(D) = \operatorname{vol}(D')\). Hence the volume descends to a well-defined function on the rational Néron-Severi space: \[
\operatorname{vol}: N^1(X)_{\mathbb{Q}} \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}.
\]


Proof. Lemma: There exists a fixed Cartier divisor \(N\) such that \(H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(N + P)) \neq 0\) for every nef divisor \(P\). Proof of Lemma: Fix a very ample divisor \(B\). By Fujita’s Vanishing Theorem (Theorem 1), there exists \(m \gg 0\) such that \(H^i(X, \mathcal{O}_X(m B + A)) = 0\) for all \(i > 0\) and any nef divisor \(A\). Setting \(A = P + (n - i) B\) for \(0 \le i \le n\), the sheaf \(\mathcal{O}_X((m+n)B + P)\) is 0-regular with respect to \(B\), hence globally generated. Choosing \(N = (m+n)B\) yields \(H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(N + P)) \neq 0\).
Now, if \(D\) is not big, then \(D'\) is not big, so \(\operatorname{vol}(D) = \operatorname{vol}(D') = 0\). Assume \(D\) is big. It suffices to show \(\operatorname{vol}(D) = \operatorname{vol}(D + P)\) for any \(P \equiv_{\mathrm{num}} 0\). Because \(-P\) is nef, the Lemma provides a fixed divisor \(N\) with \(H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(N - p P)) \neq 0\). Hence: \[
\mathcal{O}_X\big(m(p(D + P) - N)\big) \hookrightarrow \mathcal{O}_X(m p D) \implies \operatorname{vol}(p(D + P) - N) \le \operatorname{vol}(p D).
\] Dividing by \(p^n\) gives \(\operatorname{vol}(D + P - \frac{1}{p} N) \le \operatorname{vol}(D)\). Taking \(p \to \infty\), ray continuity yields \(\operatorname{vol}(D + P) \le \operatorname{vol}(D)\). By symmetry, \(\operatorname{vol}(D) = \operatorname{vol}(D + P)\).


Theorem 2 (Local Lipschitz Continuity and Extension to \(N^1(X)_{\mathbb{R}}\)) Let \(X\) be an irreducible projective variety of dimension \(n\). Fix any norm \(\|\cdot\|\) on the finite-dimensional real vector space \(N^1(X)_{\mathbb{R}}\).

There exists a constant \(C > 0\) such that for all \(\xi, \xi' \in N^1(X)_{\mathbb{Q}}\): \[
|\operatorname{vol}(\xi) - \operatorname{vol}(\xi')| \le C \cdot \big(\max\{\|\xi\|, \|\xi'\|\}\big)^{n-1} \|\xi - \xi'\|.
\]
Consequently, \(\operatorname{vol}\) is locally Lipschitz continuous on \(N^1(X)_{\mathbb{Q}}\), and extends uniquely to a continuous function: \[
\operatorname{vol}: N^1(X)_{\mathbb{R}} \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0},
\] satisfying the same Lipschitz bound for all \(\xi, \xi' \in N^1(X)_{\mathbb{R}}\).
For any nef classes \(\xi, \eta \in \operatorname{Nef}(X)\), \[
\operatorname{vol}(\xi - \eta) \ge (\xi^n) - n (\xi^{n-1} \cdot \eta).
\]
Monotonicity: If \(\xi \in N^1(X)_{\mathbb{R}}\) and \(e \in \overline{\operatorname{Eff}}(X)\), then \(\operatorname{vol}(\xi + e) \ge \operatorname{vol}(\xi)\).



Proposition 4 (Functorial Properties of Cones) Let \(f: X \to Y\) be a morphism of projective varieties.

The pullback preserves numerical triviality: if \(\alpha \equiv_{\mathrm{num}} 0\), then \((f^* \alpha \cdot C) = (\alpha \cdot f_* C) = 0\). Thus \(f\) induces a continuous linear map \(f^*: N^1(Y)_{\mathbb{R}} \to N^1(X)_{\mathbb{R}}\).
Preservation of cones:

\(f^*(\operatorname{Nef}(Y)) \subseteq \operatorname{Nef}(X)\);
\(f^*(\operatorname{SA}(Y)) \subseteq \operatorname{SA}(X)\);
\(f^*(\operatorname{Amp}(Y)) \subseteq \operatorname{Amp}(X)\) if \(f\) is finite;
\(f^*(\operatorname{Eff}(Y)) \subseteq \operatorname{Eff}(X)\) and \(f^*(\overline{\operatorname{Eff}}(Y)) \subseteq \overline{\operatorname{Eff}}(X)\) if \(f\) is surjective.




Theorem 3 (Birational Invariance of Volume) Let \(\nu: X' \to X\) be a projective birational morphism between irreducible varieties of dimension \(n\).

For every Cartier divisor \(D \in \operatorname{Div}(X)\) and \(D' = \nu^* D\): \[
\operatorname{vol}_{X'}(D') = \operatorname{vol}_X(D), \qquad D' \text{ is big} \iff D \text{ is big}.
\]
For every real class \(\xi \in N^1(X)_{\mathbb{R}}\) and \(\xi' = \nu^* \xi\): \[
\operatorname{vol}_{X'}(\xi') = \operatorname{vol}_X(\xi), \qquad \xi' \text{ is big} \iff \xi \text{ is big}.
\]




Example 1 (Non-Finitely Generated Section Ring (Zariski’s Construction)) Let \(C_0 \subseteq \mathbb{P}^2\) be a smooth plane cubic curve, and let \(\ell\) be the hyperplane class on \(\mathbb{P}^2\). Choose 12 distinct points \(P_1, \dots, P_{12} \in C_0\) such that: \[
\eta := \mathcal{O}_{C_0}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{12} P_i - 4\ell\right) \in \operatorname{Pic}^0(C_0)
\] is a non-torsion element (which is possible because the torsion group \(\operatorname{Tor}(\operatorname{Pic}^0(C_0))\) is countable while \(C_0\) is uncountable).
Let \(\mu: X = \operatorname{Bl}_{P_1, \dots, P_{12}}(\mathbb{P}^2) \to \mathbb{P}^2\) be the blow-up, with exceptional divisors \(E_i\) and \(E = \sum_{i=1}^{12} E_i\). Let \(H = \mu^* \ell\), and let \(C = 3H - E\) be the strict transform of \(C_0\). Consider the divisor: \[
D := 4H - E \sim C + H.
\] Then:

\(D\) is nef and big, because \(D \cdot H = 4 > 0\), \(D \cdot E_i = 1 > 0\), and \((D^2) = 16 - 12 = 4 > 0\).
\(\mathcal{O}_C(mD) \cong \eta^{-m}\). Because \(\eta\) is non-torsion, \(h^0(C, \mathcal{O}_C(mD)) = 0\) for all \(m \ge 1\). Hence the restriction map \(H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) \to H^0(C, \mathcal{O}_C(mD))\) is zero, so \(C \subseteq \operatorname{Bs}(|mD|)\) for all \(m \ge 1\).
By Kawamata-Viehweg vanishing, \(H^1(X, \mathcal{O}_X((m-1)D + H - C)) = 0\), so \(|mD - C|\) is base-point-free. Thus, there exist sections \(s_m \in H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD))\) with vanishing order \(\operatorname{ord}_C(s_m) = 1\) along \(C\) for all \(m \ge 1\).
If the section ring \(R(X, D) = \bigoplus_{m=0}^\infty H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD))\) were finitely generated by elements of degree \(\le d\), the vanishing orders along \(C\) for large \(m\) would be forced to grow linearly, contradicting the existence of sections with order 1 for all \(m\).

Thus, \(R(X, D)\) is not finitely generated as a \(k\)-algebra.


Lemma 1 (Cohomology and Bigness on \(\mathbb{P}(\bigoplus \mathcal{O}_V(A_i))\)) Let \(V\) be an irreducible projective variety of dimension \(v\), and let \(A_0, \dots, A_r\) be Cartier divisors on \(V\). Set \(\mathcal{E} := \bigoplus_{i=0}^r \mathcal{O}_V(A_i)\) and \(X := \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E})\) with projection \(p: X \to V\).

For every \(k \ge 0\): \[
H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(k)) \cong \bigoplus_{\sum a_i = k, \, a_i \ge 0} H^0\left(V, \mathcal{O}_V\left(\sum_{i=0}^r a_i A_i\right)\right).
\]
The tautological line bundle \(\mathcal{O}_X(1)\) is big if and only if: \[
\left( \sum_{i=0}^r \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0} A_i \right) \cap \operatorname{Big}(V) \neq \emptyset.
\]



Example 2 (Another Non-Finitely Generated Ring on a Projective Bundle) Let \(V\) be a smooth projective curve of genus \(g \ge 1\). Choose a non-torsion degree 0 bundle \(P \in \operatorname{Pic}^0(V)\) and an ample divisor \(A\) with \(\deg A \gg 0\). Set \(X = \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{O}_V(P) \oplus \mathcal{O}_V(A))\).
By Lemma 1, \(R(X, \mathcal{O}_X(1)) = \bigoplus_{i+j=k} H^0(V, \mathcal{O}_V(i P + j A))\). The subspace \(R_{k-1, 1} = H^0(V, \mathcal{O}_V((k-1)P + A))\) is non-zero for all \(k \ge 1\) by Riemann-Roch. However, for any \(2 \le p \le k\), \[
R_{k-p, 1} \otimes R_{p-1, 0} = 0
\] because \(R_{p-1, 0} = H^0(V, \mathcal{O}_V((p-1)P)) = 0\). Hence the elements in \(R_{k-1, 1}\) cannot be generated by elements of lower degrees. Therefore, \(R(X, \mathcal{O}_X(1))\) is not finitely generated.


Remark 1 (Stable Base Locus of the Projective Bundle). In Example 2, the projection \(\mathcal{E} \twoheadrightarrow \mathcal{O}_V(P)\) determines a section \(\sigma: V \hookrightarrow X\) such that \(\mathcal{O}_X(1)|_{\sigma(V)} \cong \mathcal{O}_V(P)\). Since \(H^0(V, \mathcal{O}_V(k P)) = 0\) for all \(k \ge 1\), we have \(\sigma(V) \subseteq \operatorname{Bs}(|\mathcal{O}_X(k)|)\) for every \(k\).


Example 3 (Integral Divisors with Arbitrarily Small Volume) Let \(V\) be an elliptic curve and \(x \in V\). For \(a \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}\), set \(A_0 = (1-a)x\) and \(A_1 = x\). Let \(X = \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{O}_V(A_0) \oplus \mathcal{O}_V(A_1))\). Then \(\dim X = 2\), and: \[
h^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(k)) = \sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor k/a \rfloor} h^0\big(V, \mathcal{O}_V((k - j a)x)\big) = \frac{k^2}{2a} + O(k).
\] Therefore: \[
\operatorname{vol}_X(\mathcal{O}_X(1)) = \lim_{k \to \infty} \frac{h^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(k))}{k^2 / 2!} = \frac{1}{a}.
\] As \(a \to \infty\), the volume of the integral divisor \(\mathcal{O}_X(1)\) becomes arbitrarily small.


Example 4 (A Divisor with Irrational Volume (Cutkosky)) Let \(V = E \times E\) be the product of an elliptic curve with itself. Then \(N^1(V)_{\mathbb{R}} \cong \mathbb{R}^3\), and the nef cone \(\operatorname{Nef}(V)\) is the round circular cone \(\{ \alpha \mid (\alpha^2) \ge 0, (\alpha \cdot H) \ge 0 \}\).
Let \(F_1, F_2\) be the two fibers and \(\Delta \subseteq E \times E\) the diagonal. Then \((F_1^2) = (F_2^2) = (\Delta^2) = 0\) and \((F_1 \cdot F_2) = (F_1 \cdot \Delta) = (F_2 \cdot \Delta) = 1\). Consider the ample divisors: \[
D := F_1 + F_2, \qquad H := 3(F_2 + \Delta).
\] The intersection polynomial is \(((\delta - t h)^2) = 2(9 t^2 - 9 t + 1)\). Its smallest positive root: \[
\sigma = \frac{3 - \sqrt{5}}{6} \notin \mathbb{Q}
\] marks the boundary of the nef cone along the ray \(D - t H\).
Let \(X = \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{O}_V(D) \oplus \mathcal{O}_V(-H))\) over \(V\), so \(\dim X = 3\). Then: \[
h^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(k)) = \sum_{i+j=k, \, j \le \sigma i} h^0(V, \mathcal{O}_V(i D - j H)).
\] By Kodaira vanishing and Riemann-Roch on \(V\), \(h^0(V, \mathcal{O}_V(i D - j H)) = \frac{1}{2} (i D - j H)^2\). Passing to the Riemann sum: \[
\operatorname{vol}_X(\mathcal{O}_X(1)) = 3 \int_{\frac{1}{1+\sigma}}^1 \big(t D - (1-t)H\big)^2 \, dt = 3 \int_{\frac{1}{1+\sigma}}^1 (38 t^2 - 54 t + 18) \, dt.
\] Substituting \(\sigma = \frac{3 - \sqrt{5}}{6}\) yields an irrational number. Hence, the volume of an integral divisor can be irrational!


Remark 2 (Base Locus and Non-Rational Multipliers). In Example 4, the section \(E = \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{O}_V(-H)) \subseteq X\) satisfies: \[
\mathfrak{b}(|\mathcal{O}_X(k)|) = \mathcal{O}_X\left(-\left(\left\lfloor \frac{k}{1+\sigma} \right\rfloor + 1\right) E\right) = \mathcal{O}_X(-\lceil c k \rceil E),
\] where \(c = \frac{1}{1+\sigma} = \frac{6}{9 - \sqrt{5}} \notin \mathbb{Q}\). Thus the jumping coefficients of the base ideals are irrational multiples of \(k\).

title: 22.10 Connectedness II
text:
Definition 1 (Secant and Tangent Varieties) Let \(X \subseteq \mathbb{P}^r\) be a smooth irreducible subvariety of dimension \(n\). We define the secant variety \(\operatorname{Sec}(X)\) and the tangent variety \(\operatorname{Tan}(X)\) via the secant and tangent bundles:

Tangent variety via Grassmannian incidence: Let \(G = \operatorname{Gr}(n, \mathbb{P}^r) \cong \operatorname{Gr}(n+1, r+1)\) be the Grassmannian of \(n\)-planes in \(\mathbb{P}^r\), and let: \[
\mathcal{I} := \big\{ (x, L) \in \mathbb{P}^r \times G \;\big|\; x \in L \big\} \subseteq \mathbb{P}^r \times G
\] be the universal incidence family over \(G\).
The Euler sequence on \(\mathbb{P}^r\) restricted to \(X\) gives: \[
0 \longrightarrow \mathcal{O}_X \longrightarrow \mathcal{O}_X(1)^{\oplus (r+1)} \longrightarrow T_{\mathbb{P}^r}|_X \longrightarrow 0.
\] The subbundle \(T_X(-1) \subseteq T_{\mathbb{P}^r}|_X(-1)\) lifts to a subbundle \(\widehat{T}_X \subseteq \mathcal{O}_X^{\oplus (r+1)}\) of rank \(n+1\), defining the Gauss map \(f: X \to G\), \(x \mapsto \mathbb{T}_x\). Pulling back the universal family: \[
\begin{CD}
\mathcal{I} @>{\pi_2}>> \mathbb{P}^r \\
@V{\pi_1}VV \\
G
\end{CD}
\] the tangent variety is the closed subvariety defined by: \[
\operatorname{Tan}(X) := \pi_2\big(\pi_1^{-1}(f(X))\big) \subseteq \mathbb{P}^r.
\]
Secant variety via the Hilbert scheme of two points: Let \(X^{[2]} := \operatorname{Hilb}_2(X)\) be the Hilbert scheme of length-\(2\) zero-dimensional subschemes of \(X\), and let \(\mathcal{Z} \subseteq X \times X^{[2]} \subseteq \mathbb{P}^r \times X^{[2]}\) be the universal subscheme. The projection \(\pi_2: \mathcal{Z} \to X^{[2]}\) is finite flat of degree \(2\).
The evaluation map on global sections gives a surjection: \[
\mathcal{O}_{X^{[2]}}^{\oplus (r+1)} \twoheadrightarrow \mathcal{E} := {\pi_2}_* \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{Z}}(1),
\] where \(\mathcal{E}\) is locally free of rank \(2\) on \(X^{[2]}\). This induces a morphism: \[
f: X^{[2]} \longrightarrow \operatorname{Gr}(1, \mathbb{P}^r) = \operatorname{Gr}(2, r+1),
\] mapping each length-\(2\) subscheme to the unique line it spans in \(\mathbb{P}^r\). Let \(\mathcal{U} = \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}) \subseteq \mathbb{P}^r \times X^{[2]}\) be the family of lines over \(X^{[2]}\) with projections \(p_1: \mathcal{U} \to X^{[2]}\) and \(p_2: \mathcal{U} \to \mathbb{P}^r\). The secant variety is the irreducible subvariety: \[
\operatorname{Sec}(X) := p_2(\mathcal{U}) = p_2\big(p_1^{-1}(X^{[2]})\big) \subseteq \mathbb{P}^r.
\] Under the Hilbert–Chow morphism \(\varphi: X^{[2]} \to X^{(2)} = (X \times X) / S_2\), let \(\Delta^{[2]} := \varphi^{-1}(\Delta)\) denote the exceptional divisor parameterizing non-reduced subschemes. Then the tangent variety can also be realized as: \[
\operatorname{Tan}(X) = p_2\big(p_1^{-1}(\Delta^{[2]})\big) \subseteq \operatorname{Sec}(X),
\] which is an irreducible closed subvariety of \(\mathbb{P}^r\).



Proposition 1 (Dimension of \(\operatorname{Sec}(X)\) and \(\operatorname{Tan}(X)\)) Let \(X \subseteq \mathbb{P}^r\) be a smooth irreducible subvariety of dimension \(n\). Then either: \[
\dim \operatorname{Sec}(X) = 2n + 1 \quad \text{and} \quad \dim \operatorname{Tan}(X) = 2n,
\] or: \[
\operatorname{Sec}(X) = \operatorname{Tan}(X).
\]


Proof. Assume \(\operatorname{Tan}(X) \neq \operatorname{Sec}(X)\). It suffices to prove that \(\dim \operatorname{Tan}(X) \ge 2n\). (Indeed, if \(\dim \operatorname{Tan}(X) = 2n\), then \(2n + 1 \le \dim \operatorname{Sec}(X) \le \dim X^{[2]} + 1 = 2n + 1\), forcing \(\dim \operatorname{Sec}(X) = 2n + 1\)).
Suppose for contradiction that \(\dim \operatorname{Tan}(X) < 2n\). Since \(\dim \operatorname{Sec}(X) > \dim \operatorname{Tan}(X)\), we can choose a general linear subspace \(L \subseteq \mathbb{P}^r\) of codimension \(\le 2n\) such that: \[
L \cap \operatorname{Tan}(X) = \varnothing \quad \text{but} \quad L \cap \operatorname{Sec}(X) \neq \varnothing.
\] In particular, \(L \cap X = \varnothing\). Projection away from the center \(L\) yields a morphism: \[
\varphi: X \longrightarrow \mathbb{P}^{r'}, \quad \text{where } r' \le \operatorname{codim}(L) - 1 < 2n.
\] Because \(L \cap \operatorname{Tan}(X) = \varnothing\), no tangent space of \(X\) intersects \(L\), which means the differential \(d\varphi_x\) is injective everywhere; hence \(\varphi\) is unramified. On the other hand, because \(L \cap \operatorname{Sec}(X) \neq \varnothing\), there exists a secant line of \(X\) meeting \(L\), so \(\varphi\) is not injective on closed points.
However, since \(X\) is complete and \(2n > r'\), the Ramification Theorem implies that any unramified morphism \(\varphi: X \to \mathbb{P}^{r'}\) must be a closed embedding, hence injective on points. This contradiction shows that \(\dim \operatorname{Tan}(X) \ge 2n\).



Definition 2 (Local Degree and Ramification Loci) Let \(f: X \to Y\) be a finite surjective morphism of irreducible varieties of dimension \(n\) over \(\mathbb{C}\).

Ramification and Branch Loci: If \(Y\) is smooth, the relative cotangent sheaf \(\Omega^1_{X/Y}\) has generic stalk \((\Omega^1_{X/Y})_\eta = \Omega^1_{k(X)/k(Y)} = 0\) (since \(\mathbb{C}\) is of characteristic zero). The open set: \[
U := X \setminus \operatorname{Supp}(\Omega^1_{X/Y})
\] is the unramified locus. The closed subset \(R := X \setminus U\) is the ramification locus, and \(B(f) := f(R) \subseteq Y\) is the branch locus.
Étaleness over the Unbranched Locus: Over the complement \(Y \setminus B(f)\), the restriction \(f^{-1}(Y \setminus B(f)) \to Y \setminus B(f)\) is étale. Indeed, for any \(y \in Y \setminus B(f)\) and \(x \in f^{-1}(y)\): \[
\dim X \le \dim T_x X \le \dim T_y Y = \dim Y = \dim X,
\] which implies \(\dim T_x X = \dim X\), so \(X\) is smooth at \(x\). By Miracle Flatness, a surjective morphism from a Cohen–Macaulay variety to a regular variety with equidimensional fibers is flat; hence \(f\) is flat and unramified, thus étale. (If \(Y\) is not smooth, this may fail: consider the normalization of a nodal curve \(\mathbb{A}^1 \to C\)).
Local Degree: Analytically, for every \(y \in Y\), there exists an open neighborhood \(U(y) \subseteq Y\) such that: \[
f^{-1}(U(y)) = \coprod_{x \in f^{-1}(y)} V(x),
\] where each \(V(x) \subseteq X\) is a disjoint open neighborhood of \(x\), and each restriction \(f|_{V(x)}: V(x) \to U(y)\) is finite (quasi-finite and proper). The local degree \(e_f(x)\) is defined by: \[
e_f(x) := \deg\big(V(x) \to U(y)\big).
\] Since \(B(f)\) is a proper closed subvariety of \(Y\), \(U(y) \setminus B(f)\) is dense in \(U(y)\). Taking a sequence \(y_k \to y\) in \(U(y) \setminus B(f)\), \(f|_{V(x)}\) is a topological covering of degree \(e_f(x)\) over \(y_k\), so: \[
e_f(x) = \lim_{k \to \infty} \#\big(f|_{V(x)}^{-1}(y_k)\big), \quad \text{and} \quad \deg f = \sum_{x \in f^{-1}(y)} e_f(x).
\] The function \(x \mapsto e_f(x)\) is upper semicontinuous in the analytic topology.
Higher Ramification Loci: For any integer \(l \ge 1\), the \(l\)-th higher ramification locus is: \[
R_l(f) := \big\{ x \in X \;\big|\; e_f(x) > l \big\}.
\] In particular, \(R_1(f) = R(f)\). By Serre’s GAGA, every analytic closed subset in a projective variety is Zariski closed, so \(R_l(f)\) is a Zariski closed subvariety of \(X\).



Lemma 1 (Additivity of Local Degree) Let \(f: X \to Y\) be a finite surjective morphism of complex varieties. Let \(\{x_k\}\) and \(\{z_k\}\) be two sequences of points in \(X\) such that \(x_k \neq z_k\), \(f(x_k) = f(z_k)\), and: \[
\lim_{k \to \infty} x_k = \lim_{k \to \infty} z_k = x^* \in X.
\] Then: \[
e_f(x^*) \ge \limsup_{k \to \infty} \big(e_f(x_k) + e_f(z_k)\big).
\]


Proof. Work in the analytic topology. Choose disjoint neighborhoods \(V(x^*)\) and \(U(f(x^*))\) such that \(f|_{V(x^*)}: V(x^*) \to U(f(x^*))\) is finite of degree \(e_f(x^*)\). For \(k \gg 0\), both \(x_k, z_k \in V(x^*)\), and \(y_k := f(x_k) = f(z_k) \in U(f(x^*))\).
For any point \(y \in U(f(x^*))\), the degree is the sum of local degrees over the fiber in \(V(x^*)\): \[
e_f(x^*) = \sum_{w \in V(x^*) \cap f^{-1}(y_k)} e_f(w) \ge e_f(x_k) + e_f(z_k).
\] Since \(e_f\) takes values in \(\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}\), taking the limit superior yields \(e_f(x^*) \ge \limsup_{k \to \infty} (e_f(x_k) + e_f(z_k))\).



Theorem 1 (Ramification of Coverings of Projective Space) Let \(X\) be an irreducible projective variety of dimension \(n\), and let \(f: X \to \mathbb{P}^n\) be a finite branched covering of degree \(d\).

There exists a point \(x \in X\) such that: \[
e_f(x) \ge \min\{d, \, n + 1\}.
\]
More generally, for each \(1 \le l \le \min\{d - 1, \, n\}\), the higher ramification locus satisfies: \[
\operatorname{codim}_X R_l(f) \le l.
\] In particular, for \(l = \min\{d - 1, \, n\}\), the locus \(R_l(f) = \{ x \in X \mid e_f(x) \ge \min\{d, n+1\} \}\) has codimension \(\le n\), hence is non-empty.



Proof. If \(d = 1\), the map is birational and finite, hence an isomorphism since \(\mathbb{P}^n\) is normal; the claim is trivial. Assume \(d \ge 2\). We proceed by induction on \(n\):

Base case \(n = 1\): Here \(l = 1\), and we must show \(R_1(f) \neq \varnothing\). If \(R_1(f) = \varnothing\), then \(f: X \to \mathbb{P}^1\) is a finite étale cover of degree \(d \ge 2\). But \(\mathbb{P}^1\) is simply connected (\(\pi_1^{\text{ét}}(\mathbb{P}^1) = \{e\}\)), so it admits no non-trivial connected étale covers, a contradiction.
Inductive step \(n \ge 2\): Let \(L \subseteq \mathbb{P}^n\) be a general hyperplane such that \(X' := f^{-1}(L)\) is irreducible (by Bertini’s Theorem). Let \(f' := f|_{X'}: X' \to L \cong \mathbb{P}^{n-1}\), which is a finite covering of degree \(d\).
For a general hyperplane \(L\), \(L\) meets the unbranched locus \(V \subseteq \mathbb{P}^n\), and for any \(x \in f^{-1}(L)\), we have \(e_{f'}(x) = e_f(x)\). Thus \(R_l(f') = R_l(f) \cap X'\). By induction, for all \(l \le \min\{d - 1, \, n - 1\}\): \[
\operatorname{codim}_{X'} R_l(f') \le l \implies \operatorname{codim}_X R_l(f) \le l.
\]
The case \(l = n\) (when \(d \ge n + 1\)): It remains to prove that \(R_n(f) \neq \varnothing\), i.e., there exists \(s^* \in X\) with \(e_f(s^*) \ge n + 1\). By the codimension bound for \(l = n - 1\), we have \(\operatorname{codim}_X R_{n-1}(f) \le n - 1\), so: \[
\dim R_{n-1}(f) \ge n - (n - 1) = 1.
\] Let \(S\) be an irreducible component of \(R_{n-1}(f)\) of dimension \(\ge 1\). Consider the product morphism: \[
F := f \times f|_S: X \times S \longrightarrow \mathbb{P}^n \times \mathbb{P}^n.
\] The space \(X \times S\) is irreducible of dimension \(\dim(X \times S) = n + \dim S \ge n + 1 > n\). Since \(F\) is finite, \(\dim F(X \times S) \ge n + 1 > n\). By the Fulton–Hansen Connectedness Theorem, the preimage: \[
F^{-1}(\Delta_{\mathbb{P}^n}) = X \times_{\mathbb{P}^n} S = \big\{ (x, s) \in X \times S \;\big|\; f(x) = f(s) \big\}
\] is connected.
Notice that \(\Delta_S := \{ (s, s) \mid s \in S \} \subseteq F^{-1}(\Delta_{\mathbb{P}^n})\) is an irreducible component of dimension \(\dim S\).

If \(\Delta_S = F^{-1}(\Delta_{\mathbb{P}^n})\), then \(f(x) = f(s)\) implies \(x = s\), meaning every point \(s \in S\) has a unique preimage \(\# f^{-1}(f(s)) = 1\). Thus \(e_f(s) = d \ge n + 1\), which gives \(S \subseteq R_n(f)\), so \(R_n(f) \neq \varnothing\).
If \(\Delta_S \subsetneq F^{-1}(\Delta_{\mathbb{P}^n})\), by connectedness of \(F^{-1}(\Delta_{\mathbb{P}^n})\) there exists another irreducible component \(T \neq \Delta_S\) meeting \(\Delta_S\): \[
T \cap \Delta_S \neq \varnothing.
\] Choose a point \((s^*, s^*) \in T \cap \Delta_S\) and a sequence \((x_k, s_k) \in T \setminus \Delta_S\) converging to \((s^*, s^*)\) with \(x_k \neq s_k\) and \(f(x_k) = f(s_k)\). Then \(\lim x_k = \lim s_k = s^*\). Because \(s_k \in S \subseteq R_{n-1}(f)\), we have \(e_f(s_k) \ge n\), and trivially \(e_f(x_k) \ge 1\). By Lemma 1: \[
e_f(s^*) \ge \limsup_{k \to \infty}\big(e_f(s_k) + e_f(x_k)\big) \ge n + 1.
\] Therefore, \(s^* \in R_n(f)\), completing the proof.




Corollary 1 (Geometric Consequences for Branched Coverings) Let \(X\) be an irreducible projective variety of dimension \(n\), and let \(f: X \to \mathbb{P}^n\) be a branched covering of degree \(d\).

If \(d \le n + 1\), there exists a subvariety \(T \subseteq \mathbb{P}^n\) of dimension \(\ge n + 1 - d\) over which \(f\) is bijective.
If \(X\) is normal and \(d \le n\), then the étale fundamental group of \(X\) is trivial: \[
\pi_1^{\text{ét}}(X) = \{e\}.
\]



Proof. 

For \(l = d - 1 \le n\), Theorem 1 implies that \(\operatorname{codim}_X R_{d-1}(f) \le d - 1\). For any \(x \in R_{d-1}(f)\), we have \(e_f(x) \ge d\), which forces \(f^{-1}(f(x)) = \{x\}\) because \(\sum_{x' \in f^{-1}(f(x))} e_f(x') = d\). Hence \(f\) is bijective over \(T := f(R_{d-1}(f))\), where \(\dim T \ge n - (d - 1) = n + 1 - d\).
Suppose \(p: Y \to X\) is a connected finite étale cover of degree \(m \ge 2\). Because \(X\) is normal and connected, \(Y\) is an irreducible normal variety of dimension \(n\). Consider the composite morphism: \[
g := f \circ p: Y \longrightarrow \mathbb{P}^n, \quad \deg g = m \cdot d \ge 2d.
\] Because \(d \le n\) and \(2d - 1 \ge d\), we have \(d \le \min\{\deg g - 1, \, n\}\). By Theorem 1 applied to \(g\), there exists a point \(y \in Y\) such that: \[
e_g(y) \ge d + 1.
\] However, since \(p\) is étale, \(e_g(y) = e_p(y) \cdot e_f(p(y)) = 1 \cdot e_f(p(y)) \le d\), a contradiction. Thus \(X\) has no non-trivial connected finite étale covers, so \(\pi_1^{\text{ét}}(X) = \{e\}\).



Example 1 (Sharpness of the Degree Bound) The bound \(d \le n\) is sharp. Let \(E \subseteq \mathbb{P}^n\) be an elliptic curve of degree \(n + 1\) (for \(n \ge 2\), any degree \(n+1\) line bundle on \(E\) is very ample, and \(h^0(E, \mathcal{L}) = \deg \mathcal{L} + 1 - g = n + 1\)).
Define the incidence variety: \[
X := \big\{ (x, H) \in E \times \check{\mathbb{P}}^n \;\big|\; x \in H \big\} \subseteq E \times \check{\mathbb{P}}^n.
\] The second projection \(p_2: X \to \check{\mathbb{P}}^n \cong \mathbb{P}^n\) is a finite covering of degree \(n + 1\). On the other hand, the first projection \(p_1: X \to E\) realizes \(X\) as a \(\mathbb{P}^{n-1}\)-bundle over \(E\). From the homotopy exact sequence: \[
\pi_1(\mathbb{P}^{n-1}) \longrightarrow \pi_1(X) \longrightarrow \pi_1(E) \longrightarrow \pi_0(\mathbb{P}^{n-1}) \implies \pi_1(X) \cong \pi_1(E) \cong \mathbb{Z}^2,
\] so \(\pi_1^{\text{ét}}(X) \cong \widehat{\mathbb{Z}}^2 \neq \{e\}\).



Definition 3 (Relative Secant and Tangent Varieties) Let \(X \subseteq \mathbb{P}^r\) be a smooth subvariety of dimension \(n\), and let \(V \subseteq X\) be a subvariety of dimension \(v\). 1. A linear subspace \(L \subseteq \mathbb{P}^r\) is tangent to \(X\) at \(x\) if \(x \in L \cap X\) and \(\mathbb{T}_x \subseteq L\). 2. Considering the incidence along \(V \times X \subseteq X \times X\) inside the blow-up \(\mathrm{Bl}_{\Delta}(X \times X) / S_2 \cong X^{[2]}\), the relative secant variety and relative tangent variety of \(X\) with respect to \(V\) are: \[
   \operatorname{Sec}_V(X) := \bigcup_{x \in V, \, y \in X} \overline{xy}, \qquad \operatorname{Tan}_V(X) := \bigcup_{x \in V} \mathbb{T}_x.
   \] Clearly \(\operatorname{Tan}_V(X) \subseteq \operatorname{Sec}_V(X)\) and \(X \subseteq \operatorname{Sec}_V(X)\).
