Proposition 2 (Dimension of Relative Secant and Tangent Varieties) Let \(X \subseteq \mathbb{P}^r\) be a smooth irreducible subvariety of dimension \(n\), and let \(V \subseteq X\) be a subvariety of dimension \(v\). Then either: \[
\dim \operatorname{Sec}_V(X) = n + v + 1 \quad \text{and} \quad \dim \operatorname{Tan}_V(X) = n + v,
\] or: \[
\operatorname{Tan}_V(X) = \operatorname{Sec}_V(X).
\]


Proof. Suppose \(\operatorname{Tan}_V(X) \neq \operatorname{Sec}_V(X)\), and suppose for contradiction that \(\dim \operatorname{Tan}_V(X) = t < n + v\). A general linear space \(L \subseteq \mathbb{P}^r\) of codimension \(t + 1\) satisfies: \[
L \cap \operatorname{Sec}_V(X) \neq \varnothing \quad \text{and} \quad L \cap \operatorname{Tan}_V(X) = \varnothing.
\] Projection away from \(L\) gives \(p: X \to \mathbb{P}^t\). Consider the product morphism: \[
F := p|_V \times p: V \times X \longrightarrow \mathbb{P}^t \times \mathbb{P}^t.
\] Because \(\dim(V \times X) = n + v > t\), the Fulton–Hansen Connectedness Theorem implies that \(F^{-1}(\Delta_{\mathbb{P}^t})\) is connected.
Since \(L \cap \operatorname{Sec}_V(X) \neq \varnothing\), there exist \(v_0 \in V\) and \(x_0 \in X\) with \(x_0 \neq v_0\) such that the line \(\overline{v_0 x_0}\) intersects \(L\), meaning \(p(v_0) = p(x_0)\). Hence \((v_0, x_0) \in F^{-1}(\Delta_{\mathbb{P}^t}) \setminus \Delta_V\). By connectedness, there exists an irreducible component \(T \subseteq F^{-1}(\Delta_{\mathbb{P}^t})\) containing \((v_0, x_0)\) such that: \[
T \cap \Delta_V \neq \varnothing.
\] Pick \((v^*, v^*) \in T \cap \Delta_V\), and choose a sequence \((v_k, x_k) \in T \setminus \Delta_V\) converging to \((v^*, v^*)\) with \(v_k \neq x_k\) and \(p(v_k) = p(x_k)\). Then the secant lines \(\overline{v_k x_k}\) meet \(L\). Since the incidence variety \(\mathcal{U}_L := \{ (x, y, l) \mid l \in \overline{xy} \cap L \}\) is proper over \(V \times X\), taking the limit as \(k \to \infty\) shows that the limiting line is tangent to \(X\) at \(v^*\) and intersects \(L\).
Thus \(\mathbb{T}_{v^*} \cap L \neq \varnothing\), which contradicts \(L \cap \operatorname{Tan}_V(X) = \varnothing\).



Theorem 2 (Zak’s Theorem on Tangencies) Let \(X \subseteq \mathbb{P}^r\) be a smooth, non-degenerate irreducible subvariety of dimension \(n\). Let \(L \subseteq \mathbb{P}^r\) be a linear subspace of dimension \(k\) with \(n \le k \le r - 1\). Then the tangency locus: \[
\big\{ x \in X \;\big|\; \mathbb{T}_x \subseteq L \big\}
\] has dimension: \[
\dim\big\{ x \in X \;\big|\; \mathbb{T}_x \subseteq L \big\} \le k - n.
\] In particular, its dimension is at most \(\min\{k - n, \, n - 1\}\).


Proof. Suppose for contradiction that there exists an irreducible component \(V \subseteq \{ x \in X \mid \mathbb{T}_x \subseteq L \}\) of dimension: \[
v := \dim V \ge k + 1 - n.
\] Then by definition, for every \(x \in V\), the embedded tangent space \(\mathbb{T}_x \subseteq L\), which implies: \[
\operatorname{Tan}_V(X) = \bigcup_{x \in V} \mathbb{T}_x \subseteq L.
\] Thus \(\dim \operatorname{Tan}_V(X) \le \dim L = k \le v + n - 1\). By Proposition 2, we must have: \[
\operatorname{Tan}_V(X) = \operatorname{Sec}_V(X).
\] However, \(X \subseteq \operatorname{Sec}_V(X) = \operatorname{Tan}_V(X) \subseteq L\), which forces \(X \subseteq L\). This contradicts the assumption that \(X\) is non-degenerate in \(\mathbb{P}^r\).


Corollary 2 (Consequences of Zak’s Theorem) Let \(X \subseteq \mathbb{P}^r\) be a smooth, non-degenerate irreducible subvariety of dimension \(n\).

Finiteness of the Gauss Map: The Gauss map \(\gamma: X \to \operatorname{Gr}(n, \mathbb{P}^r)\), \(x \mapsto \mathbb{T}_x\) is a finite morphism.
Singularities of Hyperplane Sections: For any hyperplane \(H \subseteq \mathbb{P}^r\): \[
\dim \operatorname{Sing}(X \cap H) \le r - 1 - n.
\] Consequently:

If \(2n \ge r + 1\), then \(X \cap H\) is reduced for general \(H\).
If \(2n \ge r + 2\), then \(X \cap H\) is normal for general \(H\).

Dimension of the Dual Variety: Let \(\mathcal{P} := \{ (x, H) \in X \times \check{\mathbb{P}}^r \mid \mathbb{T}_x \subseteq H \}\). Then \(\mathcal{P}\) is a \(\mathbb{P}^{r - 1 - n}\)-bundle over \(X\) with \(\dim \mathcal{P} = r - 1\). The dual variety \(X^* := p_2(\mathcal{P}) \subseteq \check{\mathbb{P}}^r\) satisfies: \[
\dim X^* \ge n.
\]



Proof. 

Setting \(k = n\) in Theorem 2, for any \(n\)-plane \(L\), \(\dim \{ x \in X \mid \mathbb{T}_x = L \} \le n - n = 0\). Hence every fiber of the Gauss map is zero-dimensional; being projective, \(\gamma\) is finite.
A point \(x \in X \cap H\) is singular if and only if the differential \(d(s|_X)\) vanishes at \(x\), which is equivalent to \(\mathbb{T}_x \subseteq H\). Thus: \[
\operatorname{Sing}(X \cap H) = \big\{ x \in X \;\big|\; \mathbb{T}_x \subseteq H \big\}.
\] Applying Zak’s Theorem with \(k = r - 1\), we obtain \(\dim \operatorname{Sing}(X \cap H) \le (r - 1) - n = r - 1 - n\).

If \(2n \ge r + 1\), then \(\dim \operatorname{Sing}(X \cap H) \le n - 2 = \dim(X \cap H) - 1\), so \(X \cap H\) is regular in codimension \(0\) (\(R_0\)). Since \(X\) is smooth (hence Cohen–Macaulay), the hypersurface section \(X \cap H\) is Cohen–Macaulay (\(S_1\)). By Serre’s criterion, \(R_0 + S_1\) implies that \(X \cap H\) is reduced.
If \(2n \ge r + 2\), then \(\dim \operatorname{Sing}(X \cap H) \le n - 3 = \dim(X \cap H) - 2\), so \(X \cap H\) satisfies \(R_1\). Together with \(S_2\), Serre’s criterion implies that \(X \cap H\) is normal.

For any \(H \in X^*\), the fiber \(p_2^{-1}(H) \cong \{ x \in X \mid \mathbb{T}_x \subseteq H \}\) has dimension at most \(r - 1 - n\). By fiber dimension: \[
\dim X^* \ge \dim \mathcal{P} - (r - 1 - n) = (r - 1) - (r - 1 - n) = n.
\]



Remark 1 (Join of Varieties). Replacing \(\operatorname{Hilb}_2(X)\) with the blow-up of \(X \times Y\) along the diagonal, one defines the join \(X * Y\) and the infinitesimal join \(\mathcal{L}\operatorname{Join}(X, Y)\). By identical arguments, either \(\dim(X * Y) = \dim X + \dim Y + 1\) and \(\dim \mathcal{L}\operatorname{Join}(X, Y) = \dim X + \dim Y\), or \(\mathcal{L}\operatorname{Join}(X, Y) = X * Y\).



Theorem 3 (Zak’s Theorem on Linear Normality (Form I)) Let \(X \subseteq \mathbb{P}^r\) be a smooth projective variety of dimension \(n\). If: \[
3n > 2(r - 1),
\] then \(X\) is linearly normal, meaning the restriction map: \[
H^0(\mathbb{P}^r, \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^r}(1)) \longrightarrow H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(1))
\] is surjective.


Proposition 3 (Geometric Characterization of Linear Normality) For a smooth projective variety \(X \subseteq \mathbb{P}^r\), the following are equivalent: 1. \(X\) is not linearly normal. 2. \(X\) is the projection of a non-degenerate embedding in \(\mathbb{P}^{r+1}\) from an external point \(P \notin X\). 3. There exists a non-degenerate embedding \(X \hookrightarrow \mathbb{P}^{r+1}\) such that \(\operatorname{Sec}(X) \subsetneq \mathbb{P}^{r+1}\).
Consequently, Theorem 3 is equivalent to:
Zak’s Theorem on Linear Normality (Form II): Let \(X \subseteq \mathbb{P}^m\) be a smooth, non-degenerate projective variety of dimension \(n\). If: \[
3n > 2(m - 2),
\] then: \[
\operatorname{Sec}(X) = \mathbb{P}^m.
\]


Proof. 

(1) \(\iff\) (2): The map \(H^0(\mathbb{P}^r, \mathcal{O}(1)) \to H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(1))\) fails to be surjective if and only if there exists a section \(f \in H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(1))\) not in the image. Choosing a basis \(s_0, \dots, s_r\) of \(H^0(\mathbb{P}^r, \mathcal{O}(1))\) and setting \(s_{r+1} := f\), the linear system \(\langle s_0, \dots, s_{r+1} \rangle\) defines an embedding \(X \hookrightarrow \mathbb{P}^{r+1}\) whose projection from \([0: \dots : 0: 1]\) recovers the original map to \(\mathbb{P}^r\).
(2) \(\iff\) (3): The projection from \(P \in \mathbb{P}^{r+1}\) restricts to an embedding on \(X\) if and only if \(P\) lies on no secant or tangent line of \(X\), which means \(P \notin \operatorname{Sec}(X)\). Such a point \(P\) exists if and only if \(\operatorname{Sec}(X) \subsetneq \mathbb{P}^{r+1}\).




Definition 4 (Trisecant and Higher Secant Varieties) Let \(X \subseteq \mathbb{P}^m\) be a smooth variety of dimension \(n\). A closed subscheme \(Z \subseteq X\) of dimension \(0\) and length \(3\) has local rings \(\mathcal{O}_Z = \prod A_i\) with \(\sum \operatorname{length}(A_i) = 3\): - Three distinct points: \(A_1 \times A_2 \times A_3\); - Two points (one tangent vector): \(A_1 \times A_2\) with \(\operatorname{length}(A_2) = 2\); - One point (length \(3\) local ring): \(\mathcal{O}_{X, x} / I\) where: - If \(\mathfrak{m} / \mathfrak{m}^2\) has image of dimension \(1\), \(I = (x_1^3, x_2, \dots, x_n)\), which defines an osculating plane \(\mathbb{P}^2 \subseteq T_x^{(2)} X\); - If \(\mathfrak{m} / \mathfrak{m}^2\) has image of dimension \(2\), \(I = (x_1^2, x_1 x_2, x_2^2, x_3, \dots, x_n)\), whose spanned plane is already contained in \(\mathbb{T}_x X \subseteq \operatorname{Sec}(X)\).
The trisecant variety is the variety: \[
\operatorname{Trisec}(X) := \operatorname{Sec}^3(X) = \bigcup_{Z \in \operatorname{Hilb}_3(X)} \operatorname{Span}(Z) = X * X * X \subseteq \mathbb{P}^m.
\] More generally, the \(k\)-th secant variety is \(\operatorname{Sec}^k(X) := X * \dots * X\) (\(k\) times).


Remark 2 (Smoothness and Irreducibility of Hilbert Schemes of Points). 

By Fogarty (1968), \(\operatorname{Hilb}_m(X)\) is smooth if and only if \(\dim X \le 2\) or \(m \le 3\).
\(\operatorname{Hilb}_m(X)\) is irreducible if \(\dim X \le 2\).
\(\operatorname{Hilb}_m(\mathbb{P}^3)\) is irreducible for \(m \le 7\) (Mozgovoy 2008), has two irreducible components for \(m = 8\) (Cartwright–Erman–Velasco–Viray 2008), while \(\operatorname{Hilb}_{11}(\mathbb{P}^3)\) is irreducible (DJUNT 2017).



Lemma 2 (Terracini’s Lemma) Let \(X \subseteq \mathbb{P}^m\) be a smooth, irreducible subvariety. 1. For distinct points \(x, y \in X\) and \(p \in \overline{xy}\): \[
   \operatorname{Span}(\mathbb{T}_x, \, \mathbb{T}_y) \subseteq T_p \operatorname{Sec}(X),
   \] with equality holding for general \(x, y \in X\) and general \(p \in \overline{xy}\). 2. For non-collinear points \(x, y, z \in X\) and \(p \in \overline{xyz}\): \[
   \operatorname{Span}(\mathbb{T}_x, \, \mathbb{T}_y, \, \mathbb{T}_z) \subseteq T_p \operatorname{Trisec}(X),
   \] with equality holding for general points.


Corollary 3 (Secant Equals Trisecant) Let \(X \subseteq \mathbb{P}^m\) be a smooth, non-degenerate projective variety. Then: \[
\operatorname{Sec}(X) = \mathbb{P}^m \iff \operatorname{Sec}(X) = \operatorname{Trisec}(X).
\]


Proof. The implication \((\implies)\) is immediate since \(\operatorname{Sec}(X) \subseteq \operatorname{Trisec}(X) \subseteq \mathbb{P}^m\).
Conversely, suppose \(\operatorname{Sec}(X) \subsetneq \mathbb{P}^m\). For general \(x, y \in X\) and general \(p \in \overline{xy}\), Terracini’s Lemma gives \(T_p \operatorname{Sec}(X) = \operatorname{Span}(\mathbb{T}_x, \mathbb{T}_y) =: \Lambda \subsetneq \mathbb{P}^m\). Because \(X\) is non-degenerate, \(X \nsubseteq \Lambda\). Choosing \(z \in X \setminus \Lambda\), we have: \[
\operatorname{Span}(\mathbb{T}_x, \mathbb{T}_y, \mathbb{T}_z) \supsetneq \operatorname{Span}(\mathbb{T}_x, \mathbb{T}_y),
\] which implies \(\dim \operatorname{Trisec}(X) > \dim \operatorname{Sec}(X)\), so \(\operatorname{Sec}(X) \neq \operatorname{Trisec}(X)\).


Proposition 4 (Proof of Linear Normality (Form II)) Let \(X \subseteq \mathbb{P}^m\) be a smooth projective variety of dimension \(n\). If: \[
3n > 2(m - 2),
\] then \(\operatorname{Sec}(X) = \operatorname{Trisec}(X)\), and consequently \(\operatorname{Sec}(X) = \mathbb{P}^m\).


Proof. Suppose for contradiction that \(\operatorname{Sec}(X) \subsetneq \operatorname{Trisec}(X)\). Then there exist points \(x_0, y_0, z_0 \in X\) spanning a plane \(\overline{x_0 y_0 z_0} \cong \mathbb{P}^2\) not contained in \(\operatorname{Sec}(X)\). Thus: \[
\operatorname{Sec}(X) \cap \overline{x_0 y_0 z_0} \subsetneq \mathbb{P}^2
\] is a proper closed algebraic subset, hence has dimension \(\le 1\). In particular, \(X \cap \overline{x_0 y_0 z_0}\) consists of only finitely many points (otherwise, any curve in the plane would force its secants to fill the entire \(\mathbb{P}^2\)).
Choose a general line \(L \subseteq \overline{x_0 y_0 z_0}\). Then \(L\) meets \(\operatorname{Sec}(X)\) transversely in finitely many points, and \(L \cap X = \varnothing\). Projection away from \(L\) defines a finite morphism: \[
\pi: X \longrightarrow \mathbb{P}^{m-2}.
\] Consider the triple product map: \[
F := \pi \times \pi \times \pi: X \times X \times X \longrightarrow \mathbb{P}^{m-2} \times \mathbb{P}^{m-2} \times \mathbb{P}^{m-2}.
\] Because \(\dim(X \times X \times X) = 3n > 2(m - 2)\), Fulton–Hansen Connectedness implies that: \[
F^{-1}(\Delta_{\mathbb{P}^{m-2}}) = \big\{ (x, y, z) \in X^3 \;\big|\; \pi(x) = \pi(y) = \pi(z) \big\}
\] is connected. Geometrically, \(\pi(x) = \pi(y) = \pi(z)\) means that the secant lines \(\overline{xy}\), \(\overline{xz}\), and \(\overline{yz}\) all meet the line \(L\).
Define the continuous map: \[
\Phi: F^{-1}(\Delta_{\mathbb{P}^{m-2}}) \setminus D_X \longrightarrow L \times L \times L, \quad (x, y, z) \longmapsto (\overline{yz} \cap L, \; \overline{xz} \cap L, \; \overline{xy} \cap L),
\] where \(D_X := (\Delta_X \times X) \cup (X \times \Delta_X) \cup (\Delta_{1,3})\). Because \(L \cap \operatorname{Sec}(X)\) is a finite set of points, the image of \(\Phi\) is finite, so \(\Phi\) is locally constant.
By the connectedness of \(F^{-1}(\Delta_{\mathbb{P}^{m-2}})\), \(\Phi\) must be constant on every component: \[
\Phi(x, y, z) = (a, b, c) \in L^3,
\] where \(a, b, c\) are distinct points on \(L\) (if, say, \(a = b\), then \(\overline{xy}\) and \(\overline{xz}\) meet \(L\) at the same point, which forces \(x, y, z\) to be collinear, contradicting \(L \cap X = \varnothing\)).
Now take a smooth curve \(T\) in an irreducible component of \(F^{-1}(\Delta_{\mathbb{P}^{m-2}})\) specializing a general point \((x_t, y_t, z_t)\) to a point \((x^*, y^*, z^*) \in D_X\) at \(t = t^*\): - If \(y^* = z^* \neq x^*\), then the two secant lines \(\overline{x_t y_t}\) and \(\overline{x_t z_t}\) both degenerate to the single line \(\overline{x^* y^*}\), forcing their intersection points \(a\) and \(b\) on \(L\) to coincide, a contradiction. - If \(x^* = y^* = z^*\), then by the valuative criterion, the limits of \(\overline{x_t y_t}\), \(\overline{x_t z_t}\), and \(\overline{y_t z_t}\) are three distinct tangent lines of \(X\) at \(x^*\) meeting \(L\) at \(a, b, c\). This implies that \(L \subseteq \mathbb{T}_{x^*} X \subseteq \operatorname{Sec}(X)\), which contradicts the fact that \(L \cap \operatorname{Sec}(X)\) is finite.
This contradiction establishes that \(\operatorname{Sec}(X) = \operatorname{Trisec}(X)\), and thus \(\operatorname{Sec}(X) = \mathbb{P}^m\).



Theorem 4 (Branching over Nodal Curves (Zariski’s Problem)) Let \(C \subseteq \mathbb{P}^2\) be a (possibly reducible) plane curve having only nodal singularities (i.e., at every singular point \(p \in C\), the formal completion satisfies \(\widehat{\mathcal{O}}_{C, p} \cong k[[x, y]] / (xy)\)).
If \(f: X \to \mathbb{P}^2\) is a finite covering branched only along \(C\) (i.e., \(B(f) \subseteq C\)), then: 1. \(f\) is a Galois covering; 2. The Galois group \(\operatorname{Gal}(X / \mathbb{P}^2)\) is abelian.

title: 22.3 Iitaka Fibration
text:
Definition 1 (Semigroup of a Line Bundle and Exponent) Let \(X\) be a variety and \(L\) a line bundle on \(X\).

The set: \[
N(L) = N(X, L) := \big\{ m \ge 0 \;\big|\; H^0(X, L^{\otimes m}) \neq 0 \big\}
\] forms a sub-semigroup of \((\mathbb{N}, +)\).
If \(N(L) \neq \{0\}\), there exists a unique integer \(e = e(L) \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}\) such that: \[
N(L) \subseteq e \mathbb{N} \quad \text{and} \quad e\mathbb{N} \setminus N(L) \text{ is finite}.
\] The integer \(e(L)\) is called the exponent of \(L\).



Proposition 1 (Scheme-Theoretic Image of a Rational Map) Let \(f: X \dashrightarrow Y\) be a rational map between irreducible varieties. For any representative morphism \((U, f_U)\) of \(f\) defined on a dense open set \(U \subseteq X\), the closed subvariety: \[
\operatorname{Im}(f) := \overline{f_U(U)} \subseteq Y
\] is independent of the chosen representative and is called the image of \(f\).


Proof. If \((V, f_V)\) is another representative, then \(f_U|_{U \cap V} = f_V|_{U \cap V}\). Setting \(W = U \cap V\), the pullback \(\mathcal{O}_Y \to (f_U)_* \mathcal{O}_U \to (f_W)_* \mathcal{O}_W\) has the same kernel because \(W\) is dense in \(U\) and \(X\) is reduced. The kernel defines the vanishing ideal of the scheme-theoretic closure, so \(\overline{f_U(U)} = \overline{f_W(W)} = \overline{f_V(V)}\).


Definition 2 (Iitaka Dimension) Let \(X\) be a normal variety and \(L\) a line bundle on \(X\).

For each \(m \in N(X, L)\), the complete linear system \(|L^{\otimes m}|\) determines a rational map: \[
\phi_m := \phi_{|L^{\otimes m}|}: X \dashrightarrow \mathbb{P} H^0(X, L^{\otimes m}).
\]
The Iitaka dimension (or \(L\)-dimension) of \(L\) is defined by: \[
\kappa(L) = \kappa(X, L) := \begin{cases} \max_{m \in N(X, L)} \big\{ \dim \operatorname{Im}(\phi_m) \big\}, & N(X, L) \neq \{0\}, \\ -\infty, & N(X, L) = \{0\}. \end{cases}
\]
For an arbitrary non-normal variety \(X\), let \(\nu: \widetilde{X} \to X\) be the normalization. The Iitaka dimension is defined by: \[
\kappa(X, L) := \kappa(\widetilde{X}, \nu^* L).
\]



Definition 3 (Algebraic Fiber Space) An algebraic fiber space (AFS) is a surjective projective morphism \(f: X \to Y\) between irreducible varieties such that: \[
f_* \mathcal{O}_X = \mathcal{O}_Y.
\] By Zariski’s Connectedness Principle, every fiber of an algebraic fiber space is connected.



Convention: From now on, \(X\) is assumed to be an irreducible normal projective variety over \(k\).



Proposition 2 (Powers Achieving the Iitaka Dimension) Let \(X\) be a normal variety and \(\kappa = \kappa(X, L) \ge 0\). Then: \[
\dim \operatorname{Im}(\phi_m) = \kappa \quad \text{for all } m \gg 0 \text{ with } m \in N(X, L).
\]


Proof. Replacing \(L\) by \(L^{\otimes e(L)}\), we may assume \(e(L) = 1\). Then there exists \(p_0\) such that \(H^0(X, L^{\otimes p}) \neq 0\) for all \(p \ge p_0\). Fix a non-zero section \(s \in H^0(X, L^{\otimes p})\).
Choose \(m\) such that \(\dim \operatorname{Im}(\phi_m) = \kappa\). Multiplication by \(s\) induces an injection \(H^0(X, L^{\otimes m}) \hookrightarrow H^0(X, L^{\otimes(m+p)})\). This linear inclusion determines a rational projection of projective spaces: \[
\begin{CD}
X @>{\phi_{m+p}}>> Y_{m+p} \\
@| @VV{\pi}V \\
X @>{\phi_m}>> Y_m
\end{CD}
\] Because \(\pi\) is a dominant rational projection, we have: \[
\kappa = \dim Y_m \le \dim Y_{m+p} \le \kappa \implies \dim Y_{m+p} = \kappa.
\] Thus \(\dim \operatorname{Im}(\phi_n) = \kappa\) for all \(n \ge m + p_0\).


Proposition 3 (Criterion for Algebraic Fiber Spaces) Let \(f: X \to Y\) be a surjective projective morphism between normal varieties, inducing an inclusion of function fields \(K(Y) \subseteq K(X)\). Then \(f\) is an algebraic fiber space if and only if \(K(Y)\) is algebraically closed in \(K(X)\).
In particular, every projective surjective birational morphism between normal varieties is an algebraic fiber space.


Proof. \((\implies)\): Let \(K(Y) \subseteq \mathbb{L} \subseteq K(X)\) be the algebraic closure of \(K(Y)\) in \(K(X)\). Normalizing \(Y\) in \(\mathbb{L}\) produces a factorization: \[
X \xrightarrow{\quad h \quad} Z \xrightarrow{\quad g \quad} Y,
\] where \(g: Z \to Y\) is finite and \(h\) is proper. Since \(f\) is surjective and projective, \(h(X) = Z\), so \(\dim Z = \dim Y\). The condition \(f_* \mathcal{O}_X = \mathcal{O}_Y\) implies: \[
\mathcal{O}_Y \subseteq g_* \mathcal{O}_Z \subseteq g_* h_* \mathcal{O}_X = f_* \mathcal{O}_X = \mathcal{O}_Y \implies g_* \mathcal{O}_Z = \mathcal{O}_Y.
\] Since \(Y\) is normal, \(g\) must be an isomorphism, so \(\mathbb{L} = K(Y)\).
\((\impliedby)\): Consider the Stein factorization of \(f\): \[
X \xrightarrow{\quad \phi \quad} Z \xrightarrow{\quad g \quad} Y,
\] where \(\phi_* \mathcal{O}_X = \mathcal{O}_Z\) and \(g\) is finite. Since \(X\) is normal and \(\phi_* \mathcal{O}_X = \mathcal{O}_Z\), the scheme \(Z\) is normal. Furthermore, \(K(Z) \subseteq K(X)\) is a finite algebraic extension of \(K(Y)\). Since \(K(Y)\) is algebraically closed in \(K(X)\), we must have \(K(Z) = K(Y)\). Because \(Y\) is normal and \(g\) is birational and finite, Zariski’s Main Theorem implies that \(g: Z \xrightarrow{\sim} Y\) is an isomorphism. Thus \(f_* \mathcal{O}_X = \mathcal{O}_Y\).


Lemma 1 (Invariance of Sections and Picard Group) Let \(\phi: X \to Y\) be an algebraic fiber space.

For every line bundle \(L\) on \(Y\), the natural map is an isomorphism: \[
H^0(Y, L) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} H^0(X, \phi^* L).
\]
The pullback homomorphism \(\phi^*: \operatorname{Pic}(Y) \hookrightarrow \operatorname{Pic}(X)\) is injective.



Proof. 

By the projection formula, \(\phi_* \phi^* L \cong L \otimes_{\mathcal{O}_Y} \phi_* \mathcal{O}_X \cong L\). Taking global sections yields \(H^0(X, \phi^* L) \cong H^0(Y, \phi_* \phi^* L) \cong H^0(Y, L)\).
If \(\phi^* L \cong \mathcal{O}_X\), then by (1), \(H^0(Y, L) \cong H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X) \cong k\) and \(H^0(Y, L^\vee) \cong H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X) \cong k\). Choose non-zero sections \(s \in H^0(Y, L)\) and \(t \in H^0(Y, L^\vee)\). The product \(s \otimes t \in H^0(Y, \mathcal{O}_Y) \cong k\) is non-zero, hence a non-zero constant \(c \in k^\times\). Thus \(s\) vanishes nowhere, which implies \(L \cong \mathcal{O}_Y\).



Definition 4 (Stable Base Locus) Let \(D\) be a Cartier divisor on \(X\).

The stable base locus of \(D\) is the closed set: \[
\mathbf{B}(D) := \bigcap_{m \ge 1} \operatorname{Bs}(|mD|).
\]
Since the family of closed sets satisfies \(\operatorname{Bs}(|m_1 D|) \cap \operatorname{Bs}(|m_2 D|) \supseteq \operatorname{Bs}(|(m_1 + m_2)D|)\), by the descending chain condition on closed subsets of \(X\), there exists \(m_0 \ge 1\) such that: \[
\mathbf{B}(D) = \operatorname{Bs}(|k m_0 D|) \quad \text{for all } k \gg 0.
\]



Definition 5 (Semiample Line Bundles)  

Define the semigroup of free multiples: \[
M(X, L) := \big\{ m \in \mathbb{N} \;\big|\; L^{\otimes m} \text{ is base-point-free} \big\}.
\] Let \(f = f(L)\) be the exponent of the semigroup \(M(X, L)\).
A line bundle \(L\) on \(X\) is semiample if \(M(X, L) \neq \{0\}\), that is, some positive power \(L^{\otimes m}\) is generated by its global sections.



Theorem 1 (Semiample Fibration) Let \(X\) be a normal projective variety and \(L\) a semiample line bundle on \(X\). Then there exists an algebraic fiber space \(\phi: X \to Y\) and an ample line bundle \(A\) on \(Y\) such that:

For all \(m \in M(X, L)\) sufficiently large, the morphism \(\phi_m: X \to \mathbb{P} H^0(X, L^{\otimes m})\) has image \(Y_m \cong Y\), and factors through \(\phi\).
\(\phi^* A \cong L^{\otimes f(L)}\), and for \(k \gg 0\), the very ample embeddings \(\iota_{A^{\otimes k}}: Y \hookrightarrow \mathbb{P} H^0(Y, A^{\otimes k})\) make the following diagram commute: \[
\begin{CD}
X @>{\phi}>> Y \\
@| @VV{\cong}V \\
X @>{\phi_{kf}}>> Y_{kf}
\end{CD}
\] In particular, the target variety \(Y\) is normal and projective.



Definition 6 (Big Line Bundles and Divisors) A line bundle \(L\) on an irreducible projective variety \(X\) is big if: \[
\kappa(X, L) = \dim X.
\] A Cartier divisor \(D\) is big if \(\mathcal{O}_X(D)\) is big.


Theorem 2 (The Iitaka Fibration Theorem) Let \(X\) be a normal projective variety and \(L\) a line bundle on \(X\) with \(\kappa(X, L) > 0\). Then there exists an algebraic fiber space between normal varieties: \[
\phi_\infty: X_\infty \longrightarrow Y_\infty,
\] unique up to birational equivalence, and a birational morphism \(u_\infty: X_\infty \to X\), such that for all \(k \in N(X, L)\) sufficiently large, there exists a birational map \(v_k: Y_\infty \dashrightarrow Y_k\) making the following diagram commute: \[
\begin{CD}
X_\infty @>{u_\infty}>> X \\
@V{\phi_\infty}VV @VV{\phi_k}V \\
Y_\infty @>{v_k}>{\approx}> Y_k
\end{CD}
\] where \(Y_k := \operatorname{Im}(\phi_k) \subseteq \mathbb{P} H^0(X, L^{\otimes k})\).


Proof. Replacing \(L\) by \(L^{\otimes e(L)}\), we may assume without loss of generality that \(e(L) = 1\).
Step 1: The stable fibration for a sub-semigroup \(m\mathbb{N}\). Fix \(m \in N(X, L)\) such that \(\dim Y_m = \kappa(X, L)\). Let \(\mathfrak{b} = \mathfrak{b}(|L^{\otimes m}|) \subseteq \mathcal{O}_X\) be the base ideal. Blow up \(\mathfrak{b}\) and normalize to obtain a projective birational morphism: \[
u_m: X_{(m)} := \operatorname{Bl}_{\mathfrak{b}}(X)^\nu \longrightarrow X.
\] Let \(E_m\) be the exceptional divisor on the blow-up, and \(F_m\) its pullback to \(X_{(m)}\). Define: \[
M_m := u_m^* L^{\otimes m} \otimes_{\mathcal{O}_{X_{(m)}}} \mathcal{O}_{X_{(m)}}(-F_m).
\] Because \(u_m: X_{(m)} \to X\) is a birational morphism between normal varieties, Proposition 3 implies that \(u_m\) is an algebraic fiber space. By Lemma 1, \(H^0(X, L^{\otimes m}) \cong H^0(X_{(m)}, u_m^* L^{\otimes m})\). Since all sections vanish along \(F_m\) by construction of the blow-up, restriction to \(F_m\) is zero, yielding an isomorphism: \[
H^0(X_{(m)}, M_m) \cong H^0(X, L^{\otimes m}).
\] Consequently, \(M_m\) is generated by its global sections and defines a morphism \(\phi_{M_m}: X_{(m)} \to \mathbb{P} H^0(X_{(m)}, M_m)\). By Theorem 1, the Stein factorization of \(\phi_{M_m^{\otimes k}}\) stabilizes for \(k \gg 0\) to an algebraic fiber space: \[
\phi_{(m)}: X_{(m)} \longrightarrow Y_{(m)}.
\] For every \(k \ge 1\), we have \(H^0(X_{(m)}, M_m^{\otimes k}) \subseteq H^0(X_{(m)}, u_m^* L^{\otimes mk})\), inducing a dominant rational projection \(\mu_k: Y_{mk} \dashrightarrow Y_{(m)}\). Since \(X_{(m)} \to Y_{(m)}\) is an AFS, \(K(Y_{(m)})\) is algebraically closed in \(K(X_{(m)})\). The extension \(K(Y_{mk})/K(Y_{(m)})\) is algebraic and contained in \(K(X_{(m)})\), forcing: \[
K(Y_{mk}) = K(Y_{(m)}).
\] Hence \(\mu_k: Y_{mk} \dashrightarrow Y_{(m)}\) is birational for all \(k \gg 0\).
Step 2: Construction of \(X_\infty\) and \(Y_\infty\). Choose two coprime integers \(p, q \in N(X, L)\) such that \(\dim Y_p = \dim Y_q = \kappa(X, L)\) (which is possible since \(H^0(X, L) \neq 0\)). Apply Step 1 to \(M_p\) and \(M_q\), obtaining: \[
\phi_{(p)}: X_{(p)} \longrightarrow Y_{(p)}, \qquad \phi_{(q)}: X_{(q)} \longrightarrow Y_{(q)}.
\] Let \(\widetilde{U}\) be the closure of the diagonal embedding of a common dense open set \(U \subseteq X\) into \(X_{(p)} \times_X X_{(q)}\). Let \(X_\infty\) be the normalization of \(\widetilde{U}\). The projection maps \(v_p: X_\infty \to X_{(p)}\) and \(v_q: X_\infty \to X_{(q)}\) are projective, birational morphisms between normal varieties, hence algebraic fiber spaces.
Define the semiample line bundle: \[
M_{pq} := v_p^* M_p^{\otimes m_1} \otimes v_q^* M_q^{\otimes m_2}.
\] The morphism induced by \(|M_{pq}|\) factors as: \[
X_\infty \longrightarrow Y_\infty \xrightarrow{\quad w \quad} Y_{(p)} \times Y_{(q)},
\] where \(w\) is a finite morphism onto its image. Thus \(K(Y_\infty) = K(Y_{(p)}) = K(Y_{(q)})\), and \(K(Y_\infty)\) is algebraically closed in \(K(X_\infty)\). Hence \(\phi_\infty: X_\infty \to Y_\infty\) is an algebraic fiber space with \(\dim Y_\infty = \kappa(X, L)\).
For any \(k \gg 0\), the Frobenius coin problem ensures that \(k = c p^{m_1} + d q^{m_2}\) for integers \(c, d \ge 1\). The sheaf \(u_p^* M_p^{\otimes(c-1)p^{m_1}} \otimes u_q^* M_q^{\otimes(d-1)q^{m_2}}\) has a non-zero section, inducing an inclusion: \[
H^0(X_\infty, M_{pq}) \hookrightarrow H^0(X_\infty, u_\infty^* L^{\otimes k}).
\] This gives an induced dominant rational map \(v_k: Y_\infty \dashrightarrow Y_k\). Since \(\dim Y_k = \kappa(X, L) = \dim Y_\infty\) and \(K(Y_\infty)\) is algebraically closed in \(K(X_\infty)\), \(v_k\) is birational. Uniqueness follows because any two such targets are birational to \(Y_k\).


Corollary 1 (Iitaka Dimension of the Fibers) Let \(\phi_\infty: X_\infty \to Y_\infty\) be the Iitaka fibration associated with \(L\), and let \(L_\infty := u_\infty^* L\). For a very general closed point \(y \in Y_\infty\) (that is, \(y \in Y_\infty \setminus \bigcup_{i=1}^\infty F_i\) for countable proper closed subsets \(F_i \subsetneq Y_\infty\)), the fiber \(F := X_{\infty, y} = \phi_\infty^{-1}(y)\) satisfies: \[
\kappa(F, L_\infty|_F) = 0.
\]


Proof. By generic smoothness, a very general fiber \(F = X_{\infty, y}\) is smooth and connected (by Zariski’s Main Theorem), hence integral.
For all \(k \gg 0\), the rational map \(\phi_k \circ u_\infty\) is defined along \(F\) and contracts \(F\) to a single point \(\phi_k(u_\infty(F)) = \{p_k\} \subseteq Y_k\). Thus the image of the restriction map: \[
\rho_k: H^0(X_\infty, L_\infty^{\otimes k}) \longrightarrow H^0(F, L_\infty^{\otimes k}|_F)
\] has dimension \(\le 1\) for all \(k \ge 1\).
Claim: Fix a very ample line bundle \(B\) on \(Y_\infty\). 1. There exists \(m_0 > 0\) such that \(H^0(X_\infty, L_\infty^{\otimes m_0} \otimes \phi_\infty^* B^\vee) \neq 0\). 2. For any fixed \(k\) and all \(r \gg 0\), the restriction: \[
   \beta_{k, r}: H^0(X_\infty, L_\infty^{\otimes k} \otimes \phi_\infty^* B^{\otimes r}) \longrightarrow H^0(F, L_\infty^{\otimes k} \otimes \phi_\infty^* B^{\otimes r}|_F) \cong H^0(F, L_\infty^{\otimes k}|_F)
   \] is surjective.
Proof of Claim: For (1), by the proof of Theorem 2, there exists an ample line bundle \(A\) on \(Y_\infty\) such that \(\phi_\infty^* A \subseteq L_\infty^{\otimes m_0}\). Because \(A\) is ample, \(A^{\otimes m_0} \otimes B^\vee\) has a non-zero section for \(m_0 \gg 0\), yielding a non-zero section \(s \in H^0(X_\infty, L_\infty^{\otimes m_0} \otimes \phi_\infty^* B^\vee)\). For a very general fiber \(F\), \(s|_F \neq 0\).
For (2), by generic flatness, \(X_\infty \to Y_\infty\) is flat over a neighborhood of the generic point. By Grauert’s Semicontinuity Theorem, \((\phi_\infty)_* L_\infty^{\otimes k}\) is locally free near \(y\), and the fiber cohomology satisfies: \[
H^0(F, L_\infty^{\otimes k}|_F) \cong (\phi_\infty)_* L_\infty^{\otimes k} \otimes k(y).
\] Since \(B\) is very ample on \(Y_\infty\), the sheaf \((\phi_\infty)_* L_\infty^{\otimes k} \otimes B^{\otimes r}\) is generated by its global sections for \(r \gg 0\). Hence the evaluation map \(\beta_{k, r}\) is surjective.
Now, for any \(r \ge 1\), multiplication by \(s^{\otimes r}\) yields an injection: \[
H^0(X_\infty, L_\infty^{\otimes k} \otimes \phi_\infty^* B^{\otimes r}) \xrightarrow{\quad \times s^{\otimes r} \quad} H^0(X_\infty, L_\infty^{\otimes(k + r m_0)}).
\] Restricting to the fiber \(F\), we obtain a commutative diagram: \[
\begin{CD}
H^0(X_\infty, L_\infty^{\otimes k} \otimes \phi_\infty^* B^{\otimes r}) @>>> H^0(X_\infty, L_\infty^{\otimes(k + r m_0)}) \\
@VV{\beta_{k, r}}V @VV{\rho_{k + r m_0}}V \\
H^0(F, L_\infty^{\otimes k}|_F) @>{\times (s|_F)^{\otimes r}}>> H^0(F, L_\infty^{\otimes(k + r m_0)}|_F)
\end{CD}
\] Because \(F\) is integral and \(s|_F \neq 0\), the bottom map is injective. Since \(\beta_{k, r}\) is surjective, the image of the bottom map is contained in \(\operatorname{Im}(\rho_{k + r m_0})\). However, \(\operatorname{rank}(\rho_{k + r m_0}) \le 1\), which forces: \[
h^0(F, L_\infty^{\otimes k}|_F) \le 1 \quad \text{for all } k \ge 1.
\] Since \(h^0(F, L_\infty^{\otimes k}|_F) = 1\) for all sufficiently large divisible \(k\), we conclude: \[
\kappa(F, L_\infty|_F) = 0.
\]

title: Basic Algebraic Geometry
text: Overview

title: 23.2 Representation II
text:
Proposition 1 (Stabilizer of a Subspace) Let \(r: G \to \mathrm{GL}_V\) be a finite-dimensional representation of \(G\), and let \(W \subseteq V\) be a \(k\)-subspace. Then the functor: \[
\operatorname{Stab}_G(W): k\text{-}\mathbf{Alg} \longrightarrow \mathbf{Grp}, \quad R \longmapsto \{ g \in G(R) \mid r(g)(W_R) = W_R \}
\] (also denoted by \(G_W\)) is represented by an algebraic subgroup of \(G\).


Proof. Let \((e_j)_{j \in J}\) be a \(k\)-basis of \(W\), and extend it to a basis \((e_i)_{i \in I}\) of \(V\) (with \(J \subseteq I\)). Write the comodule map on the basis elements as: \[
\rho(e_j) = \sum_{i \in I} e_i \otimes f_{ij}, \quad f_{ij} \in \mathcal{O}(G).
\] For any \(R \in k\text{-}\mathbf{Alg}\) and \(g \in G(R)\), we have: \[
\begin{aligned}
g \in \operatorname{Stab}_G(W)(R) &\iff r(g)(W_R) = W_R \\
&\iff r(g)(e_j) \in W_R \quad (\forall j \in J) \\
&\iff f_{ij}(g) = 0 \quad (\forall i \in I \setminus J, \, j \in J).
\end{aligned}
\] Therefore, \(\operatorname{Stab}_G(W)\) is represented by the closed subscheme: \[
\operatorname{Stab}_G(W) = \operatorname{Spec}\big(\mathcal{O}(G) / (f_{ij} \mid i \in I \setminus J, \, j \in J)\big),
\] which is an algebraic subgroup of \(G\).


Theorem 1 (Chevalley’s Theorem) Every algebraic subgroup \(H \leqslant G\) arises as the stabilizer of a \(1\)-dimensional subspace \(L\) in a finite-dimensional representation \(V\) of \(G\).
(This is one of the main ingredients for the existence of the quotient variety \(G/H\).)


Proof. Step 1. There exists a finite-dimensional representation \(V\) of \(G\) and a subspace \(W \subseteq V\) such that \(H = \operatorname{Stab}_G(W)\).
Step 2. Let \(d := \dim_k W\), \(\tilde{V} := \bigwedge^d V\), and \(L := \bigwedge^d W \subseteq \tilde{V}\). Show that \(\operatorname{Stab}_G(L) = H\), then the theorem is proved.

Proof of Step 2: Let \((e_j)_{1 \le j \le d}\) be a \(k\)-basis of \(W\), and extend it to a \(k\)-basis \((e_i)_{1 \le i \le n}\) of \(V\). Let: \[
\omega := e_1 \wedge \dots \wedge e_d \in L = \bigwedge^d W, \quad \text{so that } L = k\omega.
\] It suffices to prove that for all \(\alpha \in \mathrm{GL}_V(R)\): \[
\alpha(W_R) = W_R \iff \left(\bigwedge^d \alpha\right)(L_R) = L_R.
\]

\((\Longrightarrow)\) Obvious.
\((\Longleftarrow)\) Notice that \(W_R = \{ v \in V_R \mid \omega \wedge v = 0 \in \bigwedge^{d+1} V_R \}\). If \(\left(\bigwedge^d \alpha\right)(L_R) = L_R\), then: \[
\left(\bigwedge^d \alpha\right)(\omega) = c \cdot \omega \quad \text{for some } c \in R^\times.
\] For any \(v \in W_R\), \(\omega \wedge v = 0\), so: \[
0 = \left(\bigwedge^{d+1} \alpha\right)(\omega \wedge v) = \left(\bigwedge^d \alpha\right)(\omega) \wedge \alpha(v) = c \cdot (\omega \wedge \alpha(v)).
\] Since \(c \in R^\times\), this implies \(\omega \wedge \alpha(v) = 0\), hence \(\alpha(v) \in W_R\) for all \(v \in W_R\). Therefore \(\alpha(W_R) = W_R\).


Proof of Step 1: Goal: Construct a finite-dimensional representation \(r: G \to \mathrm{GL}_V\) and a subspace \(W \subseteq V\) such that \(H = \operatorname{Stab}_G(W)\).
Let \(\mathfrak{a} := \ker(\mathcal{O}(G) \to \mathcal{O}(H))\) be the defining ideal of \(H\). Since \(\mathcal{O}(G)\) is noetherian, \(\mathfrak{a}\) is finitely generated as an ideal, say by \(f_1, \dots, f_r\). Set \(W_0 := \operatorname{span}_k\{f_1, \dots, f_r\} \subseteq \mathfrak{a}\).
Since \(\mathcal{O}(G)\) is a filtered union of finite-dimensional subcomodules, there exists a finite-dimensional subcomodule \(V \subseteq \mathcal{O}(G)\) containing \(W_0\). Set \(W := V \cap \mathfrak{a}\). Then \(W\) generates \(\mathfrak{a}\) as an ideal.
Let \((f_j)_{j \in J}\) be a basis of \(W\), and extend it to a basis \((f_i)_{i \in I \cup J}\) of \(V\). Since \(V\) is a subcomodule: \[
m^*(f_j) = \sum_{i \in I \cup J} f_i \otimes a_{ij}, \quad a_{ij} \in \mathcal{O}(G).
\] Then \(\operatorname{Stab}_G(W) = \operatorname{Spec}\big(\mathcal{O}(G)/\mathfrak{a}'\big)\), where \(\mathfrak{a}' := (a_{ij} \mid i \in I, \, j \in J)\). We claim that \(\mathfrak{a} = \mathfrak{a}'\):

Since \(\mathfrak{a}\) is a Hopf ideal, \(m^*(\mathfrak{a}) \subseteq \mathfrak{a} \otimes \mathcal{O}(G) + \mathcal{O}(G) \otimes \mathfrak{a}\). For each \(j \in J\), \(f_j \in W \subseteq \mathfrak{a}\), so: \[
m^*(f_j) = \sum_{i \in I \cup J} f_i \otimes a_{ij} \equiv 0 \pmod{\mathfrak{a} \otimes \mathcal{O}(G) + \mathcal{O}(G) \otimes \mathfrak{a}} \implies \sum_{i \in I} f_i \otimes a_{ij} \equiv 0 \pmod{\mathfrak{a} \otimes \mathcal{O}(G)}.
\] Since the images of \((f_i)_{i \in I}\) in \(V/W \subseteq \mathcal{O}(G)/\mathfrak{a}\) are linearly independent, we obtain \(a_{ij} \in \mathfrak{a}\) for all \(i \in I, j \in J\). Thus \(\mathfrak{a}' \subseteq \mathfrak{a}\).
Conversely, applying \((\mathrm{id} \otimes e^*) \circ m^* = \mathrm{id}\) to \(f_j\), we have: \[
f_j = \sum_{i \in I \cup J} f_i(e) a_{ij} \equiv \sum_{j' \in J} f_{j'}(e) a_{j' j} \pmod{\mathfrak{a}'}.
\] Since \(f_{j'} \in \mathfrak{a}\), we have \(f_{j'}(e) = 0\) for all \(j' \in J\). Thus \(f_j \equiv 0 \pmod{\mathfrak{a}'}\), meaning \(f_j \in \mathfrak{a}'\) for all \(j \in J\). Because \(W = \operatorname{span}_k\{f_j\}\) generates \(\mathfrak{a}\) as an ideal, this shows \(\mathfrak{a} \subseteq \mathfrak{a}'\).

Hence \(\mathfrak{a} = \mathfrak{a}'\), which implies \(H = \operatorname{Stab}_G(W)\).



Definition 1 (Character) A character of a linear algebraic group \(G\) over \(k\) is a homomorphism: \[
\chi: G \longrightarrow \mathbb{G}_m.
\] Then \(\chi\) is determined by the comorphism: \[
\chi^*: k[T, T^{-1}] \longrightarrow \mathcal{O}(G), \quad T \longmapsto a := \chi^*(T) \in \mathcal{O}(G)^\times.
\] The compatibility of \(\chi\) with group multiplication implies \(m^*(a) = a \otimes a\), corresponding to the commutative diagram: \[
\begin{CD}
k[T, T^{-1}] @>{\chi^*}>> \mathcal{O}(G) \\
@VV{T \mapsto T \otimes T}V @VV{m^*}V \\
k[T, T^{-1}] \otimes k[T, T^{-1}] @>{\chi^* \otimes \chi^*}>> \mathcal{O}(G) \otimes \mathcal{O}(G)
\end{CD}
\]


Proposition 2 (Group-like Elements and Characters)  

There are natural bijections: \[
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Grp}}(G, \mathbb{G}_m) \xleftrightarrow{\quad 1:1 \quad} \{ a \in \mathcal{O}(G)^\times \mid m^*(a) = a \otimes a \} \xleftrightarrow{\quad 1:1 \quad} \{ \text{$1$-dimensional representations of } G \}.
\] An element \(a \in \mathcal{O}(G)\) satisfying \(m^*(a) = a \otimes a\) is called a group-like element.
Group-like elements in \(\mathcal{O}(G)\) are linearly independent over \(k\).



Proof. (Proof of 2) Suppose distinct group-like elements \(a_1, \dots, a_n\) are linearly dependent. Without loss of generality, assume any \(n-1\) of them are linearly independent. We may assume \(k = \bar{k}\). Suppose there exists a non-trivial relation: \[
\sum_{i=1}^n c_i a_i = 0 \quad \text{with } c_i \in k^\times.
\] Applying \(m^*\) to this equation gives: \[
0 = m^*\left(\sum_{i=1}^n c_i a_i\right) = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i \, a_i \otimes a_i.
\] Since \(a_1 \neq a_2\), there exists \(x \in G(k)\) such that \(a_1(x) \neq a_2(x)\). Applying \((\mathrm{id} \otimes x)\) to the equation above gives: \[
\sum_{i=1}^n c_i a_i(x) a_i = 0.
\] Multiplying the original relation \(\sum c_i a_i = 0\) by \(a_1(x)\) and subtracting yields: \[
\sum_{i=2}^n c_i \big(a_i(x) - a_1(x)\big) a_i = 0.
\] Since \(c_2 \neq 0\) and \(a_2(x) - a_1(x) \neq 0\), the coefficient of \(a_2\) is non-zero. This provides a non-trivial linear relation among \(a_2, \dots, a_n\), contradicting the minimality of \(n\).


Definition 2 (Eigenspaces)  

Let \(r: G \to \mathrm{GL}_V\) be a representation of \(G\), and \(\chi: G \to \mathbb{G}_m\) a character. We say that \(G\) acts on \(V\) through \(\chi\) (\(G \circlearrowright V\) through \(\chi\)) if \(r\) factors as: \[
\begin{CD}
G @>{r}>> \mathrm{GL}(V) \\
@V{\chi}VV @AA{a \mapsto a \cdot \mathrm{id}_V}A \\
\mathbb{G}_m @= \mathbb{G}_m
\end{CD}
\] i.e., \(\rho(v) = v \otimes a(\chi)\), where \(a(\chi) := \chi^*(T) \in \mathcal{O}(G)\).
If \(W \subseteq V\) is a \(G\)-stable subspace, we say \(G \circlearrowright W\) through \(\chi\) if the restricted representation acts through \(\chi\). The largest subspace of \(V\) on which \(G\) acts through \(\chi\) is called the \(\chi\)-eigenspace (or \(\chi\)-weight space), denoted by \(V_\chi\).



Proposition 3 (Sum of Eigenspaces is Direct) Let \(r: G \to \mathrm{GL}_V\) be a representation of \(G\). If \(V = \sum_\chi V_\chi\), then the sum is direct: \[
V = \bigoplus_\chi V_\chi.
\]


Proof. Suppose \(v_1 + \dots + v_s = 0\) with \(v_i \in V_{\chi_i}\) (\(1 \le i \le s\)), where \(\chi_1, \dots, \chi_s\) are pairwise distinct characters. We want to show that \(v_i = 0\) for all \(1 \le i \le s\). Applying the comodule map \(\rho\) to the relation: \[
0 = \rho(v_1 + \dots + v_s) = v_1 \otimes a(\chi_1) + \dots + v_s \otimes a(\chi_s).
\] For any linear functional \(f \in V^\vee\), applying \(f \otimes \mathrm{id}\) yields: \[
f(v_1) a(\chi_1) + \dots + f(v_s) a(\chi_s) = 0 \quad \text{in } \mathcal{O}(G).
\] By Proposition 2(2), the distinct group-like elements \(a(\chi_i)\) are linearly independent over \(k\). Hence \(f(v_i) = 0\) for all \(f \in V^\vee\) and all \(1 \le i \le s\). Thus \(v_i = 0\) for each \(i\), showing that the sum is direct.



Definition 3 (Category of Representations) Let \(\mathbf{Rep}_k G\) denote the category of linear representations of \(G\) on finite-dimensional \(k\)-vector spaces. - It is a tensor category equipped with: \[
  \otimes: \mathbf{Rep}_k G \times \mathbf{Rep}_k G \longrightarrow \mathbf{Rep}_k G, \quad (V, W) \longmapsto V \otimes W,
  \] and identity object \(\mathbf{1} := (G \to \mathrm{GL}_1(k))\) (the trivial \(1\)-dimensional representation). - \(\mathbf{Rep}_k G\) is a neutral Tannakian category equipped with the natural forgetful functor: \[
  \omega: \mathbf{Rep}_k G \longrightarrow \mathbf{Vect}_k, \quad (G \to \mathrm{GL}_V) \longmapsto V.
  \] - A tensor functor between tensor categories is a functor \(F\) satisfying: \[
  F(V \otimes W) = F(V) \otimes F(W), \quad F(f \otimes g) = F(f) \otimes F(g), \quad F(\mathbf{1}) = \mathbf{1}.
  \] - A natural transformation of tensor functors is a natural transformation \(\eta: F \to F'\) such that: \[
  \eta_{\mathbf{1}} = \mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{1}}, \quad \eta_{X \otimes Y} = \eta_X \otimes \eta_Y \quad \text{with respect to } F(X \otimes Y) \xrightarrow{\sim} F(X) \otimes F(Y).
  \]


Definition 4 (Automorphism Functor of the Fibre Functor) Define the functor of tensor automorphisms of \(\omega\): \[
\underline{\operatorname{Aut}}^\otimes(\omega): k\text{-}\mathbf{Alg} \longrightarrow \mathbf{Grp}
\] \[
R \longmapsto \underline{\operatorname{Aut}}^\otimes(\omega)(R) := \operatorname{Aut}^\otimes(\omega_R) = \operatorname{Aut}^\otimes(\mathbf{Rep}_k G \otimes R \xrightarrow{\;\omega_R\;} \mathbf{Vect}_k \otimes R),
\] where: - \(\mathbf{Rep}_k G \otimes R\) is \(\mathbf{Rep}_k G / R\), whose objects are \(V \otimes R\) and morphisms are \(f \otimes \mathrm{id}_R\) for \(V \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathbf{Rep}_k G)\) and \(f \in \operatorname{Mor}(\mathbf{Rep}_k G)\); - \(\mathbf{Vect}_k \otimes R\) consists of \(\{ V \otimes R, \, f \otimes \mathrm{id}_R \}_{V \in \mathbf{Vect}_k, f \in \operatorname{Mor}}\).
Explicitly, an element \(\lambda \in \underline{\operatorname{Aut}}^\otimes(\omega)(R)\) is a family of \(R\)-linear isomorphisms: \[
\lambda = (\lambda_X)_{X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathbf{Rep}_k G)}, \quad \lambda_X: X \otimes R \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} X \otimes R
\] such that: 1. \(\lambda_{\mathbf{1}} = \mathrm{id}_R\); 2. \(\lambda_{X_1 \otimes X_2} = \lambda_{X_1} \otimes_R \lambda_{X_2}\); 3. For every morphism \(f: X \to Y\) in \(\mathbf{Rep}_k G\), the diagram commutes: \[
   \begin{CD}
   X \otimes R @>{\lambda_X}>> X \otimes R \\
   @V{f \otimes \mathrm{id}}VV @VV{f \otimes \mathrm{id}}V \\
   Y \otimes R @>{\lambda_Y}>> Y \otimes R
   \end{CD}
   \]
For any \(k\)-algebra homomorphism \(R \to R'\), the induced map: \[
\underline{\operatorname{Aut}}^\otimes(\omega)(R) \longrightarrow \underline{\operatorname{Aut}}^\otimes(\omega)(R'), \quad (\lambda_X) \longmapsto (\lambda_X \otimes_R R')
\] makes \(\underline{\operatorname{Aut}}^\otimes(\omega)\) into a group functor.


Theorem 2 (Tannakian Reconstruction of \(G\)) The natural morphism: \[
G \longrightarrow \underline{\operatorname{Aut}}^\otimes(\omega), \quad G(R) \longrightarrow \underline{\operatorname{Aut}}^\otimes(\omega)(R), \quad g \longmapsto (\rho_g \otimes R)
\] is an isomorphism of group functors.


Proof. It suffices to prove that for all \(R \in k\text{-}\mathbf{Alg}\), \(G(R) \xrightarrow{\sim} \underline{\operatorname{Aut}}^\otimes(\omega)(R)\) is a bijection.
Step 1. Extension to infinite-dimensional representations: Let \(r: G \to \mathrm{GL}_V\) be a representation with \(\dim V = \infty\). Write \(V = \bigcup_i V_i\) as the union of its finite-dimensional subcomodules. For any two finite-dimensional subcomodules \(V_i, V_j \subseteq V\), the intersection \(V_i \cap V_j\) is a finite-dimensional subcomodule, and by functoriality: \[
\begin{CD}
(V_i \cap V_j) \otimes R @>{\lambda_{V_i \cap V_j}}>> (V_i \cap V_j) \otimes R \\
@VVV @VVV \\
V_i \otimes R @>{\lambda_{V_i}}>> V_i \otimes R
\end{CD}
\] Passing to the colimit yields a unique \(R\)-linear isomorphism \(\lambda_V: V \otimes R \xrightarrow{\sim} V \otimes R\) such that \(\lambda_V|_{V_i \otimes R} = \lambda_{V_i}\).
Step 2. The regular representation: For \(R \in k\text{-}\mathbf{Alg}\), let \(X_0 := \mathcal{O}(G)\) be the regular representation of \(G\).
Claim: \(\lambda_{X_0}: \mathcal{O}(G) \otimes R \to \mathcal{O}(G) \otimes R\) equals \(r_0(g)\) for some unique \(g \in G(R) = \operatorname{Hom}_{k\text{-alg}}(\mathcal{O}(G), R)\).
(Proof of Claim: Since \(\lambda\) commutes with all comodule endomorphisms and preserves the algebra structure via tensor compatibility, \(\lambda_{X_0}\) is an algebra automorphism commuting with the right \(G\)-action, hence is given by left translation by some element \(g \in G(R)\)).
Step 3. Surjectivity: The regular representation settles the case \(R = \mathcal{O}(G)\). For any \((V, r) \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathbf{Rep}_k G)\), \(V \hookrightarrow \mathcal{O}(G)^n\) for some \(n\) as a \(G\)-representation. Then: \[
\begin{CD}
V \otimes R @>>> \mathcal{O}(G)^n \otimes R \\
@V{\lambda_V}VV @VV{\lambda_{X_0^n} = (r_0(g), \dots, r_0(g))}V \\
V \otimes R @>>> \mathcal{O}(G)^n \otimes R
\end{CD}
\] By functoriality with respect to the embedding \(V \hookrightarrow \mathcal{O}(G)^n\), we deduce \(\lambda_V = r(g)\) for all \(V\). Thus the map is surjective.
Step 4. Injectivity: The element \(g \in G(R)\) is uniquely determined by any faithful representation: if \(V\) is faithful, i.e., \(G \hookrightarrow \mathrm{GL}_V\), then \(G(R) \hookrightarrow \mathrm{GL}_V(R)\) for all \(R\), via \(g \mapsto \lambda_V\). (Since every representation \(W\) is obtained from \(V\) via tensor products, duals, direct sums, and subquotients, functoriality forces \(\lambda_W = r(g)\)).



Remark 1 (Equivalence of Categories via Tannakian Duality). (Reference: [Milne, §4.7])
Let \((\mathcal{C}, \otimes)\) be a neutral Tannakian category over \(k\) with a \(k\)-valued fibre functor \(\omega: \mathcal{C} \to \mathbf{Vect}_k\). Then: 1. \(\underline{\operatorname{Aut}}^\otimes(\omega): k\text{-}\mathbf{Alg} \to \mathbf{Grp}\) is representable by an affine group scheme \(G\) over \(k\). 2. The functor \(\mathcal{C} \to \mathbf{Rep}_k(G)\) defined by \(\omega\) is an equivalence of tensor categories.


Remark 2 (Neutral Tannakian Categories). A tuple \((\mathcal{C}, \otimes, \Phi, \Psi)\) is a neutral Tannakian category over \(k\) if:

\(\mathcal{C}\) is a \(k\)-linear abelian category (a subabelian category of \(\mathbf{Vect}_k\)).
\(\otimes: \mathcal{C} \times \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{C}\) is a \(k\)-bilinear functor.
Associativity and symmetry constraints: \[
\Phi_{X,Y,Z}: X \otimes (Y \otimes Z) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} (X \otimes Y) \otimes Z, \quad \Psi_{X,Y}: X \otimes Y \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} Y \otimes X,
\] which imply the existence of an identity object \(\mathbf{1}\) such that \(\mathcal{C} \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathcal{C}\), \(X \mapsto \mathbf{1} \otimes X\).
Existence of duals: for every \(X \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\), there exists \(X^\vee \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\) and an evaluation morphism: \[
\operatorname{ev}: X^\vee \otimes X \longrightarrow \mathbf{1}
\] inducing an isomorphism: \[
\operatorname{Hom}_\mathcal{C}(T, X^\vee) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \operatorname{Hom}_\mathcal{C}(T \otimes X, \mathbf{1}), \quad \alpha \longmapsto \operatorname{ev} \circ (\alpha \otimes \mathrm{id}_X).
\]
There exists a \(k\)-valued fibre functor \(\omega: (\mathcal{C}, \otimes) \to \mathbf{Vect}_k\), which is an exact, faithful \(k\)-linear functor preserving tensor products.

title: 23.4 Quotients
text:
Theorem 1 (Universal Property of Quotients) Let \(k\) be a field, and let \(G, G'\) be linear algebraic groups over \(k\).

A homomorphism \(p: G \to Q\) of linear algebraic groups is a quotient map if and only if it is faithfully flat of finite presentation (fppf). Equivalently, at the level of coordinate Hopf algebras, \(A = \mathcal{O}(Q) \hookrightarrow B = \mathcal{O}(G)\) is an injective Hopf subalgebra map such that \(B\) is faithfully flat over \(A\).
Let \(p: G \to Q\) be a quotient map of linear algebraic groups, and let \(N = \ker p\). Every homomorphism \(\varphi: G \to G'\) such that \(\ker \varphi \supseteq \ker p\) factors uniquely through \(p\): \[
\begin{CD}
G @>{p}>> Q \\
@V{\varphi}VV @VV{\exists!\,\bar{\varphi}}V \\
G' @= G'
\end{CD}
\]



Proof. To prove (2), consider the kernel pair diagram (coequalizer): \[
G \times_Q G \;\rightrightarrows\; G \xrightarrow{\;\varphi\;} G'.
\] We check this condition on points: for every \(R \in \mathbf{Alg}_{/k}\), \[
\begin{CD}
G(R) \times_{Q(R)} G(R) @>{p_1, p_2}>> G(R) @>{\varphi}>> G'(R) \\
@V{p \times p}VV @VV{p}V @VV{\varphi}V \\
Q(R) \times Q(R) @>>> Q(R) @>>> G'(R)
\end{CD}
\] Since \(\ker p \subseteq \ker \varphi\), for every \(R \in \mathbf{Alg}_{/k}\) we have \(\ker p(R) \subseteq \ker \varphi(R)\). For any pair \((g_1, g_2) \in G(R) \times_{Q(R)} G(R)\), we have \(p(g_1) = p(g_2)\), so: \[
g_1 g_2^{-1} \in \ker p(R) \subseteq \ker \varphi(R) \implies \varphi(g_1 g_2^{-1}) = 1 \implies \varphi(g_1) = \varphi(g_2).
\] Hence the two compositions \(G \times_Q G \rightrightarrows G \xrightarrow{\varphi} G'\) coincide.
At the level of coordinate rings, let \(B = \mathcal{O}(G)\) and \(A = \mathcal{O}(Q)\). Since \(B\) is faithfully flat over \(A\), the Amitsur complex \[
A \longrightarrow B \;\rightrightarrows\; B \otimes_A B
\] is exact (i.e., \(A = \{ b \in B \mid b \otimes 1 = 1 \otimes b \}\)). The equality of the two pullbacks on \(B \otimes_A B\) ensures that the comorphism \(\varphi^\sharp: \mathcal{O}(G') \to B\) has image landing in the equalizer \(A = \mathcal{O}(Q)\): \[
\begin{CD}
B \otimes B @<<< B @<{\varphi^\sharp}<< \mathcal{O}(G') \\
@AAA @AAA @| \\
B \otimes_A B @<<< A @<<{\exists!\,\bar{\varphi}^\sharp}< \mathcal{O}(G')
\end{CD}
\] Thus, there exists a unique \(k\)-algebra homomorphism \(\bar{\varphi}^\sharp: \mathcal{O}(G') \to \mathcal{O}(Q)\), inducing the unique group homomorphism \(\bar{\varphi}: Q \to G'\).


Definition 1 Let \(G\) be a linear algebraic group and \(N \unlhd G\) a normal closed subgroup. If there exists a quotient map \(q: G \to Q\) such that \(\ker q = N\), then \(Q\) is called the quotient group of \(G\) by \(N\), denoted \(G/N\). By Theorem 1, \(Q\) is unique up to unique isomorphism.


Definition 2 Let \(G\) be a linear algebraic group, and let \(r: G \to \mathrm{GL}_V\) be a representation of \(G\) on a finite-dimensional \(k\)-vector space \(V\). The subspace of invariants (or fixed points) is defined by: \[
V^G := \big\{ v \in V \;\big|\; g \cdot v_R = v_R \quad \forall R \in \mathbf{Alg}_{/k}, \, \forall g \in G(R) \big\},
\] where \(v_R = v \otimes 1 \in V \otimes_k R\).


Lemma 1 For every \(k\)-algebra \(R \in \mathbf{Alg}_{/k}\), the formation of invariants commutes with base change: \[
V^G \otimes_k R = \big\{ v' \in V \otimes_k R \;\big|\; g \cdot v'_S = v'_S \quad \forall S \in \mathbf{Alg}_{/R}, \, \forall g \in G(S) \big\}.
\]


Proof. The inclusion \(\mathrm{LHS} \subseteq \mathrm{RHS}\) is clear. Conversely, choose a \(k\)-basis \(\{e_i\}_{i \in I}\) of \(R\). Any element \(v' \in V \otimes_k R\) can be uniquely written as a finite sum: \[
v' = \sum_{i \in I} v_i \otimes e_i, \quad v_i \in V.
\] Suppose \(v' \in \mathrm{RHS}\). We want to show that \(v_i \in V^G\) for each \(i \in I\). For any \(S \in \mathbf{Alg}_{/k}\) and any \(g \in G(S)\), consider the canonical base extension \(S \to S \otimes_k R\) given by \(a \mapsto a \otimes 1\). This induces a map \(G(S) \to G(S \otimes_k R)\), sending \(g \mapsto g'\). Viewing \(S \otimes_k R\) as an \(R\)-algebra, the assumption on \(v'\) implies: \[
g' \cdot v'_{S \otimes_k R} = v'_{S \otimes_k R} \quad \text{in } V \otimes_k S \otimes_k R.
\] Expanding in the basis \(\{e_i\}\): \[
\sum_{i \in I} \big( g \cdot (v_i)_S \big) \otimes e_i = \sum_{i \in I} (v_i)_S \otimes e_i \quad \text{in } (V \otimes_k S) \otimes_k R.
\] Since the elements \(e_i\) are linearly independent over \(k\), we deduce that for each \(i \in I\): \[
g \cdot (v_i)_S = (v_i)_S \quad \text{in } V \otimes_k S.
\] Because this holds for all \(S\) and all \(g \in G(S)\), it follows that \(v_i \in V^G\) for all \(i \in I\). Thus \(v' \in V^G \otimes_k R\).


Lemma 2 Let \(G\) be a linear algebraic group, \(N \unlhd G\) a normal subgroup, and \((V, r) \in \mathbf{Rep}_k(G)\). Then the invariant subspace \(V^N\) is stable under \(G\) (i.e., \(g \cdot V^N = V^N\) for all \(g \in G\)).


Proof. Let \(R \in \mathbf{Alg}_{/k}\) and \(v \in V^N \otimes_k R\). For any \(R\)-algebra \(R'\) and any \(g \in G(R')\), we must show that: \[
(g \cdot v_R)_{R'} \in V^N \otimes_k R'.
\] By Lemma 1, it suffices to show that for any \(n' \in N(R')\): \[
n' \cdot (g \cdot v_R)_{R'} = (g \cdot v_R)_{R'}.
\] Writing \(g'\) for the image of \(g\) in \(G(R')\), since \(N \unlhd G\) is normal, \(g'^{-1} n' g' \in N(R')\). Since \(v \in V^N \otimes_k R\), \((g'^{-1} n' g') \cdot v_{R'} = v_{R'}\). Therefore: \[
n' \cdot (g' \cdot v_{R'}) = g' \cdot \big( (g'^{-1} n' g') \cdot v_{R'} \big) = g' \cdot v_{R'} = (g \cdot v_R)_{R'}.
\] Thus \((g \cdot v_R) \in V^N \otimes_k R\), so \(V^N\) is stable under \(G\).


Proposition 1 Let \(k = \bar{k}\), let \(G\) be a linear algebraic group, and let \(H \unlhd G\) be a closed normal subgroup. Then there exists a representation \((V, r) \in \mathbf{Rep}_k(G)\) and a \(1\)-dimensional subspace \(L \subseteq V\) such that: \[
H = \operatorname{Stab}_G(L) \quad \text{and } H \text{ acts trivially on } L.
\]

To prove Proposition 1, we establish two preliminary lemmas.

Lemma 3 (Lemma B) Let \(G\) be a linear algebraic group over \(k\), and let \((V, r) \in \mathbf{Rep}_k(G)\). If \(V = \sum_{i \in I} S_i\) is a sum of simple subrepresentations, then for every subrepresentation \(W \subseteq V\), there exists a subset \(J \subseteq I\) such that: \[
V = W \oplus \bigoplus_{j \in J} S_j.
\] In particular, \(V\) is a direct sum of simple representations, and every subrepresentation \(W\) is a direct summand.


Lemma 4 (Lemma A) Let \(k = \bar{k}\), let \(G\) be a linear algebraic group, and let \(H \unlhd G\) be a closed normal subgroup. If a character \(\chi \in X^*(H)\) occurs in a representation \((V, r)\) of \(G\) (meaning there is an \(H\)-stable line \(L \subseteq V\) on which \(H\) acts via \(\chi\)), then there exists an integer \(m \ge 1\) such that \(-m\chi\) occurs in a representation (possibly different) of \(G\).


Proof. Step 1: Reduction using Lemma B. Suppose \(\chi\) occurs on a line \(L \subseteq V\). It suffices to find a representation \((W, r_W) \in \mathbf{Rep}_k(G)\) containing a \(1\)-dimensional subspace \(L_1 \subseteq W\) such that:

\(H \le \operatorname{Stab}_G(L_1)\) with \(H\) acting on \(L_1\) via \(m\chi\);
\(L_1\) is a direct summand of \(W\) as a representation of \(H\).

If such a \(W\) exists, then in the dual representation \(W^\vee \in \mathbf{Rep}_k(G)\), the dual line \(L_1^\vee\) is an \(H\)-subrepresentation on which \(H\) acts via \(-m\chi\).
Step 2: Case 1 — \(G(k)\) is Zariski dense in \(G\). This occurs, for example, when \(G\) is smooth or reduced over an algebraically closed field. Let \(W \subseteq V\) be the sum of all \(1\)-dimensional \(H\)-stable subspaces of \(V\). We claim that \(W\) is \(G\)-stable: Since \(H \unlhd G\), for any \(g \in G(k)\) and \(h \in H(k)\), \(g^{-1} h g \in H(k)\). For any \(v \in L_\chi \subseteq W\), \[
h \cdot (g \cdot v) = g \cdot (g^{-1} h g \cdot v) = g \cdot \big(\chi(g^{-1} h g) v\big) = \chi(g^{-1} h g) (g \cdot v).
\] Hence \(g \cdot v\) is an eigenvector for \(H\), so \(g \cdot W \subseteq W\). Since \(G(k)\) is Zariski dense in \(G\), \(\operatorname{Stab}_G(W) = G\), so \((W, r|_W) \in \mathbf{Rep}_k(G)\). By definition, \(W\) is a sum of \(1\)-dimensional (hence simple) \(H\)-representations. By Lemma 3 (Lemma B), \(L\) is a direct summand of \(W\) as an \(H\)-representation. Thus \(L^\vee \subseteq W^\vee\) is a subrepresentation with character \(-\chi\) (here \(m = 1\)).
Step 3: Case 2 — General case (characteristic \(p > 0\)). If \(\operatorname{char} k = 0\), \(G\) is always smooth, so Case 1 applies. Assume \(\operatorname{char} k = p > 0\). For a sufficiently large integer \(r \ge 1\), let \(F_G^r: G \to G^{(p^r)}\) be the \(r\)-th Frobenius morphism, and let \(N = \ker F_G^r\) be the Frobenius kernel. Consider the representation \(S^{p^r}(V) \in \mathbf{Rep}_k(G)\) and the line \(L^{\otimes p^r} \subseteq S^{p^r}(V)\). Choose a basis \(\{e_1, \dots, e_n\}\) of \(V\) such that \(L = k e_1\). Under \(r: G \to \mathrm{GL}_n\), the elements \(n \in N(R)\) satisfy \(r(n) = (a_{ij})\) with \(a_{ij}^{p^r} = \delta_{ij}\). In the symmetric power \(S^{p^r}(V)\), \[
n \cdot e_1^{\otimes p^r} = \left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_{i1} e_i\right)^{\!\![p^r]} = \sum_{i=1}^n a_{i1}^{p^r} e_i^{[p^r]} = e_1^{[p^r]}.
\] Therefore, \(L^{\otimes p^r} \subseteq \big(S^{p^r}(V)\big)^N\). By Lemma 2, \(V_1 := \big(S^{p^r}(V)\big)^N\) is a subrepresentation of \(G\). Since \(N\) acts trivially on \(V_1\), the action of \(G\) on \(V_1\) factors through the quotient \(Z := G/N \cong \operatorname{Im}(F_G^r)\). For \(r \gg 0\), \(Z\) is reduced, and since \(k = \bar{k}\), \(Z(k)\) is Zariski dense in \(Z\). Applying Case 1 to \(Z\), there exists a subrepresentation \(W \subseteq V_1\) containing a line \(L_1\) on which \(H\) acts via \(\chi^{p^r}\), and \(L_1\) is a direct summand of \(W\). Thus the dual representation yields the character \(-p^r \chi\) (with \(m = p^r\)).


Proof. (Proof of Proposition 1) By Chevalley’s theorem (Theorem 5.2.1), there exists a representation \((V, r_V) \in \mathbf{Rep}_k(G)\) and a \(1\)-dimensional subspace \(L \subseteq V\) such that \(H = \operatorname{Stab}_G(L)\). The subgroup \(H\) acts on \(L\) via a character \(\chi: H \to \mathrm{GL}(L) \cong \mathbb{G}_m\). If \(\chi = 1\) is trivial, the statement is already satisfied. If \(\chi \ne 1\), by Lemma 4 (Lemma A), there exists a representation \((W, r_W) \in \mathbf{Rep}_k(G)\) and a line \(L' \subseteq W\) such that \(H \le \operatorname{Stab}_G(L')\) and \(H\) acts on \(L'\) via \(-m\chi\) for some \(m \ge 1\). Consider the representation \[
\widetilde{V} := V^{\otimes m} \otimes_k W \in \mathbf{Rep}_k(G),
\] and the \(1\)-dimensional subspace \(\widetilde{L} := L^{\otimes m} \otimes_k L' \subseteq \widetilde{V}\). The character by which \(H\) acts on \(\widetilde{L}\) is: \[
\chi^m \cdot (-m\chi) = 1 \quad (\text{trivial}).
\] Furthermore, \(\operatorname{Stab}_G(\widetilde{L}) \ge \operatorname{Stab}_G(L) \cap \operatorname{Stab}_G(L') \ge H\). To ensure the stabilizer is exactly \(H\), we take \(V' = V \oplus \widetilde{V}\) and \(L'' = \widetilde{L}\) inside a suitable direct sum, or simply replace \(V\) with \(V^{\oplus m} \oplus \widetilde{V}\) so that \(\operatorname{Stab}_G(\widetilde{L}) = H\).


Definition 3 (Weil Restriction of Scalars) Let \(A\) be a finite \(k\)-algebra, and let \(X\) be a quasi-projective scheme over \(A\). The Weil restriction of scalars of \(X\) from \(A\) to \(k\), denoted \(\operatorname{Res}_{A/k} X\), is the functor: \[
\operatorname{Res}_{A/k} X: \mathbf{Alg}_{/k} \longrightarrow \mathbf{Sets}, \quad R \longmapsto X(A \otimes_k R).
\] The functor \(\operatorname{Res}_{A/k}: \mathbf{Sch}_{/A} \to \mathbf{Sch}_{/k}\) is the right adjoint to base change: \[
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Sch}_{/A}}(Y_A, X) \cong \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Sch}_{/k}}(Y, \operatorname{Res}_{A/k} X).
\]


Proposition 2 Let \(A\) be a finite \(k\)-algebra.

If \(G\) is an algebraic group over \(A\), then \(\operatorname{Res}_{A/k} G\) is an algebraic group over \(k\).
If \(G\) is a linear algebraic group over \(A\), then \(\operatorname{Res}_{A/k} G\) is a linear algebraic group over \(k\).



Example 1  

For any \(k\)-algebraic group \(G\), the unit of the adjunction gives a canonical homomorphism: \[
i_G: G \longrightarrow \operatorname{Res}_{A/k}(G_A),
\] which on \(R\)-points is given by: \[
i_G(R): G(R) \longrightarrow G_A(A \otimes_k R) = G(A \otimes_k R),
\] induced by the natural \(k\)-algebra homomorphism \(R \to A \otimes_k R\), \(r \mapsto 1 \otimes r\).
If \(f: G_A \to H\) is a homomorphism of \(A\)-algebraic groups, the adjunction gives: \[
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Grp}/A}(G_A, H) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Grp}/k}\big(G, \operatorname{Res}_{A/k} H\big), \quad f \longmapsto \operatorname{Res}_{A/k}(f) \circ i_G.
\]



Theorem 2 (Existence of Quotients) Every closed normal subgroup \(H\) of a linear algebraic group \(G\) over a field \(k\) is the kernel of a quotient map \(p: G \to Q\), where \(Q\) is a linear algebraic group.


Proof. Case 1: \(k = \bar{k}\). By Proposition 1, there exists a representation \((V, r_V) \in \mathbf{Rep}_k(G)\) and a line \(L \subseteq V\) such that \(\operatorname{Stab}_G(L) = H\) and \(H\) acts trivially on \(L\). Since \(H\) acts trivially on \(L\), we have \(L \subseteq V^H\). By Lemma 2, \(V^H\) is a \(G\)-subrepresentation of \(V\). Let \(\alpha: G \to \mathrm{GL}(V^H)\) be the restriction of \(r_V\) to \(V^H\). Since \(H\) acts trivially on \(V^H\), we have \(H \le \ker \alpha\). On the other hand, since \(L \subseteq V^H\), any \(g \in \ker \alpha\) fixes \(L\) pointwise, which means: \[
\ker \alpha \le \operatorname{Stab}_G(L) = H.
\] Thus \(\ker \alpha = H\). Setting \(Q := \operatorname{Im}(\alpha) \subseteq \mathrm{GL}(V^H)\) (the scheme-theoretic image), the map \(p: G \to Q\) is faithfully flat (fppf), and \(\ker p = H\). Thus \(Q \cong G/H\) is a linear algebraic group.
Case 2: Arbitrary ground field \(k\). Over \(\bar{k}\), by Case 1 there exists a quotient \(G_{\bar{k}} \to Q_{\bar{k}}\) with kernel \(H_{\bar{k}}\), and choosing a faithful representation of \(Q_{\bar{k}}\) yields a representation \(r: G_{\bar{k}} \to \mathrm{GL}_{n,\bar{k}}\) such that \(\ker r = H_{\bar{k}}\). Since \(G\) and \(H\) are defined over \(k\), the representation \(r\) is defined over some finite field extension \(k'/k\): \[
r': G_{k'} \longrightarrow \mathrm{GL}(V') \quad \text{such that} \quad \ker r' = H_{k'},
\] where \(V'\) is a finite-dimensional \(k'\)-vector space. Applying Weil restriction \(\operatorname{Res}_{k'/k}\) to \(r'\) and precomposing with the canonical map \(i_G: G \to \operatorname{Res}_{k'/k} G_{k'}\), we obtain a homomorphism of linear algebraic groups over \(k\): \[
\alpha: G \xrightarrow{\;i_G\;} \operatorname{Res}_{k'/k}(G_{k'}) \xrightarrow{\;\operatorname{Res}_{k'/k}(r')\;} \operatorname{Res}_{k'/k}\big(\mathrm{GL}(V')\big).
\] For every \(k\)-algebra \(R \in \mathbf{Alg}_{/k}\), the map on \(R\)-points is: \[
\alpha(R): G(R) \longrightarrow G(R \otimes_k k') \xrightarrow{\;r'(R \otimes_k k')\;} \mathrm{GL}_{V'}(R \otimes_k k').
\] Its kernel is: \[
\ker \alpha(R) = G(R) \cap \ker\big(r'(R \otimes_k k')\big) = G(R) \cap H(R \otimes_k k') = H(R).
\] Hence \(\ker \alpha = H\). Defining \(Q := \operatorname{Im} \alpha\) as the scheme-theoretic image of \(\alpha\) inside \(\operatorname{Res}_{k'/k}(\mathrm{GL}(V'))\), we obtain a quotient map \(p: G \to Q\) with \(\ker p = H\). By Proposition 2, \(\operatorname{Res}_{k'/k}(\mathrm{GL}(V'))\) is a linear algebraic group, so its closed subgroup \(Q\) is also a linear algebraic group.


Corollary 1  

For every closed normal subgroup \(H \unlhd G\), there exists a representation \((V, r)\) of \(G\) such that \(H = \ker r\).
Let \(0 \to H \to G \xrightarrow{\pi} Q \to 0\) be a sequence of linear algebraic groups. The following are equivalent:

It is an exact sequence of group sheaves in the fppf topology on \((\mathbf{Sch}_{/k})_{\text{fppf}}\);
\(Q\) is the quotient group \(G/H\);
\(\pi\) is fppf and \(H = \ker \pi\).




Proof. 

By Theorem 2, \(Q = G/H\) is a linear algebraic group. Choosing a faithful representation \(\rho: Q \hookrightarrow \mathrm{GL}_V\), the composite \(r = \rho \circ \pi: G \to \mathrm{GL}_V\) satisfies \(\ker r = \ker \pi = H\).
The equivalence (b) \(\iff\) (c) is the definition of a quotient map.


\(\implies\) (c): Since \(G \to Q\) is an fppf epimorphism, \(Q\) is an \(H\)-torsor over \(G\), which implies \(\pi\) is fppf and \(H = \ker \pi\).
\(\implies\) (a): For every \(R \in \mathbf{Alg}_{/k}\) and every \(\bar{g} \in Q(R)\), the fiber product \(R' := R \times_Q G\) is an fppf \(R\)-algebra, and the image of \(\bar{g}\) in \(Q(R')\) lifts to \(G(R')\). Hence \(G \to Q\) is an epimorphism of fppf sheaves. Exactness at \(G\) follows from \(H = \ker \pi\).



Proposition 3  

Let \(f: X \to Y\) be a \(G\)-equivariant morphism of \(k\)-schemes of finite type. Then the image \(f(X)\) is locally closed in \(Y\). If \(X\) is reduced, \(f\) factors as: \[
X \xrightarrow{\;\text{fppf}\;} f(X) \hookrightarrow Y.
\]
In particular, for any action \(G \times X \to X\) and any \(k\)-point \(x \in X(k)\), the orbit map induces a morphism: \[
G \xrightarrow{\;\text{fppf}\;} G \cdot x \hookrightarrow X.
\] If \(G\) is reduced, the orbit \(G \cdot x\) is locally closed and stable under \(G\). The sequence \[
0 \longrightarrow G_x \longrightarrow G \longrightarrow G \cdot x \longrightarrow 0
\] is an exact sequence of fppf sheaves. If \(G\) is smooth, then \(G \cdot x\) is smooth.



Theorem 3 (Quotient by an Arbitrary Subgroup) Let \(G\) be a smooth linear algebraic group, and let \(H \le G\) be any closed subgroup (not necessarily normal). Then the fppf quotient sheaf \(G/H\) is representable by a smooth quasi-projective scheme over \(k\).


Proof. By Chevalley’s theorem (Theorem 5.2.1), there exists a representation \((V, r) \in \mathbf{Rep}_k(G)\) and a \(1\)-dimensional subspace \(L \subseteq V\) such that: \[
H = \operatorname{Stab}_G(L).
\] Consider the projective space \(\mathbb{P}(V)\) and the point \(x := [L] \in \mathbb{P}(V)(k)\). The representation \(r\) induces a regular algebraic action \(G \times \mathbb{P}(V) \to \mathbb{P}(V)\). The stabilizer scheme of the point \(x\) is: \[
G_x = \operatorname{Stab}_G(L) = H.
\] By Proposition 3, the orbit \(G \cdot x \subseteq \mathbb{P}(V)\) is a locally closed subscheme of \(\mathbb{P}(V)\) (hence a quasi-projective variety), and the orbit map \[
G \longrightarrow G \cdot x
\] is faithfully flat (fppf). Consequently, the sequence of fppf sheaves \[
0 \longrightarrow H \longrightarrow G \longrightarrow G \cdot x \longrightarrow 0
\] is exact. Therefore, the orbit \(G \cdot x\) represents the fppf quotient sheaf \(G/H\). Since \(G\) is smooth, the homogeneous space \(G/H \cong G \cdot x\) is also smooth.

title: 23.3 Jordan Decomposition
text:
Motivation (Matrix case): Let \(x \in \mathrm{GL}_n(\bar{k})\). The Jordan normal form of \(x\) is given by: \[
x = s^{-1} \begin{pmatrix} B_{a_1}^{n_1} & & \\ & \ddots & \\ & & B_{a_r}^{n_r} \end{pmatrix} s,
\] where each \(B_{a_i}^{n_i}\) is a Jordan block of size \(n_i \times n_i\) with eigenvalue \(a_i\): \[
B_{a_i}^{n_i} = \begin{pmatrix}
a_i & 1 & & \\
& a_i & \ddots & \\
& & \ddots & 1 \\
& & & a_i
\end{pmatrix}.
\] Define: \[
x_s := s^{-1} \begin{pmatrix} a_1 I_{n_1} & & \\ & \ddots & \\ & & a_r I_{n_r} \end{pmatrix} s \in \mathrm{GL}_n(\bar{k}) \quad (\text{semisimple element}),
\] \[
x_u := s^{-1} \begin{pmatrix} a_1^{-1} B_{a_1}^{n_1} & & \\ & \ddots & \\ & & a_r^{-1} B_{a_r}^{n_r} \end{pmatrix} s \in \mathrm{GL}_n(\bar{k}) \quad (\text{unipotent element}).
\] Then: \[
x = x_s x_u = x_u x_s
\] is called the Jordan decomposition of \(x\).
Generalization:

Replace the algebraically closed field \(\bar{k}\) with an arbitrary perfect field \(k\).
Replace \(\mathrm{GL}_n\) with an arbitrary linear algebraic group \(G\). <<<<<<< HEAD

======= ::: >>>>>>> 2fa6ddb (awd)

Definition 1 Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional vector space over \(k\), and let \(\alpha \in \mathrm{GL}_V(k) = \mathrm{GL}_n(k)\). Let \(P_\alpha(T) := \det(T \cdot \mathrm{id} - \alpha) \in k[T]\) be the characteristic polynomial of \(\alpha\).

The eigenvalues of \(\alpha\) lie in \(k\) if \(P_\alpha(T)\) splits over \(k\): \[
P_\alpha(T) = (T - a_1)^{m_1} \cdots (T - a_r)^{m_r}, \quad a_i \in k.
\]
For each eigenvalue \(a \in k\) of \(\alpha\), the primary space (generalized eigenspace) is defined by: \[
V^{(a)} := \{ v \in V \mid (\alpha - a \cdot \mathrm{id})^N v = 0 \text{ for some } N \ge 1 \}.
\] Then \(V = \bigoplus_{i=1}^r V^{(a_i)}\), and the usual Jordan decomposition works on each subspace.
An element \(\alpha\) is semisimple if \(\alpha_{\bar{k}} \in \operatorname{End}_{\bar{k}}(V_{\bar{k}})\) is diagonalizable.
An element \(\alpha\) is unipotent if there exists an integer \(N \ge 1\) such that \((\alpha - \mathrm{id})^N = 0\).



Theorem 1 Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional vector space over a perfect field \(k\). Let \(\alpha \in \operatorname{Aut}_k(V) = \mathrm{GL}_V(k)\). Then there exist unique elements \(\alpha_s, \alpha_u \in \operatorname{Aut}_k(V)\) such that:

\(\alpha = \alpha_s \alpha_u = \alpha_u \alpha_s\) (equivalently, \(\alpha = \alpha_s + \alpha_s(\alpha_u - \mathrm{id})\), where \(\alpha_s(\alpha_u - \mathrm{id})\) is nilpotent);
\(\alpha_s\) is semisimple, and \(\alpha_u\) is unipotent.

In this case, \(\alpha_s\) and \(\alpha_u\) are polynomials in \(\alpha\), i.e., \(\alpha_s, \alpha_u \in k[\alpha]\).


Proof. Case 1: All eigenvalues of \(\alpha\) lie in \(k\).
The characteristic polynomial splits over \(k\): \[
P_\alpha(T) = \prod_{i=1}^r (T - a_i)^{m_i}, \quad a_i \in k.
\] Then \(V = \bigoplus_{i=1}^r V^{(a_i)}\), where \(V^{(a_i)} = \ker(\alpha - a_i \cdot \mathrm{id})^{m_i}\).
Define \(\alpha_s \in \operatorname{Aut}_k(V)\) by: \[
\alpha_s\big|_{V^{(a_i)}} := a_i \cdot \mathrm{id}_{V^{(a_i)}}.
\] Define \(\alpha_u := \alpha \alpha_s^{-1}\). For each \(v_i \in V^{(a_i)}\), we have: \[
(\alpha_u - \mathrm{id})^{m_i}(v_i) = (a_i^{-1} \alpha - \mathrm{id})^{m_i}(v_i) = a_i^{-m_i} (\alpha - a_i \cdot \mathrm{id})^{m_i}(v_i) = 0.
\] Hence \(\alpha_u\) is unipotent.
To find a polynomial \(Q(T) \in k[T]\) such that \(Q(\alpha) = \alpha_s\), it suffices to require: \[
\big(Q(\alpha) - a_i \cdot \mathrm{id}\big)\big|_{V^{(a_i)}} = 0 \quad \text{for all } 1 \le i \le r,
\] which is guaranteed if: \[
(T - a_i)^{m_i} \mid \big(Q(T) - a_i\big), \quad \text{i.e., } Q(T) \equiv a_i \pmod{(T - a_i)^{m_i}}.
\] By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, such a polynomial \(Q(T)\) exists.
Similarly, there exists a polynomial \(\widetilde{Q}(T) \in k[T]\) such that \(\widetilde{Q}(\alpha) = \alpha_s^{-1}\). Then: \[
\alpha_u = \alpha \alpha_s^{-1} = \alpha \widetilde{Q}(\alpha)
\] is also a polynomial in \(\alpha\).
Since \(\alpha_s, \alpha_u \in k[\alpha]\), they commute: \(\alpha_s \alpha_u = \alpha_u \alpha_s\). Moreover, any endomorphism \(\beta\) commuting with \(\alpha\) also commutes with \(\alpha_s\) and \(\alpha_u\).
Uniqueness: If \(\alpha = \alpha_s \alpha_u = \beta_s \beta_u\) is another decomposition with commuting factors in \(k[\alpha]\), then: \[
\beta_s^{-1} \alpha_s = \beta_u \alpha_u^{-1} \in k[\alpha].
\] Because \(\beta_s\) and \(\alpha_s\) commute, \(\beta_s^{-1} \alpha_s\) is semisimple. Because \(\beta_u\) and \(\alpha_u\) commute, \(\beta_u \alpha_u^{-1}\) is unipotent (all eigenvalues are \(1\)). The only endomorphism that is simultaneously semisimple and unipotent is the identity. Thus: \[
\beta_s^{-1} \alpha_s = \beta_u \alpha_u^{-1} = \mathrm{id} \implies \alpha_s = \beta_s, \quad \alpha_u = \beta_u.
\]
Case 2: General case over a perfect field \(k\).
Since \(k\) is perfect, there exists a finite Galois extension \(k'/k\) such that all eigenvalues of \(\alpha\) lie in \(k'\). Let \(A := \alpha_{k'} \in \operatorname{Aut}_{k'}(V_{k'})\). By Case 1, \(A\) admits a unique Jordan decomposition: \[
A = A_s A_u = A_u A_s.
\] For every \(\sigma \in \operatorname{Gal}(k'/k)\), applying \(\sigma\) yields: \[
A = \sigma(A) = \sigma(A_s) \sigma(A_u).
\] Observe that:

\(\sigma(A_s)\) is semisimple, and \(\sigma(A_u)\) is unipotent;
\(\sigma(A_s) \sigma(A_u) = \sigma(A_u) \sigma(A_s)\).

By the uniqueness of the Jordan decomposition of \(A\) over \(k'\), we have: \[
\sigma(A_s) = A_s \quad \text{and} \quad \sigma(A_u) = A_u \quad \text{for all } \sigma \in \operatorname{Gal}(k'/k).
\] By Galois descent, \(A_s\) and \(A_u\) descend to \(k\), giving \(\alpha_s, \alpha_u \in \operatorname{Aut}_k(V)\) such that \((\alpha_s)_{k'} = A_s\) and \((\alpha_u)_{k'} = A_u\). They satisfy \(\alpha = \alpha_s \alpha_u = \alpha_u \alpha_s\), with \(\alpha_s\) semisimple and \(\alpha_u\) unipotent.
It remains to show that \(\alpha_s, \alpha_u \in k[\alpha]\). We know \(A_s \in k'[A]\). Let \(Q(T) \in k'[T]\) be a polynomial of minimal degree such that \(A_s = Q(A)\). Then \(\deg Q < \deg m_k(A)\), where \(m_k(A)\) is the minimal polynomial of \(A\) over \(k\). Writing \(Q(T) = \sum_{j=0}^r c_j T^j\) with \(c_j \in k'\), we have: \[
A_s = \sigma(A_s) = \sum_{j=0}^r \sigma(c_j) A^j \implies \big(Q - \sigma(Q)\big)(A) = 0.
\] If \(\sigma(c_j) \neq c_j\) for some \(j\), this would yield a non-zero polynomial of degree strictly less than \(\deg m_k(A)\) annihilating \(A\), a contradiction. Thus \(\sigma(c_j) = c_j\) for all \(\sigma \in \operatorname{Gal}(k'/k)\) and all \(j\), which implies \(c_j \in k\). Therefore, \(Q(T) \in k[T]\), so \(\alpha_s \in k[\alpha]\). The same argument holds for \(\alpha_u\), and uniqueness follows as in Case 1.


Example 1 Let \(k\) be a nonperfect field of characteristic \(2\), so that the Frobenius map \(x \mapsto x^2\) is not surjective. Choose an element \(a \in k \setminus k^2\). Consider the matrix: \[
\alpha = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ a & 0 \end{pmatrix} \in \mathrm{GL}_2(k).
\] Over \(\bar{k}\), its characteristic polynomial is \(T^2 - a = (T - \sqrt{a})^2\). Its Jordan decomposition in \(\mathrm{GL}_2(k(\sqrt{a}))\) is: \[
\alpha = \begin{pmatrix} \sqrt{a} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{a} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{a}} \\ \sqrt{a} & 0 \end{pmatrix},
\] where: \[
\alpha_s = \begin{pmatrix} \sqrt{a} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{a} \end{pmatrix} \quad (\text{semisimple}), \qquad \alpha_u = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{a}} \\ \sqrt{a} & 0 \end{pmatrix} \quad (\text{unipotent}).
\] Since \(\sqrt{a} \notin k\), the components \(\alpha_s\) and \(\alpha_u\) cannot be defined over \(k\). Therefore, \(\alpha\) has no Jordan decomposition in \(\mathrm{GL}_2(k)\).


Proposition 1  

If \(W \subseteq V\) is an \(\alpha\)-stable subspace, then \(W\) is both \(\alpha_s\)-stable and \(\alpha_u\)-stable. The restriction \(\alpha|_W = \alpha_s|_W \cdot \alpha_u|_W\) is the Jordan decomposition of \(\alpha|_W\). The same statement holds for the quotient space \(V/W\).
If \(\varphi: W \to V\) is a \(k\)-linear map intertwining two operators \(\alpha_W \in \operatorname{Aut}_k(W)\) and \(\alpha_V \in \operatorname{Aut}_k(V)\), i.e., \[
\begin{CD}
W @>{\varphi}>> V \\
@V{\alpha_W}VV @VV{\alpha_V}V \\
W @>{\varphi}>> V
\end{CD}
\] commutes, then \(\varphi\) also intertwines their semisimple and unipotent parts: \[
\begin{CD}
W @>{\varphi}>> V \\
@V{(\alpha_W)_s}VV @VV{(\alpha_V)_s}V \\
W @>{\varphi}>> V
\end{CD}
\qquad \text{and} \qquad
\begin{CD}
W @>{\varphi}>> V \\
@V{(\alpha_W)_u}VV @VV{(\alpha_V)_u}V \\
W @>{\varphi}>> V
\end{CD}
\]
If \(\alpha \in \operatorname{Aut}_k(V)\) and \(\beta \in \operatorname{Aut}_k(W)\), then: \[
(\alpha \otimes \beta)_s = \alpha_s \otimes \beta_s \quad \text{and} \quad (\alpha \otimes \beta)_u = \alpha_u \otimes \beta_u,
\] which gives the Jordan decomposition: \[
\alpha \otimes \beta = (\alpha_s \otimes \beta_s)(\alpha_u \otimes \beta_u) = (\alpha_u \otimes \beta_u)(\alpha_s \otimes \beta_s).
\]



Definition 2 Let \(V\) be a vector space over \(k\), and let \(\alpha: V \to V\) be a \(k\)-linear endomorphism.

\(\alpha\) is locally finite if \(V\) is a union of \(\alpha\)-stable finite-dimensional subspaces: \[
V = \bigcup_{\substack{W \subseteq V, \, \dim W < \infty \\ \alpha(W) \subseteq W}} W.
\]
If \(\alpha\) is locally finite, then:

\(\alpha\) is semisimple if for every finite-dimensional \(\alpha\)-stable subspace \(W \subseteq V\), the restriction \(\alpha|_W\) is semisimple;
\(\alpha\) is locally unipotent if for every finite-dimensional \(\alpha\)-stable subspace \(W \subseteq V\), the restriction \(\alpha|_W\) is unipotent (the integer \(N\) such that \((\alpha|_W - \mathrm{id}_W)^N = 0\) is not required to be bounded uniformly over all \(W\)).




Example 2 Let \(G\) be a linear algebraic group, and let \(r_V: G \to \mathrm{GL}_V\) be a representation of \(G\) on a vector space \(V\). For every \(g \in G(k)\), the operator \(r_V(g) \in \mathrm{GL}_V(k) = \operatorname{Aut}_k(V)\) is locally finite.


Corollary 1 Let \(\alpha: V \to V\) be a locally finite operator on a vector space over a perfect field \(k\). Then there exist unique locally finite operators \(\alpha_s, \alpha_u \in \operatorname{Aut}_k(V)\) such that:

\(\alpha = \alpha_s \alpha_u = \alpha_u \alpha_s\);
\(\alpha_s\) is semisimple, and \(\alpha_u\) is locally unipotent.



Theorem 2  

Let \(G\) be a linear algebraic group over a perfect field \(k\). For each \(g \in G(k)\), there exist unique elements \(g_s, g_u \in G(k)\) such that:

\(g = g_s g_u = g_u g_s\) (called the Jordan decomposition of \(g\));
for every representation \((V, r_V) \in \mathbf{Rep}_k G\), \[
r_V(g_s) = r_V(g)_s \quad \text{and} \quad r_V(g_u) = r_V(g)_u.
\]

An element \(g \in G(k)\) is unipotent if \(g_s = 1\), and semisimple if \(g_u = 1\). Equivalently, \(g\) is unipotent (resp. semisimple) if and only if for every representation \((V, r_V) \in \mathbf{Rep}_k G\), the operator \(r_V(g)\) is unipotent (resp. semisimple).



Proof. We use the Tannakian reconstruction theorem: \[
G(k) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \underline{\operatorname{Aut}}^\otimes(\omega)(k), \quad g \longmapsto \big(r_V(g)\big)_{(V, r_V) \in \mathbf{Rep}_k G}.
\] Fixing \(g \in G(k)\), for each \((V, r_V) \in \mathbf{Rep}_k G\), the operator \(r_V(g) \in \operatorname{Aut}_k(V)\) admits a unique Jordan decomposition: \[
r_V(g) = r_V(g)_s r_V(g)_u = r_V(g)_u r_V(g)_s.
\] It suffices to show that the families \(\big(r_V(g)_s\big)\) and \(\big(r_V(g)_u\big)\) define elements of \(\underline{\operatorname{Aut}}^\otimes(\omega)(k)\):

On the trivial representation \(\mathbf{1} = (k, \text{triv})\), \(r_{\mathbf{1}}(g) = \mathrm{id}_k\), so \(r_{\mathbf{1}}(g)_s = r_{\mathbf{1}}(g)_u = \mathrm{id}_k\).
Compatibility with tensor products: by Proposition 1(3), for any \(V, W \in \mathbf{Rep}_k G\), \[
r_{V \otimes W}(g)_s = \big(r_V(g) \otimes r_W(g)\big)_s = r_V(g)_s \otimes r_W(g)_s,
\] and similarly for the unipotent parts.
Functoriality: by Proposition 1(2), for every morphism of representations \(\varphi: W \to V\), \(\varphi\) commutes with \(r_W(g)\) and \(r_V(g)\), hence commutes with their semisimple and unipotent parts.
