Thus, \(\big(r_V(g)_s\big), \big(r_V(g)_u\big) \in \underline{\operatorname{Aut}}^\otimes(\omega)(k)\). Tracing back via the Tannakian isomorphism yields unique elements \(g_s, g_u \in G(k)\) such that: \[
r_V(g) = r_V(g)_s r_V(g)_u = r_V(g)_u r_V(g)_s \implies g = g_s g_u = g_u g_s.
\]


Corollary 2 Let \(\phi: G \to H\) be a homomorphism of linear algebraic groups over a perfect field \(k\). Then for all \(g \in G(k)\): \[
\phi(g_s) = \phi(g)_s \quad \text{and} \quad \phi(g_u) = \phi(g)_u.
\]


Proof. Choose a faithful representation of \(H\), \(r_V: H \hookrightarrow \mathrm{GL}_V\). Then \(r_V \circ \phi\) is a representation of \(G\). By Theorem 2: \[
r_V\big(\phi(g)_s\big) = \big(r_V(\phi(g))\big)_s = \big((r_V \circ \phi)(g)\big)_s = (r_V \circ \phi)(g_s) = r_V\big(\phi(g_s)\big),
\] \[
r_V\big(\phi(g)_u\big) = \big(r_V(\phi(g))\big)_u = \big((r_V \circ \phi)(g)\big)_u = (r_V \circ \phi)(g_u) = r_V\big(\phi(g_u)\big).
\] Since \(r_V\) is faithful, it is injective on \(k\)-points. Therefore: \[
\phi(g_s) = \phi(g)_s \quad \text{and} \quad \phi(g_u) = \phi(g)_u.
\]


Remark 1. An alternative proof of Theorem 2 can be given without Tannakian categories:

By Theorem 5.1.18, choose a faithful representation \(r_V: G \hookrightarrow \mathrm{GL}_V\). In \(\mathrm{GL}_V(k)\), \(r_V(g)\) has a Jordan decomposition \(r_V(g) = r_V(g)_s r_V(g)_u\).

\rho\big(r_V(g)_s\big) = \rho\big(r_V(g)\big)_s \quad \text{and} \quad \rho\big(r_V(g)_u\big) = \rho\big(r_V(g)\big)_u.
\] Since \(r_V(g) \in G(k)\), \(\rho(r_V(g))\) preserves \(L\). As \(L\) is a \(1\)-dimensional invariant subspace, its semisimple and unipotent parts must also preserve \(L\): \[
\rho\big(r_V(g)_s\big)(L) = L \quad \text{and} \quad \rho\big(r_V(g)_u\big)(L) = L.

Definition 3 (Schematically Dense Subsets (Def 5.3.10)) Let \(X\) be an algebraic scheme over a field \(k\).

A subset \(S \subseteq X(k)\) is schematically dense in \(X\) if the only closed subscheme \(Z \subseteq X\) containing \(S\) (i.e., \(S \subseteq Z(k)\)) is \(X\) itself. Equivalently:

\(X\) is reduced (\(X = X^{\mathrm{red}}\)) and \(S\) is topologically dense in \(|X|\) (\(\overline{S} = |X|\));
The canonical evaluation morphism \[
\mathcal{O}_X \longrightarrow \prod_{s \in S} i_{s*} k, \quad f \longmapsto \big(f(s)\big)_{s \in S}
\] is injective.

A subset \(S\) is schematically dense in \(X\) if and only if it is locally schematically dense (i.e., for any open affine cover \(\{U_i\}\) of \(X\), \(S \cap U_i(k)\) is schematically dense in \(U_i\)).
Schematic density is stable under base change of the base field (by taking the inverse image). In particular, if \(S \subseteq X(k)\) is schematically dense in \(X\), then \(X\) is geometrically reduced.
For a field extension \(k'/k\), a subset \(S \subseteq X(k')\) is schematically dense in \(X\) if the only closed subscheme \(Z \subseteq X\) such that \(S \subseteq Z(k')\) is \(X\) itself.



Proposition 2 (Geometric Reducedness Criterion (Prop 5.3.11)) An algebraic scheme \(X\) over \(k\) is geometrically reduced if and only if \(X(k^s)\) is schematically dense in \(X\), where \(k^s\) denotes the separable closure of \(k\).


Proof. \((\implies)\) Since \(X\) is geometrically reduced, the smooth locus \(X^{\mathrm{sm}}\) is a dense open subscheme of \(X\). Thus it suffices to show that \(X^{\mathrm{sm}}(k^s)\) is dense in \(X^{\mathrm{sm}}\), so we may assume without loss of generality that \(X\) is smooth over \(k\).
Then the base change \(X_{k^s}\) is smooth over \(k^s\). For each point \(x \in X_{k^s}\), there exists an étale neighborhood \(U \xrightarrow{f} \mathbb{A}^d_{k^s}\). Since \(k^s\) is separably closed, every non-empty étale \(k^s\)-scheme has \(k^s\)-rational points, which implies that the rational points are topologically dense: \[
\overline{X_{k^s}(k^s)} = |X_{k^s}|.
\] Under the projection morphism \(\pi: X_{k^s} \to X\), the image of \(X_{k^s}(k^s)\) is \(X(k^s)\). Hence: \[
\overline{X(k^s)} = \overline{\pi\big(X_{k^s}(k^s)\big)} = \pi\big(\overline{X_{k^s}(k^s)}\big) = \pi(|X_{k^s}|) = |X|.
\] Because \(X\) is reduced and \(X(k^s)\) is dense in \(|X|\), \(X(k^s)\) is schematically dense in \(X\).
\((\impliedby)\) If \(X(k^s)\) is schematically dense in \(X\), then by stability under base change (Definition 3(3)), \(X_{k^s}(k^s)\) is dense in \(X_{k^s}\), which implies that \(X_{\bar{k}}(\bar{k})\) is dense in \(X_{\bar{k}}\). A scheme containing a dense set of reduced points is reduced, hence \(X_{\bar{k}}\) is reduced, which means \(X\) is geometrically reduced.


Definition 4 (Frobenius Morphisms (Def 5.3.12)) Let \(k\) be a field of characteristic \(p > 0\).

For a \(k\)-algebra \(R\), the \(p\)-th power map \(\sigma: R \to R\), \(x \mapsto x^p\) is a ring homomorphism (the Frobenius endomorphism), but it is not a \(k\)-algebra homomorphism unless \(k = \mathbb{F}_p\). Geometrically, this induces the absolute Frobenius morphism: \[
\begin{CD}
\operatorname{Spec} R @>{\sigma^*}>> \operatorname{Spec} R \\
@VVV @VVV \\
\operatorname{Spec} k @>{\sigma^*}>> \operatorname{Spec} k
\end{CD}
\]
For a \(k\)-scheme \(X\), the Frobenius twist \(X^{(p)}\) is defined by the fiber product (base change by \(\sigma: k \to k\), \(a \mapsto a^p\)): \[
\begin{CD}
X^{(p)} @>>> X \\
@VVV @VVV \\
\operatorname{Spec} k @>{\sigma}>> \operatorname{Spec} k
\end{CD}
\] By the universal property of fiber products, the absolute Frobenius \(F_{\mathrm{abs}}: X \to X\) and the structure morphism \(X \to \operatorname{Spec} k\) induce a unique morphism of \(k\)-schemes: \[
F_{X/k}: X \longrightarrow X^{(p)},
\] called the relative Frobenius morphism.
In terms of functors of points: for a \(k\)-algebra \(R\), let \({}_\sigma R\) (or \({}_f R\)) denote the \(k\)-algebra with underlying ring \(R\) whose \(k\)-algebra structure is twisted by \(\sigma\) (i.e., \(a \cdot r := \sigma(a) r = a^p r\)). Then the \(p\)-th power map \(R \to {}_\sigma R\), \(x \mapsto x^p\) is a homomorphism of \(k\)-algebras, and: \[
X^{(p)}(R) \cong X({}_\sigma R).
\]



Proposition 3 (Properties of Relative Frobenius (Prop 5.3.13))  

Functoriality: For any morphism of \(k\)-schemes \(\varphi: X \to Y\), the relative Frobenius is functorial; that is, the following diagram commutes: \[
\begin{CD}
X @>{\varphi}>> Y \\
@V{F_{X/k}}VV @VV{F_{Y/k}}V \\
X^{(p)} @>{\varphi^{(p)}}>> Y^{(p)}
\end{CD}
\]
Compatibility with products: \[
F_{(X \times_k Y)/k} = F_{X/k} \times F_{Y/k}.
\]
Compatibility with base change: For any field extension \(k'/k\), \[
(F_{X/k})_{k'} = F_{X_{k'}/k'}.
\]
Group scheme structure: If \(G\) is an algebraic group over \(k\), then the functor \[
G^{(p)}: \mathbf{Alg}_k \longrightarrow \mathbf{Grp}, \quad R \longmapsto G^{(p)}(R) = G({}_\sigma R)
\] defines an algebraic group over \(k\), and the relative Frobenius morphism \(F_G: G \to G^{(p)}\) is a homomorphism of algebraic groups.



Proof. Part (4) follows from applying (1) and (2) to the multiplication map \(m: G \times G \to G\). Specifically, the diagram: \[
\begin{CD}
G \times G @>{m}>> G \\
@V{F_G \times F_G}VV @VV{F_G}V \\
G^{(p)} \times G^{(p)} @>{m^{(p)}}>> G^{(p)}
\end{CD}
\] commutes, showing that \(F_G\) preserves multiplication, hence is a homomorphism of algebraic groups.


Proposition 4 (Relative Frobenius of Smooth Connected Groups (Prop 5.3.14)) If \(G\) is a smooth and connected (i.e., geometrically integral) algebraic group over \(k\), then \(G^{(p)}\) is also smooth and connected. Moreover, the relative Frobenius morphism \(F_G: G \to G^{(p)}\) is fppf (faithfully flat of finite presentation).


Proof. By descent of smoothness and fppf descent of fppf morphisms, we may assume without loss of generality that \(k = \bar{k}\).
When \(k = \bar{k}\) (hence perfect), \(\sigma: k \xrightarrow{\sim} k\) is an isomorphism of fields, so \(G^{(p)} \cong G\) as schemes; in particular, \(G^{(p)}\) is smooth and connected.
On coordinate rings, the pullback map \((F_G)^*: \mathcal{O}(G^{(p)}) \hookrightarrow \mathcal{O}(G)\) is the Frobenius map (\(a \mapsto a^p\)), which is integral (every element \(a\) satisfies \(T^p - a^p = 0\)). By generic flatness and the homogeneity of algebraic groups, since \(G^{(p)}\) is regular/reduced, \(F_G\) is flat everywhere. Because it is dominant and integral, it is surjective on points. Hence \(F_G: G \to G^{(p)}\) is fppf.


Corollary 3 (Iterated Frobenius (Corollary 5.3.15)) For each \(n \ge 1\), define the \(n\)-th Frobenius twist inductively by \(G^{(p^n)} := (G^{(p^{n-1})})^{(p)}\) with \(G^{(p^0)} := G\). Then the \(n\)-th iterate of relative Frobenius: \[
F_G^n: G \xrightarrow{F_G} G^{(p)} \xrightarrow{F_{G^{(p)}}} \cdots \xrightarrow{F_{G^{(p^{n-1})}}} G^{(p^n)}
\] is a homomorphism of algebraic groups. If \(G\) is smooth and connected, then \(G^{(p^n)}\) is smooth and connected, and \(F_G^n\) is fppf.


Proposition 5 (Hopf Subalgebra \(\mathcal{O}(G)^{p^n}\) (Prop 5.3.16)) Let \(G\) be a linear algebraic group over a perfect field \(k\) of characteristic \(p > 0\). For \(n \ge 1\), let \(\mathcal{O}(G)^{p^n} := \operatorname{Im}(f^n)\), where \(f^n: \mathcal{O}(G) \to \mathcal{O}(G)\) is the \(p^n\)-th power map \(a \mapsto a^{p^n}\). Then \(\mathcal{O}(G)^{p^n}\) is a Hopf subalgebra of \(\mathcal{O}(G)\), which is geometrically reduced for all \(n \gg 0\).


Proof. Let \(A := \mathcal{O}(G)\) be the coordinate Hopf algebra of \(G\). The comorphism of the \(n\)-th relative Frobenius is: \[
(F_G^n)^*: A \otimes_{k, \sigma^n} k \longrightarrow A, \quad a \otimes b \longmapsto a^{p^n} b.
\] Since \(k\) is perfect, every \(b \in k\) has a unique \(p^n\)-th root \(b^{1/p^n} \in k\), so \(a^{p^n} b = (a b^{1/p^n})^{p^n}\). Thus: \[
\operatorname{Im}\big((F_G^n)^*\big) = A^{p^n} = \mathcal{O}(G)^{p^n}.
\] Since \(F_G^n: G \to G^{(p^n)}\) is a homomorphism of algebraic groups, the image of its comorphism is a Hopf subalgebra of \(A\).
Because \(A\) is a Noetherian ring, its nilradical \(\operatorname{nil}(A)\) is finitely generated, hence nilpotent: there exists an integer \(n_0 \ge 1\) such that \(\operatorname{nil}(A)^{p^{n_0}} = 0\). Taking \(n \gg 0\) such that \(p^n > n_0\), any nilpotent element in \(A\) has its \(p^n\)-th power equal to \(0\). Therefore, \(\mathcal{O}(G)^{p^n}\) has no non-zero nilpotent elements, so it is reduced. Because \(k\) is perfect, reduced implies geometrically reduced (reduced over \(k = k^{p^n} \iff\) reduced over \(\bar{k}\)).


Corollary 4 (Factorization via Smooth Algebraic Groups (Corollary 5.3.17)) Let \(G\) be a linear algebraic group over a perfect field \(k\) of characteristic \(p > 0\). Consider the \(n\)-th relative Frobenius \(F_G^n: G \to G^{(p^n)}\), and let \(I_n := \operatorname{Spec}\big(\mathcal{O}(G)^{p^n}\big) = \operatorname{Spec}\big(\operatorname{Im}((F_G^n)^*)\big)\) be its scheme-theoretic image: \[
\begin{CD}
G @>{F_G^n}>> G^{(p^n)} \\
@V{\text{fppf}}VV @AAA \\
I_n @= I_n
\end{CD}
\]

If \(G\) is smooth and connected, then \(F_G^n\) is fppf, hence \(I_n = G^{(p^n)}\), which is smooth and connected.
In general, for all \(n \gg 0\), \(I_n\) is a smooth linear algebraic group over \(k\), and the canonical morphism \(G \to I_n\) is fppf.



Lemma 1 (Smoothness Criterion via Nilradical (Lemma 5.3.18)) Let \(G\) be a linear algebraic group over an algebraically closed field \(k\). If \(\operatorname{nil}(\mathcal{O}(G)) \subseteq \mathfrak{m}_e^2\), where \(\mathfrak{m}_e\) is the maximal ideal at the identity element \(e \in G\), then \(G\) is smooth.


Proof. An algebraic group \(G\) is smooth if and only if \(\dim T_e G = \dim G\). Let \(G^{\mathrm{red}}\) be the associated reduced algebraic group. Over an algebraically closed field \(k\), \(G^{\mathrm{red}}\) is a smooth algebraic group, so: \[
\dim T_e G^{\mathrm{red}} = \dim G^{\mathrm{red}} = \dim G.
\] Thus it suffices to show that \(\dim T_e G = \dim T_e G^{\mathrm{red}}\).
The maximal ideal of the local ring of \(G^{\mathrm{red}}\) at \(e\) is \(\mathfrak{m}_e^{\mathrm{red}} = \mathfrak{m}_e / \operatorname{nil}(\mathcal{O}(G))\). The canonical quotient morphism on Zariski cotangent spaces: \[
\mathfrak{m}_e / \mathfrak{m}_e^2 \longrightarrow \mathfrak{m}_e^{\mathrm{red}} / (\mathfrak{m}_e^{\mathrm{red}})^2 \cong \mathfrak{m}_e / \big(\mathfrak{m}_e^2 + \operatorname{nil}(\mathcal{O}(G))\big)
\] is an isomorphism because \(\operatorname{nil}(\mathcal{O}(G)) \subseteq \mathfrak{m}_e^2\) implies \(\mathfrak{m}_e^2 + \operatorname{nil}(\mathcal{O}(G)) = \mathfrak{m}_e^2\). Dualizing gives an isomorphism on tangent spaces \(T_e G^{\mathrm{red}} \xrightarrow{\sim} T_e G\), so: \[
\dim T_e G = \dim T_e G^{\mathrm{red}} = \dim G.
\] Hence \(G\) is smooth at \(e\), and by group translations, \(G\) is smooth everywhere.


Theorem 3 (Cartier’s Theorem (Theorem 5.3.19)) Every linear algebraic group (and indeed every group scheme of finite type) over a field \(k\) of characteristic zero is smooth.


Proof. By fppf descent of smoothness, we may assume without loss of generality that \(k = \bar{k}\).
Write \(G = \operatorname{Spec} A\), where \(A = \mathcal{O}(G)\) is the coordinate Hopf algebra of \(G\), and let \(\mathfrak{p} := \mathfrak{m}_e = \ker(\epsilon: A \to k)\) be the augmentation ideal corresponding to the identity element \(e \in G\). By Lemma 1, it suffices to show that every nilpotent element \(a \in A\) satisfies \(a \in \mathfrak{p}^2\).
Since \(A/\mathfrak{p} \cong k\) has no non-zero nilpotents, \(a \in \mathfrak{p}\). If the image of \(a\) in the localization \(A_{\mathfrak{p}}\) is zero, then its image in \(A_{\mathfrak{p}}/(\mathfrak{p}A_{\mathfrak{p}})^2 \cong A/\mathfrak{p}^2\) is zero, which implies \(a \in \mathfrak{p}^2\), and there is nothing to prove.
Thus, we may assume that the image of \(a\) in \(A_{\mathfrak{p}}\) is non-zero. Let \(n \ge 2\) be an integer such that: \[
a^n = 0 \text{ in } A_{\mathfrak{p}}, \quad \text{but} \quad a^{n-1} \neq 0 \text{ in } A_{\mathfrak{p}}.
\] Since \(a^n = 0\) in \(A_{\mathfrak{p}}\), there exists an element \(s \in A \setminus \mathfrak{p}\) such that \(s a^n = 0\) in \(A\). Replacing \(a\) with \(sa\) (note that \(sa \equiv s(e) a \pmod{\mathfrak{p}^2}\) with \(s(e) \in k^\times\), so \(a \in \mathfrak{p}^2 \iff sa \in \mathfrak{p}^2\), and \((sa)^{n-1} = s^{n-1} a^{n-1} \neq 0\) in \(A_{\mathfrak{p}}\)), we may assume: \[
a^n = 0 \text{ in } A, \quad \text{and} \quad a^{n-1} \neq 0 \text{ in } A_{\mathfrak{p}}.
\]
Claim: \(m^*(a) - a \otimes 1 - 1 \otimes a \in \mathfrak{p} \otimes \mathfrak{p}\), where \(m^*: A \to A \otimes_k A\) is the comultiplication map.
Proof of Claim: The counit axioms state that: \[
(\epsilon \otimes \mathrm{id}) \circ m^* = \mathrm{id} \quad \text{and} \quad (\mathrm{id} \otimes \epsilon) \circ m^* = \mathrm{id}.
\] Since \(\mathfrak{p} = \ker \epsilon\), we have: \[
m^*(a) \equiv 1 \otimes a \pmod{\mathfrak{p} \otimes A} \quad \text{and} \quad m^*(a) \equiv a \otimes 1 \pmod{A \otimes \mathfrak{p}}.
\] Under the decomposition \(A = k \cdot 1 \oplus \mathfrak{p}\), \[
A \otimes_k A = (k \cdot 1 \otimes 1) \oplus (k \cdot 1 \otimes \mathfrak{p}) \oplus (\mathfrak{p} \otimes k \cdot 1) \oplus (\mathfrak{p} \otimes \mathfrak{p}).
\] Comparing with the congruences above yields: \[
m^*(a) = a \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes a + y \quad \text{for some } y \in \mathfrak{p} \otimes_k \mathfrak{p}.
\] This establishes the Claim.
Now, because \(m^*\) is a \(k\)-algebra homomorphism and \(a^n = 0\) in \(A\): \[
0 = m^*(a^n) = \big(m^*(a)\big)^n = (a \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes a + y)^n.
\] Expanding this product modulo \(A \otimes \mathfrak{p}^2\), note that any term containing \((1 \otimes a + y)^k\) with \(k \ge 2\) lies in \(A \otimes \mathfrak{p}^2\) because \(1 \otimes a + y \in A \otimes \mathfrak{p}\). Therefore: \[
0 \equiv a^n \otimes 1 + n (a^{n-1} \otimes 1)(1 \otimes a + y) \pmod{A \otimes \mathfrak{p}^2}.
\] Since \(a^n = 0\) in \(A\), this reduces to: \[
n a^{n-1} \otimes a + n (a^{n-1} \otimes 1) y \in A \otimes \mathfrak{p}^2.
\] Because \(y \in \mathfrak{p} \otimes \mathfrak{p}\), we have \((a^{n-1} \otimes 1) y \in a^{n-1}\mathfrak{p} \otimes \mathfrak{p}\). Thus: \[
n a^{n-1} \otimes a \in a^{n-1}\mathfrak{p} \otimes \mathfrak{p} + A \otimes \mathfrak{p}^2.
\] Passing to the quotient \(A \otimes (\mathfrak{p}/\mathfrak{p}^2)\), and denoting the image of \(a\) by \(\bar{a} \in \mathfrak{p}/\mathfrak{p}^2\), we obtain: \[
n a^{n-1} \otimes \bar{a} \in a^{n-1}\mathfrak{p} \otimes (\mathfrak{p}/\mathfrak{p}^2) \quad \text{in } A \otimes_k (\mathfrak{p}/\mathfrak{p}^2).
\] If \(\bar{a} \neq 0\) in \(\mathfrak{p}/\mathfrak{p}^2\), then \(\bar{a}\) can be extended to a basis of \(\mathfrak{p}/\mathfrak{p}^2\), which forces: \[
n a^{n-1} \in a^{n-1}\mathfrak{p}.
\] Since \(\operatorname{char}(k) = 0\), the integer \(n\) is invertible in \(k\), so: \[
a^{n-1} \in a^{n-1}\mathfrak{p}.
\] Thus there exists an element \(x \in \mathfrak{p}\) such that \(a^{n-1} = a^{n-1} x\), which implies: \[
a^{n-1}(1 - x) = 0.
\] Because \(x \in \mathfrak{p} = \mathfrak{m}_e\), the element \(1 - x\) is a unit in the local ring \(A_{\mathfrak{p}}\). Multiplying by its inverse in \(A_{\mathfrak{p}}\) yields: \[
a^{n-1} = 0 \quad \text{in } A_{\mathfrak{p}},
\] which directly contradicts our choice of \(n\) (that \(a^{n-1} \neq 0\) in \(A_{\mathfrak{p}}\)).
Therefore, we must have \(\bar{a} = 0\) in \(\mathfrak{p}/\mathfrak{p}^2\), which means \(a \in \mathfrak{p}^2\). By Lemma 1, \(G\) is smooth.

title: How to Edit These Notes
text: 你平时只需要编辑扩展名为 .qmd 的源文件。它和 Markdown 几乎一样，但对数学公式、目录和提示框支持得更好。侧边栏、首页卡片、主题目录和 HTML 都由 Quarto 根据这些源文件自动生成。

title: How to Edit These Notes
text:
修改一篇笔记
在 VS Code 左侧文件列表中打开对应的 .qmd 文件，直接修改文字并保存即可：
## A new section

普通文字写在这里，行内公式写成 $X \to Y$。

$$
\Omega_{X/Y}=0
$$
以 --- 包围的文件开头是页面信息。每篇正式笔记都需要填写：
---
title: "A New Note"
subtitle: ""
description: "A short description shown on the topic page."
order: 80
---

title 是页面标题以及侧边栏中的名称。
description 是主题目录中显示的一句话简介。
order 是阅读顺序，必须写成数字。现有页面以 10 为间隔排列，因此可以把新页面插入中间，例如在 40 和 50 之间使用 45。
subtitle 可以留空。

修改并保存后，本地预览会自动重新生成相应的 HTML。

title: How to Edit These Notes
text:
删除一篇笔记
删除对应的 .qmd 文件即可。下一次预览或构建时，Quarto 会自动把它从侧边栏和主题目录移除。
如果其他笔记的正文中手动链接了被删除的页面，那些正文链接仍需自行修改。

title: How to Edit These Notes
text:
新增一篇笔记
在已有主题的文件夹中，新建一个 .qmd 文件并填写 title、description 和 order。例如：
---
title: "Examples"
description: "Examples illustrating the main definitions and geometric intuition."
order: 45
---
文件保存后，不需要修改 _quarto.yml 或主题的 index.qmd：新页面会自动出现在侧边栏、主题目录和生成的网站中。

title: How to Edit These Notes
text:
新增一个大主题
新建一个主题文件夹，并在其中创建 index.qmd。文件夹名称最好使用小写英文和连字符，例如 perfectoid-spaces。主题首页可以使用下面的模板：
---
title: "Perfectoid Spaces"
subtitle: ""
description: "Notes on perfectoid spaces and their applications."
order: 30
start-page: "perfectoid-spaces/first-note.qmd"
toc: false
listing:
  id: topic-pages
  contents: "*.qmd"
  template: "../_templates/topic-pages.ejs.md"
  fields: [title, description, order]
  sort: "order asc"
  sort-ui: false
  filter-ui: false
---

Write the introduction to this topic here.

## Contents

::: {#topic-pages}
:::
其中 start-page 是首页卡片上 “Start reading” 指向的第一篇笔记。创建主题首页和第一篇笔记后，新主题会自动出现在网站首页与侧边栏中。






Tip最省事的工作方式



你也可以复制同一主题中的现有 .qmd，只修改文件名、页面信息和正文。只要 title、description 和 order 完整，目录不需要手工维护。

title: How to Edit These Notes
text:
本地预览
在英文路径的工作目录 C:\notes\p-adic-geometry-note 中打开 VS Code，然后在终端运行：
.\preview-local.ps1
终端会显示一个 http://localhost:... 地址。保持这个终端运行，保存 .qmd 文件后网页会自动刷新；结束预览时按 Ctrl+C。
确认预览无误后，把修改 commit 并 push 到 main。GitHub Actions 会重新构建并发布网站。

title: 23.1 Representation I
text:
Definition 1 (Action)  

An action of an algebraic group \(G\) on a scheme \(X\) over \(k\) is a morphism: \[
G \times X \longrightarrow X
\] or equivalently, a natural transformation: \[
\forall R \in k\text{-alg}, \quad G(R) \circlearrowright X(R) \quad \text{naturally}.
\]
A linear representation of \(G\) is a homomorphism of algebraic groups: \[
G \longrightarrow \mathrm{GL}_n
\] for some \(n\), i.e., \(G \circlearrowright \mathbb{A}^n\).



Lemma 1 (Properties of Action Morphisms) Let \(\varphi: G \times X \to X\) be an action. Then \(\varphi\) is fppf. Moreover, \(\varphi\) is smooth (resp. finite) if \(G\) is smooth (resp. finite).


Proof. Consider the commutative diagram: \[
\begin{CD}
G \times X @>{\sim}>{(g, x) \mapsto (g, gx)}> G \times X @>>> G \\
@V{\varphi}VV @VV{\mathrm{pr}_2}V @VVV \\
X @= X @>>> \operatorname{Spec} k
\end{CD}
\] The right square is Cartesian, so \(\mathrm{pr}_2\) inherits the respective property (fppf, smooth, finite) from \(G \to \operatorname{Spec} k\) by base change. Since the first horizontal map is an isomorphism, \(\varphi = \mathrm{pr}_2 \circ \sim\) satisfies these properties.


Proposition 1 (Orbit)  

Let \(\varphi: G \times X \to X\) be an action, and \(x \in X(k)\). Define the orbit map: \[
\varphi_x: G = G \times \operatorname{Spec} k \xrightarrow{\;\mathrm{id} \times x\;} G \times X \xrightarrow{\;\varphi\;} X.
\] The orbit of \(x\) is defined set-theoretically as \(\operatorname{Im} \varphi_x\).
\(\operatorname{Im} \varphi_x\) is always locally closed. \(G \cdot x\) is open dense in \(\overline{G \cdot x}\).



Proof. Since \(X_{\bar{k}} \to X\) is a quotient open map of topological spaces, without loss of generality we may assume \(k = \bar{k}\).
Apply Chevalley’s Theorem to \(\varphi_x\): \(G \cdot x\) is constructible. Thus there exists an open dense subset \(U \subseteq \overline{G \cdot x}\) such that \(U \subseteq G \cdot x\). Then: \[
G \cdot x = G \cdot U = \bigcup_{g \in G} g \cdot U \subseteq \overline{G \cdot x}.
\] Since each \(g \cdot U\) is open in \(\overline{G \cdot x}\), the union \(G \cdot x\) is open in \(\overline{G \cdot x}\). Therefore, \(G \cdot x\) is an open subset of a closed subset, hence locally closed.


Proposition 2 (Closed Orbits) If \(k = \bar{k}\) and \(G \circlearrowright X\), every orbit of minimal dimension is closed. In particular, closed orbits always exist.



Theorem 1 (Structure of General Algebraic Groups) (Reference: [Milne, Chapter 8])

There exists an exact sequence: \[
0 \longrightarrow G^\circ \longrightarrow G \longrightarrow \pi_0(G) \longrightarrow e
\] with \(G^\circ\) geometrically connected.
(Barsotti–Chevalley) For every connected algebraic group \(G\) over \(k\), there exists an exact sequence: \[
0 \longrightarrow N \longrightarrow G \longrightarrow Q \longrightarrow 0
\] where \(N\) is connected linear and \(Q\) is an abelian variety. If \(k\) is perfect, then \(N\) is unique.



Theorem 2 (Maximal Affine Quotient) Every algebraic group \(G\) has a maximal affine quotient, defined by: \[
G \xrightarrow{\;\phi\;} \operatorname{Spec}\mathcal{O}(G)
\] since \(\mathcal{O}(G)\) is a commutative Hopf \(k\)-algebra.
Facts:

\(\mathcal{O}(G)\) is a finitely generated \(k\)-algebra, and \(G_{\mathrm{aff}} := \operatorname{Spec}\mathcal{O}(G)\) is a linear algebraic group (LAG).
\(G \to G_{\mathrm{aff}}\) is universal: for every linear algebraic group \(H\) and every homomorphism \(G \to H\), there exists a unique factorization: \[
\begin{CD}
G @>{\phi}>> G_{\mathrm{aff}} \\
@VVV @VV{\exists!}V \\
H @= H
\end{CD}
\]
\(\phi\) is fppf.
\(\mathcal{O}(\ker \phi) = k\). If \(\mathcal{O}(G) = k\), \(G\) is called anti-affine (\(G\) is commutative anti-affine).




Definition 2 (Hopf Subalgebra) Let \(B\) be a Hopf algebra over \(k\). A \(k\)-subalgebra \(A \subseteq B\) is called a Hopf subalgebra if: \[
m^*(A) \subseteq A \otimes A \quad \text{and} \quad i^*(A) \subseteq A.
\] Then \(m_A^* = m_B^*|_A\), \(i_A^* = i_B^*|_A\), and \(e_A^* = e_B^*|_A\).


Proposition 3 (Image, Kernel, and Hopf Ideals)  

If \(f: A \to B\) is a morphism of Hopf algebras, then \(\operatorname{Im} f = f(A)\) is a Hopf subalgebra of \(B\).
A Hopf ideal in a Hopf \(k\)-algebra \(A\) is an ideal \(\mathfrak{a} \subseteq A\) such that: \[
m^*(\mathfrak{a}) \subseteq \mathfrak{a} \otimes A + A \otimes \mathfrak{a}, \quad i^*(\mathfrak{a}) \subseteq \mathfrak{a}, \quad \text{and} \quad e^*(\mathfrak{a}) = 0.
\]
If \(f: A \to B\) is a morphism of Hopf algebras, then \(\ker f\) is a Hopf ideal of \(A\).
If \(\mathfrak{a} \subseteq A\) is a Hopf ideal, then \(A/\mathfrak{a}\) has a natural Hopf algebra structure and \(A \to A/\mathfrak{a}\) is a morphism in the category of Hopf \(k\)-algebras. For every \(f: A \to B\) such that \(\ker f \supseteq \mathfrak{a}\), there exists a unique \(\bar{f}\): \[
\begin{CD}
A @>{f}>> B \\
@VVV @AA{\exists! \bar{f}}A \\
A/\mathfrak{a} @= A/\mathfrak{a}
\end{CD}
\]
For every morphism of Hopf algebras \(f: A \to B\), there is a canonical isomorphism: \[
A/\ker f \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} f(A) \subseteq B.
\]



Corollary 1 (Factorization of Morphisms of LAG) A homomorphism \(\varphi: G \to H\) of linear algebraic groups factors as: \[
\begin{CD}
G @>{\varphi}>> H \\
@V{q}VV @AA{i}A \\
I @= I
\end{CD}
\qquad
\begin{CD}
\operatorname{Spec} B @>{\varphi}>> \operatorname{Spec} A \\
@V{q}VV @AA{i}A \\
\operatorname{Spec}(A/\mathfrak{a}) @= \operatorname{Spec}(A/\mathfrak{a})
\end{CD}
\] where \(q\) is fppf and \(i\) is a closed immersion.
Fact: If \(A \subseteq B\) is a Hopf subalgebra, then \(B\) is fppf over \(A\) (i.e., \(\operatorname{Spec} B \to \operatorname{Spec} A\) is fppf).


Proposition 4 (Closed Immersion Criterion) Let \(\varphi: G \to H\) be a morphism of linear algebraic groups. If \(\ker \varphi = \operatorname{Spec} k\), then \(\varphi\) is a closed immersion.


Proof. It suffices to prove that \(q: G \to I\) is an isomorphism.
Since \(\ker q = \ker \varphi = \operatorname{Spec} k\), for every \(R \in k\text{-alg}\), the map \(\varphi(R): G(R) \hookrightarrow I(R)\) is injective.
Claim: \(\varphi(R)\) is surjective for all \(R\).
For any \(y \in I(R)\), there exists an fppf extension \(R' \in k\text{-alg}\) over \(R\) and \(x \in G(R')\) such that \(\varphi(R')(x) = y|_{R'}\). (Take \(R' = R \otimes_{\mathcal{O}(I)} \mathcal{O}(G)\) via the pullback): \[
\begin{CD}
R' @<<< G \\
@AAA @VV{\mathrm{fppf}}V \\
R @>>> I
\end{CD}
\] Now the sequence \(0 \to R \to R' \rightrightarrows R' \otimes_R R'\) is exact, giving the exact sequence: \[
0 \longrightarrow G(R) \longrightarrow G(R') \rightrightarrows G(R' \otimes_R R')
\] \[
\operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal{O}(G), R) \longhookrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal{O}(G), R') \rightrightarrows \operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal{O}(G), R' \otimes_R R')
\] Consider the commutative diagram: \[
\begin{CD}
\operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal{O}(G), R) @>>> \operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal{O}(G), R') @>>> \operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal{O}(G), R' \otimes_R R') \\
@V{\varphi(R)}VV @V{\varphi(R')}VV @VVV \\
I(R) @>>> I(R') @>>> I(R' \otimes_R R')
\end{CD}
\] \[
y \longmapsto y|_{R'} \longmapsto 0
\] Then \(x \in G(R')\) maps to \(y|_{R'}\), and its difference in \(G(R' \otimes_R R')\) maps to \(0\) in \(I(R' \otimes_R R')\). By injectivity, the difference is \(0\). By descent, \(x\) descends to \(x_0 \in G(R)\) with \(x_0 \mapsto y\). Thus \(\varphi(R)\) is surjective.



Definition 3 (Representations)  

Let \(V\) be a \(k\)-vector space. Define the affine algebraic group functor: \[
\mathrm{GL}_V: k\text{-alg} \longrightarrow \mathbf{Grp}, \quad R \longmapsto \mathrm{GL}_V(R) = \operatorname{Aut}_R(V \otimes R).
\] If \(V\) is finite-dimensional, then after fixing a basis, \(\mathrm{GL}_V \cong \mathrm{GL}_n\).
A linear representation of \(G\) is a morphism of algebraic groups: \[
r: G \longrightarrow \mathrm{GL}_V.
\]

\(r\) is faithful if \(\ker r = \operatorname{Spec} k \iff r\) is a closed immersion.
\(r\) is trivial if \(r(G) = e\).




Definition 4 (Comodule) A right comodule is a \(k\)-vector space \(V\) equipped with a \(k\)-linear map \(\rho: V \to V \otimes \mathcal{O}(G)\) such that:

\((\mathrm{id}_V \otimes e^*) \circ \rho = \mathrm{id}_V\): \[
\begin{CD}
V @>{\rho}>> V \otimes \mathcal{O}(G) \\
@| @VV{\mathrm{id}_V \otimes e^*}V \\
V @= V
\end{CD}
\]
\((\mathrm{id}_V \otimes m^*) \circ \rho = (\rho \otimes \mathrm{id}_{\mathcal{O}(G)}) \circ \rho\): \[
\begin{CD}
V @>{\rho}>> V \otimes \mathcal{O}(G) \\
@V{\rho}VV @VV{\mathrm{id}_V \otimes m^*}V \\
V \otimes \mathcal{O}(G) @>{\rho \otimes \mathrm{id}}>> V \otimes \mathcal{O}(G) \otimes \mathcal{O}(G)
\end{CD}
\]



Definition 5 (Comodule Morphism and Submodule) Let \((V, \rho)\) be an \(\mathcal{O}(G)\)-comodule.

A morphism of \(\mathcal{O}(G)\)-comodules is a \(k\)-linear map \(f: V \to W\) such that: \[
\begin{CD}
V @>{f}>> W \\
@V{\rho_V}VV @VV{\rho_W}V \\
V \otimes \mathcal{O}(G) @>{f \otimes \mathrm{id}}>> W \otimes \mathcal{O}(G)
\end{CD}
\]
A submodule (subcomodule) is a subspace \(W \subseteq V\) such that \(\rho(W) \subseteq W \otimes \mathcal{O}(G)\).



Theorem 3 (Bijection between Representations and Comodules) Let \(r: G \to \mathrm{GL}_V\) be a representation and \(A := \mathcal{O}(G)\). \[
r(A): G(A) = \operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal{O}(G), A) \longrightarrow \mathrm{GL}_V(A) = \operatorname{Aut}_A(V \otimes A)
\] \[
\mathrm{id} \longmapsto (u: V \otimes A \xrightarrow{\sim} V \otimes A) \in \operatorname{Aut}_A(V \otimes A).
\] Consider \(\rho: V \xrightarrow{v \mapsto v \otimes 1} V \otimes A \xrightarrow{u} V \otimes A\). There is a bijection: \[
\big\{ \text{Representations } r: G \to \mathrm{GL}_V \big\} \xleftrightarrow{\quad 1:1 \quad} \big\{ \mathcal{O}(G)\text{-comodule structures on } V \big\}, \quad r \longleftrightarrow \rho_r.
\]


Proof. By Yoneda’s Lemma on \(G\) and \(\mathrm{GL}_V(-)\), for every \(R \in k\text{-alg}\) and \(f: A \to R\) (\(f \in G(R)\)), we have: \[
\begin{CD}
G(A) @>{r(A)}>> \mathrm{GL}_V(A) \\
@V{f_*}VV @VV{f_*}V \\
G(R) @>{r(R)}>> \mathrm{GL}_V(R)
\end{CD}
\qquad
\begin{array}{rcl}
\mathrm{id} & \longmapsto & u \\
f & \longmapsto & f_* u
\end{array}
\] Then \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Grp}}(G, \mathrm{GL}_V) \cong \dots\)
Given a \(k\)-morphism \(V \xrightarrow{\rho} V \otimes A\), one has \(V \otimes A \to V \otimes A\), \((v, a) \mapsto a\rho(v)\). Then: \[
\operatorname{Hom}_k(V, V \otimes A) = \operatorname{Hom}_k(V, \operatorname{Hom}_A(A, V \otimes A)) = \operatorname{Hom}_A(V \otimes A, V \otimes A).
\] We narrow down to \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Grp}}(G, \mathrm{GL}_V) = \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{comod}}(V, V \otimes A)\).


Proposition 5 (Filtered Union of Finite-Dimensional Submodules) Every \(\mathcal{O}(G)\)-comodule \((V, \rho)\) is a filtered union of finite-dimensional submodules.


Proof. If \(W_1, W_2 \subseteq V\) are submodules, then \(W_1 + W_2\) is a submodule. It suffices to show that every \(v \in V\) is contained in a finite-dimensional submodule of \(V\).
Let \((f_i)_{i \in I}\) be a \(k\)-basis of \(\mathcal{O}(G)\), then: \[
\rho(v) = \sum_{i \in I} v_i \otimes f_i \in V \otimes \mathcal{O}(G) \quad (\text{finite sum}).
\] Set \(W := \operatorname{span}_k\{v_i\}\).
Claim: \(W\) is a subcomodule of \(V\) containing \(v\).
First, \(v = \sum_{i \in I} v_i f_i(e) \in W\). It remains to show that \(\rho(v_i) \in W \otimes \mathcal{O}(G)\) for all \(v_i\). From the coassociativity diagram: \[
\begin{CD}
V @>{\rho}>> V \otimes \mathcal{O}(G) \\
@V{\rho}VV @VV{\mathrm{id} \otimes m^*}V \\
V \otimes \mathcal{O}(G) @>{\rho \otimes \mathrm{id}}>> V \otimes \mathcal{O}(G) \otimes \mathcal{O}(G)
\end{CD}
\] we have: \[
\sum v_i \otimes m^*(f_i) = \sum a_{ijl} \, v_i \otimes f_j \otimes f_l
\] \[
\sum \rho(v_i) \otimes f_i = \sum \rho(v_l) \otimes f_l.
\] Then \(\rho(v_l) = \sum a_{ijl} \, v_i \otimes f_j \in W \otimes \mathcal{O}(G)\).


Remark 1 (Algebraic Action). If \(V = \mathcal{O}(X)\) with \(X\) affine over \(k\), then \(V\) is an \(\mathcal{O}(G)\)-comodule. Given \(\rho: V \to V \otimes \mathcal{O}(G)\), suppose \(\rho\) is a morphism of \(k\)-algebras. Then \(X \times G \xrightarrow{a} X\): \[
\begin{CD}
\mathcal{O}(X) @>{\rho}>> \mathcal{O}(X) \otimes \mathcal{O}(G) \\
@| @VV{\mathrm{id} \otimes e^*}V \\
\mathcal{O}(X) @= \mathcal{O}(X)
\end{CD}
\qquad
\begin{CD}
\mathcal{O}(X) @>{\rho}>> \mathcal{O}(X) \otimes \mathcal{O}(G) \\
@V{\rho}VV @VV{\mathrm{id} \otimes m^*}V \\
\mathcal{O}(X) \otimes \mathcal{O}(G) @>{\rho \otimes \mathrm{id}}>> \mathcal{O}(X) \otimes \mathcal{O}(G) \otimes \mathcal{O}(G)
\end{CD}
\] \(\implies a\) is a right algebraic action, which is in fact: \[
G \longrightarrow \operatorname{Aut}_X \longrightarrow \mathrm{GL}_{\mathcal{O}(X)}
\] \[
\begin{array}{rcl}
\operatorname{Aut}_X(R) & \longrightarrow & \mathrm{GL}_{\mathcal{O}(X)}(R) \\
\operatorname{Aut}(X \times R) & \longrightarrow & \mathrm{GL}(\mathcal{O}(X) \otimes R) \\
f & \longmapsto & f^*: \mathcal{O}(X \times R) \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathcal{O}(X \times R).
\end{array}
\]



Definition 6 (Simple Representation) A representation \(V\) of \(G\) is simple if \(V \neq 0\) and has no non-trivial subrepresentations.
Then every simple representation of a linear algebraic group is finite-dimensional.


Definition 7 (Regular Representation) Let \(X = G\), with \(m: X \times G \to X\) the right action. Then \(\mathcal{O}(X) = \mathcal{O}(G)\) is an \(\mathcal{O}(G)\)-comodule. The morphism: \[
G \longrightarrow \mathrm{GL}_A
\] is called the regular representation, where \(A = \mathcal{O}(G)\).


Theorem 4 (Finite-Dimensional Faithful Action) The regular representation of \(G\) has a faithful finite-dimensional subrepresentation. In particular, the regular representation is faithful and \(G \hookrightarrow \mathrm{GL}_n\).


Proof. For any finite-dimensional submodule \(V \subseteq \mathcal{O}(G)\), if \(f_1, \dots, f_n\) is a basis of \(V\), then \(\mathrm{GL}_V \cong \mathrm{GL}_n\): \[
\begin{CD}
V @>>> V \otimes \mathcal{O}(G) \\
@VVV @VVV \\
\mathcal{O}(G) @>{m^*}>> \mathcal{O}(G) \otimes \mathcal{O}(G)
\end{CD}
\] Suppose \(m^*(f_i) = \sum_j f_j \otimes b_{ij}\). Then: \[
G \longrightarrow \mathrm{GL}_V \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \mathrm{GL}_n, \quad g \longmapsto (b_{ij}(g)).
\] Then we want: \[
\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{GL}_n) = k[T_{ij}, \det{}^{-1}] \longrightarrow \mathcal{O}(G), \quad T_{ij} \longmapsto b_{ij}
\] to be surjective. It suffices to find \(b_{ij}\) generating \(\mathcal{O}(G)\).
Since \(\mathrm{id}: G \xrightarrow{e \times \mathrm{id}} G \times G \xrightarrow{m} G \implies f_i = \sum_j f_j(e) b_{ij}\), it suffices to choose \(V \subseteq \mathcal{O}(G)\) such that: - \(V\) generates \(\mathcal{O}(G)\), - \(V\) is a submodule of \(\mathcal{O}(G)\), - \(\dim_k V < +\infty\).



Definition 8 (Free Comodule) For a vector space \(V/k\), \(V \otimes \mathcal{O}(G)\) equipped with: \[
V \otimes \mathcal{O}(G) \xrightarrow{\;\mathrm{id} \otimes m^* \;} V \otimes \mathcal{O}(G) \otimes \mathcal{O}(G)
\] is an \(\mathcal{O}(G)\)-comodule, called the free comodule.


Proposition 6 (Finite-Dimensional Comodules Embed into Free Comodules) Every finite-dimensional \(\mathcal{O}(G)\)-comodule \(V\) is a submodule of \((\mathcal{O}(G)^n, m^*)\).


Proof. \(\rho: V \to V \otimes \mathcal{O}(G)\) is injective (since \((\mathrm{id} \otimes e^*) \circ \rho = \mathrm{id}_V\)), and: \[
\begin{CD}
V @>{\rho}>> V \otimes \mathcal{O}(G) \\
@V{\rho}VV @VV{\mathrm{id} \otimes m^*}V \\
V \otimes \mathcal{O}(G) @>{\rho \otimes \mathrm{id}}>> V \otimes \mathcal{O}(G) \otimes \mathcal{O}(G)
\end{CD}
\] is a morphism of comodules.


Theorem 5 (Generating Representation) Let \(G \hookrightarrow \mathrm{GL}_V\) be a faithful finite-dimensional representation of \(G\). Every finite-dimensional representation \(W\) of \(G\) can be constructed from \(V\) by tensor, direct sum, dual, and subquotient.


Proof. See [Milne].

Instructor: Prof. Miaofen Chen (陈苗芬)
Credits: 3.0 (54 Total Credit Hours)

title: Algebraic Groups
text:
Course Overview
Linear algebraic groups are fundamental objects and tools in mathematics, with wide applications in number theory, representation theory, automorphic forms, and dynamical systems on homogeneous spaces.
The goal of this course is to systematically develop the theory of linear algebraic groups, focusing on their structural properties, representations, and root-theoretic classifications, laying a solid foundation for research in arithmetic geometry, the Langlands program, and related areas.


Syllabus & Lecture Schedule
The notes are organized according to the 7 main modules of the course:

title: Algebraic Groups
section: [Weeks 1–2] Linear Algebraic Groups: Foundations & Jordan Decomposition
text:
[Weeks 1–2] Linear Algebraic Groups: Foundations & Jordan Decomposition

Affine varieties and the definition of linear algebraic groups
Subgroups, homomorphisms, and canonical examples (\(\mathrm{GL}_n\), \(\mathrm{SL}_n\), \(\mathrm{Sp}_{2n}\), \(\mathrm{SO}_n\))
Jordan-Chevalley decomposition (additive and multiplicative) in \(\mathrm{GL}(V)\) and in abstract linear algebraic groups

title: Algebraic Groups
text:
[Weeks 3–4] Tannakian Formalism and Lie Algebras

Group actions on affine coordinate algebras \(\mathcal{O}(G)\) and locally finite representations
Tannakian perspective: reconstructing an algebraic group from its representation category
The Lie algebra \(\mathfrak{g} = \operatorname{Lie}(G)\) as invariant derivations
The adjoint representation \(\mathrm{Ad}: G \to \mathrm{GL}(\mathfrak{g})\)

title: Algebraic Groups
text:
[Week 5] Tori in Algebraic Groups

Diagonalizable groups and Cartier duality
Character lattice \(X^*(T)\) and cocharacter lattice \(X_*(T)\)
Algebraic tori (split vs. non-split)
Rigidity of tori, centralizers, and normalizers

title: Algebraic Groups
text:
[Week 6] Quotients of Algebraic Groups

Actions on algebraic varieties, orbits, and stabilizers
Chevalley’s Theorem on constructing subgroups as stabilizers of lines
Existence and geometric construction of homogeneous spaces and quotient varieties \(G/H\)

title: Algebraic Groups
text:
[Weeks 7–8] Reductive Groups

The radical \(R(G)\) and the unipotent radical \(R_u(G)\)
Definitions and characterizations of semisimple and reductive groups
Action of maximal tori on \(\operatorname{Lie}(G)\) and the root space decomposition
Basic properties of roots and root systems

title: Algebraic Groups
text:
[Weeks 10–11] Parabolic Subgroups of Reductive Groups

The Borel Fixed-Point Theorem for complete varieties
Maximal connected solvable subgroups (Borel subgroups \(B\))
The flag variety \(G/B\) and its projectivity/completeness
Parabolic subgroups: standard parabolic subgroups and their classification

title: Algebraic Groups
text:
[Weeks 12–13] Various Decompositions of Reductive Groups

The Bruhat decomposition: \(G = \bigsqcup_{w \in W} B w B\)
Relative root systems and decompositions over non-algebraically closed fields
Connections to the Iwasawa and Cartan decompositions in Lie groups and arithmetic groups

title: 23.0 Basics
text:
Throughout this chapter:

Let \(k\) be a fixed base field.
A \(k\)-variety is defined as a geometrically reduced, separated scheme of finite type over \(k\).
We denote by \(\mathrm{Sch}/k\) the category of schemes of finite type over \(k\), and by \(\mathrm{Var}/k\) the full subcategory of \(k\)-varieties.
For an affine scheme \(X = \operatorname{Spec} A\), \(A\) is a finitely generated \(k\)-algebra.



Definition 1 (Algebraic Group and Abelian Variety)  

An algebraic group over \(k\) is a group object in the category \(\mathrm{Sch}/k\). That is, it is a scheme \(G\) of finite type over \(k\) equipped with \(k\)-morphisms:

Multiplication: \(m: G \times_k G \to G\),
Inverse: \(i: G \to G\),
Identity section: \(e: \operatorname{Spec} k \to G\),

satisfying the usual group axioms.
An abelian variety is an algebraic variety \(A \in \mathrm{Var}/k\) which is a proper, geometrically connected group object in \(\mathrm{Sch}/k\).



Lemma 1 (Smoothness of Geometrically Reduced Groups) Any geometrically reduced algebraic group \(G\) over \(k\) is smooth. Consequently, its connected components coincide with its irreducible components.


Proof. Proof sketch. Since \(G_{\bar{k}}\) is reduced and of finite type over an algebraically closed field, its smooth locus \(\operatorname{Sm}(G_{\bar{k}})\) is open and non-empty. For any closed point \(g \in G(\bar{k})\), the group translation \(L_g: G_{\bar{k}} \to G_{\bar{k}}\) is an automorphism mapping smooth points to smooth points. Transitivity of translations implies that every point of \(G_{\bar{k}}\) is smooth. Thus \(G\) is smooth over \(k\). Because smooth schemes are locally irreducible, the connected components must coincide with the irreducible components.


Lemma 2 (Rigidity Lemma) Let \(X, Y, Z\) be varieties over \(k\) with \(X\) proper and geometrically irreducible, and \(Y\) geometrically irreducible. Let \[
f: X \times_k Y \to Z
\] be a \(k\)-morphism. Suppose there exists a \(k\)-rational point \(y_0 \in Y(k)\) such that \(f(X \times \{y_0\}) = \{z_0\}\) for some \(z_0 \in Z(k)\).
Then \(f\) factors through the canonical projection \(p_2: X \times_k Y \to Y\). That is, there exists a morphism \(g: Y \to Z\) such that \(f = g \circ p_2\).


Proof. Fix a rational point \(x_0 \in X(k)\) (extending scalars to \(\bar{k}\) if necessary). Define \(g: Y \to Z\) by the composition: \[
Y \xrightarrow{x_0 \times \mathrm{id}_Y} X \times_k Y \xrightarrow{f} Z.
\] We show that \(f(x, y) = g(y)\) for all \(x \in X, y \in Y\).

Choose an affine open neighborhood \(U \subseteq Z\) containing \(z_0\). The complement \(Z \setminus U\) is closed in \(Z\), so \(f^{-1}(Z \setminus U)\) is closed in \(X \times_k Y\).
Since \(X\) is proper over \(k\), the projection \(p_2: X \times_k Y \to Y\) is universally closed. Thus: \[
W := p_2\big(f^{-1}(Z \setminus U)\big) = \{ y \in Y \mid \exists x \in X \text{ with } f(x, y) \notin U \}
\] is a closed subset of \(Y\).
By hypothesis, \(f(X \times \{y_0\}) = \{z_0\} \subseteq U\), so \(y_0 \notin W\). Hence \(Y \setminus W\) is an open neighborhood of \(y_0\). Pick an affine open neighborhood \(V \subseteq Y \setminus W\) containing \(y_0\).
By construction, \(f(X \times V) \subseteq U\). Since \(U\) is affine, we may choose a closed embedding \(U \hookrightarrow \mathbb{A}^n\). For every closed point \(y \in V\), the fiber \(X \times \{y\} \cong X\) is proper and connected. Its image in the affine space \(\mathbb{A}^n\) under \(f\) must be both proper and affine, hence it must be a single point: \[
f(X \times \{y\}) = \{f(x_0, y)\} = \{g(y)\}.
\]
Therefore, \(f|_{X \times V} = (g \circ p_2)|_{X \times V}\). Because \(X \times_k Y\) is reduced and \(Z\) is separated, two morphisms agreeing on a non-empty open subscheme are identical everywhere (Reduced-to-Separated Theorem). Thus \(f = g \circ p_2\).



Proposition 1 (Proper Connected Groups are Abelian) Any proper connected smooth algebraic group \(G\) over \(k\) is abelian. In particular, abelian varieties are commutative.


Proof. Consider the commutator morphism: \[
f: G \times_k G \to G, \quad (x, y) \mapsto x y x^{-1} y^{-1}.
\] Observe that \(f(G \times \{e\}) = \{e\}\). Since \(G\) is proper and connected, Lemma 2 implies that \(f\) factors through the projection to the second factor: \[
f(x, y) = f(e, y) = e y e^{-1} y^{-1} = e.
\] Hence \(xyx^{-1}y^{-1} = e\) for all \(x, y \in G\), meaning \(xy = yx\). Thus \(G\) is abelian.



Proposition 2 (Separatedness of Group Schemes) Every group scheme \(G\) of finite type over a field \(k\) is separated.


Proof. A morphism \(G \to \operatorname{Spec} k\) is separated if and only if the diagonal \(\Delta: G \to G \times_k G\) is a closed immersion.
Consider the difference morphism \(\mu: G \times_k G \to G\) defined by \((g_1, g_2) \mapsto g_1 g_2^{-1}\). The diagonal \(\Delta(G)\) is the scheme-theoretic pullback of the identity section \(e: \operatorname{Spec} k \to G\) along \(\mu\): \[
\begin{CD}
G @>{\Delta}>> G \times_k G \\
@VVV @VV{\mu}V \\
\operatorname{Spec} k @>{e}>> G
\end{CD}
\] Because base change preserves closed immersions, it suffices to prove that \(e: \operatorname{Spec} k \to G\) is a closed immersion. The image of \(e\) is a single point \(e \in G\). Since \(G\) is of finite type over \(k\), the point \(e\) has residue field \(k(e) \cong k\) and is closed. Thus \(e\) is a closed immersion, which implies \(\Delta\) is a closed immersion. Therefore, \(G\) is separated over \(k\).


Lemma 3 (Open Subgroups are Closed)  

If \(G\) is a group scheme over \(k\) such that \(G_{\mathrm{red}} \times_k G_{\mathrm{red}}\) is reduced, then \(G_{\mathrm{red}} \hookrightarrow G\) is a closed subgroup scheme. In particular, if \(G_{\mathrm{red}}\) is geometrically reduced (e.g., if \(k\) is perfect), then \(G_{\mathrm{red}} \hookrightarrow G\) is a smooth closed subgroup scheme of \(G\).
Let \(\varphi: G' \to G\) be a homomorphism of group schemes over \(k\). If the image \(\varphi(G')\) is open in \(G\), then \(\varphi(G')\) is also closed in \(G\).



Proof. Proof of (2). Let \(U = \varphi(G') \subseteq G\) be open. Endow the complement \(Z := G \setminus U\) with the reduced subscheme structure. It suffices to show that \(Z\) is open.
Consider the action map \(Z \times_k G' \to G\) given by \((z, g') \mapsto z \cdot \varphi(g')\). For any \(g' \in G'\), the translation \(x \mapsto x \cdot \varphi(g')\) is an automorphism of \(G\). Since \(U = \varphi(G')\) is stable under right multiplication by \(\varphi(G')\), its complement \(Z\) is also stable under multiplication by \(\varphi(G')\).
Because translations are open morphisms, the image of \(Z \times_k G' \to G\) is a union of translates of \(Z\), which is open. But this image is precisely \(Z\) itself. Hence \(Z\) is open, which proves \(U = G \setminus Z\) is closed.


Lemma 4 (Immersions of Group Schemes are Closed) Let \(i: G' \hookrightarrow G\) be an immersion of group schemes over \(k\). Then \(i\) is a closed immersion.


Proof. Without loss of generality, assume \(G\) and \(G'\) are reduced. Let \(\overline{G'}\) denote the scheme-theoretic closure of \(i(G')\) in \(G\) equipped with the reduced structure. Since multiplication \(m: G \times_k G \to G\) is continuous and maps \(G' \times_k G'\) into \(G'\), it maps the closure \(\overline{G'} \times_k \overline{G'}\) into \(\overline{G'}\). Thus \(\overline{G'}\) is a closed subgroup scheme of \(G\).
Since \(i\) is an immersion, \(i(G')\) is an open subscheme of \(\overline{G'}\). By Lemma 3, an open subgroup scheme of \(\overline{G'}\) is closed in \(\overline{G'}\). Hence \(i(G') = \overline{G'}\), so \(i(G')\) is closed in \(G\).


Lemma 5 (Connected Implies Irreducible) Let \(G\) be a group scheme of finite type over \(k\).

If \(G\) is irreducible, then \(G\) is quasi-compact.
If \(G\) is connected, then \(G\) is irreducible.


(Reference: The Stacks Project, Tag 047R, Tag 047S).


Proposition 3 (Subgroup Schemes and Kernels)  

A closed subscheme \(H \subseteq G\) is a normal subgroup scheme (denoted \(H \trianglelefteq G\)) if for all \(T \in \mathrm{Sch}/k\), \(H(T)\) is a normal subgroup of \(G(T)\) (equivalently, \(H(R) \trianglelefteq G(R)\) for all \(R \in \mathrm{Alg}_k\)).
Let \(\varphi: G \to G'\) be a homomorphism of group schemes. The scheme-theoretic kernel is defined as the fiber product: \[
\ker \varphi := \operatorname{Spec} k \times_{e, G', \varphi} G = \varphi^{-1}(e).
\] Then \(\ker \varphi\) is a closed normal subgroup scheme of \(G\).
On functor of points, \(\ker(\varphi)(R) = \ker(G(R) \to G'(R))\) for all \(R \in \mathrm{Alg}_k\).



Proposition 4 (Homomorphisms and Dimensions) Let \(\varphi: G \to G'\) be a homomorphism of algebraic groups over \(k\).

The scheme-theoretic image \(\varphi(G)\) is closed in \(G'\). We denote \(\operatorname{Im} \varphi := \varphi(G)_{\mathrm{red}}\).
Dimension Formula: \[
\dim G = \dim \ker \varphi + \dim \operatorname{Im} \varphi.
\]



Proof. Idea of Proof. By Chevalley’s Theorem on constructible sets, \(\varphi(G)\) contains a dense open subset of its closure. Group translations then show that \(\varphi(G)\) is open in its closure \(\overline{\varphi(G)}\). By Lemma 3, an open subgroup of \(\overline{\varphi(G)}\) is closed, whence \(\varphi(G) = \overline{\varphi(G)}\).


Proposition 5 (Image Factorization and Flatness)  

If \(G'\) is reduced and \(\varphi: G \to G'\) is dominant, then \(\varphi\) is an fppf morphism (faithfully flat locally of finite presentation).
If \(G\) is smooth, any homomorphism \(\varphi: G \to H\) factors canonically as: \[
G \xrightarrow{p} I \xrightarrow{i} H
\] where \(p\) is fppf and \(i\) is a closed immersion into \(H\).



Proof. Set \(I := \varphi(G)\) with reduced subscheme structure. By generic flatness, there exists a dense open subscheme \(U \subseteq I\) over which \(\varphi^{-1}(U) \to U\) is flat. Since translations by rational points (over \(\bar{k}\)) act transitively on \(I\), translates of \(U\) cover \(I\). Therefore, \(\varphi_{\bar{k}}\) is flat everywhere. Being surjective (image is closed) between noetherian schemes, it is fppf.



Remark 1 (Hopf Algebras and Functor of Points). An affine scheme \(G = \operatorname{Spec} A\) is a group scheme if and only if its coordinate ring \(A = \mathcal{O}(G)\) is a commutative Hopf algebra over \(k\), equipped with:

Comultiplication \(\Delta: A \to A \otimes_k A\),
Counit \(\varepsilon: A \to k\),
Antipode \(S: A \to A\).

We have an anti-equivalence of categories: \[
\{\text{Commutative f.g. Hopf } k\text{-algebras}\}^{\mathrm{op}} \xrightarrow{\sim} \{\text{Affine / Linear } k\text{-algebraic groups}\}.
\]
Via the functor of points, the Yoneda embedding yields a fully faithful functor: \[
\mathbf{GrpSch}/k \hookrightarrow \mathrm{Fun}(\mathrm{Alg}_k, \mathbf{Grp}), \quad G \mapsto (R \mapsto G(R) = \operatorname{Hom}_{k\text{-alg}}(A, R)).
\]


Example 1 (Basic Examples)  

Finite Constant Group: Let \(\Gamma\) be a finite abstract group. The coordinate algebra is \(A = \prod_{g \in \Gamma} k \cdot e_g\) with orthogonal idempotents \(e_g\).

Comultiplication: \(\Delta(e_x) = \sum_{yz = x} e_y \otimes e_z\),
Antipode: \(S(e_x) = e_{x^{-1}}\),
Counit: \(\varepsilon(e_x) = \delta_{x, e}\).

On \(R\)-points: \[
G(R) = \left\{ (r_g)_{g \in \Gamma} \in R^\Gamma \;\middle|\; \sum_{g \in \Gamma} r_g = 1, \, r_g r_h = 0 \text{ for } g \neq h \right\}.
\]
Standard Matrix Groups (for \(n \in \mathbb{N}\)):

General Linear Group \(\mathrm{GL}_n\) (Reductive): \[
\mathrm{GL}_n(R) = \{ M \in \mathrm{Mat}_{n \times n}(R) \mid \det(M) \in R^\times \}.
\]
Standard Borel Subgroup \(B_n\) (Solvable): \[
B_n(R) = \{ (x_{ij}) \in \mathrm{GL}_n(R) \mid x_{ij} = 0 \text{ for all } i > j \}.
\]
Standard Unipotent Subgroup \(U_n\) (Unipotent): \[
U_n(R) = \{ (x_{ij}) \in B_n(R) \mid x_{ii} = 1 \text{ for all } 1 \le i \le n \}.
\]
Standard Maximal Torus \(T_n\) (Split Torus): \[
T_n(R) = \{ (x_{ij}) \in B_n(R) \mid x_{ij} = 0 \text{ for all } i \neq j \} \cong (\mathbb{G}_{m, R})^n.
\]

These satisfy the inclusion hierarchy: \[
U_n \trianglelefteq B_n \subseteq \mathrm{GL}_n, \quad T_n \subseteq B_n, \quad B_n = T_n \ltimes U_n.
\]




Proposition 6 (Existence of the Largest Étale Subalgebra) Let \(X\) be a scheme of finite type over \(k\). Then there exists a unique largest étale \(k\)-subalgebra \(\pi_0(X) \subseteq \mathcal{O}(X)\).


Proof. 

If \(A_1, A_2 \subseteq \mathcal{O}(X)\) are étale \(k\)-subalgebras, the subring generated by them is the image of the canonical map \(A_1 \otimes_k A_2 \to \mathcal{O}(X)\). Since the tensor product of étale algebras is étale and any quotient of an étale algebra over a field is étale, the composite is étale.
For any étale subalgebra \(A \subseteq \mathcal{O}(X)\), base change to the separable closure satisfies: \[
A \otimes_k k^{\mathrm{sep}} \subseteq \mathcal{O}(X) \otimes_k k^{\mathrm{sep}} = \mathcal{O}(X_{k^{\mathrm{sep}}}).
\] Since \(A \otimes_k k^{\mathrm{sep}} \cong \prod_{i=1}^m k^{\mathrm{sep}}\), it admits a complete system of orthogonal idempotents \(e_1, \dots, e_m\). Each \(e_i\) defines a non-empty open and closed subscheme \(V(1 - e_i)\) of \(X_{k^{\mathrm{sep}}}\). Thus \(m \le \#\{\text{connected components of } X_{k^{\mathrm{sep}}}\}\).
Because \(X\) is of finite type, it has finitely many connected components. The dimension \(\dim_k A\) is uniformly bounded, guaranteeing the existence of a unique maximal étale subalgebra.



Definition 2 (The Scheme \(\pi_0(X)\))  

Let \(A \subseteq \mathcal{O}(X)\) be the largest étale \(k\)-subalgebra. We define: \[
\pi_0(X) := \operatorname{Spec} A.
\] The inclusion \(A \hookrightarrow \mathcal{O}(X)\) induces a canonical morphism \(X \to \pi_0(X)\).
Universal Property: For any étale \(k\)-scheme \(Y\) and any \(k\)-morphism \(f: X \to Y\), there exists a unique morphism \(\bar{f}: \pi_0(X) \to Y\) such that the following diagram commutes: \[
\begin{CD}
X @>{f}>> Y \\
@VVV @| \\
\pi_0(X) @>{\exists! \bar{f}}>> Y
\end{CD}
\]
Properties:

The fibers of \(X \to \pi_0(X)\) are the connected components of \(X\).
For every \(y \in \pi_0(X)\), the fiber \(X_y\) is geometrically connected over the residue field \(k(y)\).
\(\pi_0\) preserves finite products: \(\pi_0(X \times_k Y) \cong \pi_0(X) \times_k \pi_0(Y)\).
The canonical morphism \(X \to \pi_0(X)\) is fppf.




Proposition 7 (Geometric Connectedness Criteria)  

If \(X\) is connected and \(X(k) \neq \emptyset\), then \(X\) is geometrically connected.
If \(X\) is geometrically connected and \(Y\) is connected, then \(X \times_k Y\) is connected.



Proof. 

If \(X\) is connected, \(\pi_0(X) = \operatorname{Spec} L\), where \(L/k\) is a finite separable field extension. A rational point \(x \in X(k)\) provides a section \(\operatorname{Spec} k \to X \to \operatorname{Spec} L\), forcing \(L \cong k\). Thus \(\pi_0(X) = \operatorname{Spec} k\), so \(X\) is geometrically connected.
We have \(\pi_0(X) \cong \operatorname{Spec} k\). By product preservation, \[
\pi_0(X \times_k Y) \cong \pi_0(X) \times_k \pi_0(Y) \cong \operatorname{Spec} k \times_k \pi_0(Y) \cong \pi_0(Y).
\] Since \(Y\) is connected, \(\pi_0(Y) = \operatorname{Spec} L\) for a field \(L\). Thus \(\pi_0(X \times_k Y) \cong \operatorname{Spec} L\), which shows \(X \times_k Y\) is connected.



Definition 3 (The Identity Component \(G^\circ\))  

The identity component \(G^\circ\) of an algebraic group \(G\) is the connected component containing the identity section \(e\). Endowed with its open subscheme structure, \(G^\circ\) is a smooth, geometrically connected, open and closed normal subgroup scheme of \(G\).
For any open subgroup \(G' \subseteq G\) of finite index, \(G^\circ \subseteq G' \subseteq G\), and \((G^\circ)^\circ = G^\circ\).



Proposition 8 (\(\pi_0(G)\) and the Connected Component) Let \(G\) be an algebraic group over \(k\).

\(\pi_0(G)\) is a finite étale group scheme over \(k\), and the canonical morphism \(G \to \pi_0(G)\) is a homomorphism of algebraic groups.
The identity component \(G^\circ := \ker(G \to \pi_0(G))\) is a geometrically connected, normal closed and open subgroup scheme of \(G\). For any field extension \(L/k\), we have \((G_L)^\circ = (G^\circ)_L\).
\(G\) is connected \(\iff \pi_0(G) \cong \operatorname{Spec} k \iff G\) is geometrically connected.
Formation of the identity component commutes with products: \((G \times_k H)^\circ \cong G^\circ \times_k H^\circ\).
If \(H\) is a connected group scheme over \(k\), any homomorphism \(\psi: H \to G\) factors uniquely through \(G^\circ \hookrightarrow G\).



Proof. 

Since \(\pi_0\) commutes with finite products, the group morphisms \(m, i, e\) on \(G\) induce group structure morphisms on \(\pi_0(G)\) by functoriality.
For (3), since \(e \in G^\circ(k)\), \(G^\circ\) has a \(k\)-rational point. Proposition 7(1) implies that \(G^\circ\) is geometrically connected.
For (5), since \(H\) is connected, \(\pi_0(H) \cong \operatorname{Spec} k\). Functoriality yields a commutative diagram: \[
\begin{CD}
H @>{\psi}>> G \\
@VVV @VVV \\
\pi_0(H) \cong \operatorname{Spec} k @>{e}>> \pi_0(G)
\end{CD}
\] Thus the composition \(H \to G \to \pi_0(G)\) is the trivial map, which implies that \(\psi\) factors uniquely through \(G^\circ = \ker(G \to \pi_0(G))\).



Definition 4 (Exact Sequences of Group Schemes) A sequence of homomorphisms of group schemes over \(k\): \[
1 \longrightarrow N \xrightarrow{\quad i \quad} G \xrightarrow{\quad p \quad} Q \longrightarrow 1
\] is said to be exact if:

\(i: N \hookrightarrow G\) is a closed immersion identifying \(N\) with a normal subgroup scheme of \(G\);
\(p: G \to Q\) is an fppf morphism;
\(i(N) = \ker(p)\).

title: 22.0 Preliminaries
text:
Definition 1 (Cartier Divisor) Let \(X\) be an irreducible complex variety. Let \(\mathcal{M}_X := \mathcal{K}_X\) be the constant sheaf of rational functions on \(X\), and \(\mathcal{O}_X \subseteq \mathcal{M}_X\) the structure sheaf.

A Cartier divisor on \(X\) is a global section of the quotient sheaf of units \(\mathcal{M}_X^* / \mathcal{O}_X^*\). The abelian group of Cartier divisors on \(X\) is denoted by: \[
\operatorname{Div}(X) := \Gamma(X, \mathcal{M}_X^* / \mathcal{O}_X^*).
\]
In terms of local data, a Cartier divisor \(D \in \operatorname{Div}(X)\) is represented by a collection of pairs \(\{(U_i, f_i)\}_{i \in I}\), where \(\{U_i\}\) is an open covering of \(X\), \(f_i \in \Gamma(U_i, \mathcal{M}_X^*)\), and on overlaps \(U_{ij} = U_i \cap U_j\), \[
\frac{f_i}{f_j} = g_{ij} \in \Gamma(U_{ij}, \mathcal{O}_X^*).
\] Two such collections \(\{(U_i, f_i)\}\) and \(\{(V_j, g_j)\}\) determine the same Cartier divisor if they agree on a common refinement \(\{W_k\}\), that is, \(f_k / g_k \in \Gamma(W_k, \mathcal{O}_X^*)\).
The support of \(D\) is the closed subset: \[
\operatorname{Supp}(D) := \big\{ x \in X \;\big|\; (f_i)_x \notin \mathcal{O}_{X, x}^* \text{ for } x \in U_i \big\}.
\]
The group operation is written additively: for \(D = \{(U_i, f_i)\}\) and \(D' = \{(U_i, f_i')\}\), \[
D + D' = \{(U_i, f_i f_i')\}.
\]
A Cartier divisor \(D\) is effective (denoted \(D \ge 0\)) if it can be represented by local equations \(f_i \in \Gamma(U_i, \mathcal{O}_X)\) for all \(i\). We write \(D \ge D'\) if and only if \(D - D' \ge 0\).



Remark 1 (Sheaf of Meromorphic Functions on Non-Reduced Schemes). If \(X\) is not necessarily reduced, \(\mathcal{M}_X\) is defined as the sheaf of total quotient rings: for an affine open \(U = \operatorname{Spec} A\), \[
\mathcal{M}_X(U) := A_{\mathrm{tot}},
\] where \(A_{\mathrm{tot}} = S^{-1}A\) is the localization of \(A\) at the multiplicatively closed set \(S \subseteq A\) of all non-zero-divisors. Then \(\mathcal{O}_X^* \subseteq \mathcal{M}_X^*\), and Cartier divisors are defined identically.


Definition 2 (Cycles and Weil Divisors)  

Let \(X\) be a variety (or scheme) of pure dimension \(n\). A \(k\)-cycle on \(X\) is a formal \(\mathbb{Z}\)-linear combination of \(k\)-dimensional irreducible subvarieties of \(X\). The abelian group of \(k\)-cycles is denoted by \(Z_k(X)\).
A Weil divisor on \(X\) is an \((n-1)\)-cycle, so the group of Weil divisors is \(\operatorname{WDiv}(X) := Z_{n-1}(X)\).
If \(X\) is irreducible, for any \(f \in \mathcal{K}(X)^*\) and any prime divisor \(V \in Z_{n-1}(X)\), we define: \[
\operatorname{ord}_V(f) := \operatorname{ord}_{\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}_{X, V}}(f),
\] where \(\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}_{X, V}\) is the normalization of the local ring \(\mathcal{O}_{X, V}\) in \(\mathcal{K}(X)\). The rational function \(f\) defines a principal Weil divisor: \[
\operatorname{div}(f) = \sum_{V \subseteq X} \operatorname{ord}_V(f) [V].
\]



Proposition 1 (Cycle Map) There is a canonical cycle homomorphism: \[
\operatorname{cyc}: \operatorname{Div}(X) \longrightarrow \operatorname{WDiv}(X), \quad D \longmapsto [D] := \sum_{V \subseteq X} \operatorname{ord}_V(D) \cdot [V],
\] where \(\operatorname{ord}_V(D) = \operatorname{ord}_V(f_i)\) whenever the generic point \(\eta_V \in U_i\).

The map \(\operatorname{cyc}\) is injective if \(X\) is normal.
The map \(\operatorname{cyc}\) is an isomorphism if \(X\) is non-singular (regular).



Definition 3 (Principal Divisors and Rational Sections)  

For any global section \(f \in \Gamma(X, \mathcal{M}_X^*)\), \(f\) defines a principal Cartier divisor: \[
\operatorname{div}(f) \in \Gamma(X, \mathcal{M}_X^* / \mathcal{O}_X^*) = \operatorname{Div}(X).
\] The subgroup of principal divisors is denoted by \(\operatorname{PDiv}(X) \subseteq \operatorname{Div}(X)\).
Two Cartier divisors \(D_1, D_2\) are linearly equivalent (denoted \(D_1 \sim D_2\) or \(D_1 \equiv_{\mathrm{lin}} D_2\)) if: \[
D_1 - D_2 \in \operatorname{PDiv}(X).
\]
Let \(L\) be a line bundle on \(X\). For any global section \(s \in \Gamma(X, L)\), choosing local trivializations \(\psi_i: L|_{U_i} \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathcal{O}_{U_i}\) defines an effective Cartier divisor \(\{ (U_i, \psi_i(s)) \} \in \operatorname{Div}(X)\), denoted \(\operatorname{div}(s)_0\).
More generally, any non-zero rational section \(s \in \Gamma(X, L \otimes_{\mathcal{O}_X} \mathcal{M}_X)\) determines a Cartier divisor \(\operatorname{div}(s) \in \operatorname{Div}(X)\).



Definition 4 (The Sheaf \(\mathcal{O}_X(D)\))  

Every Cartier divisor \(D = \{(U_i, f_i)\} \in \operatorname{Div}(X)\) determines an invertible sheaf \(\mathcal{O}_X(D)\) (or \(\mathcal{L}(D)\)) whose local sections are: \[
\mathcal{O}_X(D)(U) := \big\{ s \in \Gamma(U, \mathcal{M}_X) \;\big|\; \operatorname{div}(s)|_U + D|_U \ge 0 \big\}.
\] Locally on each open set \(U_i\), multiplication by \(f_i\) yields an isomorphism: \[
\mathcal{O}_X(D)(U_i) \xrightarrow{\quad \times f_i \quad} \mathcal{O}_X(U_i), \quad s \longmapsto f_i \cdot s,
\] since \(\operatorname{div}(f_i s) = \operatorname{div}(f_i) + \operatorname{div}(s) \ge 0 \implies f_i s \in \mathcal{O}_X(U_i)\).
From the short exact sequence of sheaves on \(X\): \[
0 \longrightarrow \mathcal{O}_X^* \longrightarrow \mathcal{M}_X^* \longrightarrow \mathcal{M}_X^* / \mathcal{O}_X^* \longrightarrow 0,
\] the connecting homomorphism gives: \[
\delta: \operatorname{Div}(X) = \Gamma(X, \mathcal{M}_X^* / \mathcal{O}_X^*) \longrightarrow H^1(X, \mathcal{O}_X^*) = \operatorname{Pic}(X).
\] Furthermore, \(\mathcal{O}_X(D_1) \cong \mathcal{O}_X(D_2) \iff D_1 \sim D_2\).
This construction induces an isomorphism: \[
\operatorname{CaCl}(X) := \operatorname{Div}(X) / \operatorname{PDiv}(X) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \operatorname{Pic}(X)
\] whenever \(X\) is reduced or projective.



Definition 5 (Linear Series and Base Locus)  

Let \(X\) be a variety and \(L\) a line bundle on \(X\). Let \(V \subseteq H^0(X, L)\) be a non-zero finite-dimensional subspace. The linear series associated with \(V\) is: \[
|V| := \mathbb{P}(V^*) = \mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{sub}}(V),
\] the projective space of 1-dimensional subspaces in \(V\). If \(H^0(X, L)\) is finite-dimensional, \(|H^0(X, L)|\) is denoted by \(|L|\) and called the complete linear series.
The evaluation homomorphism is given by: \[
\mathrm{eval}_V: V \otimes_k \mathcal{O}_X \longrightarrow L, \quad s \otimes f \longmapsto f \cdot s|_U.
\]
The base ideal \(\mathfrak{b}(|V|) \subseteq \mathcal{O}_X\) of \(|V|\) is the image of the dualized evaluation: \[
V \otimes_k L^\vee \longrightarrow \mathcal{O}_X, \quad s \otimes \phi \longmapsto \phi(s).
\] The base scheme is the closed subscheme \(\operatorname{Bs}(|V|) \subseteq X\) defined by \(\mathfrak{b}(|V|)\). For a divisor \(D\), we write \(\mathfrak{b}(|D|)\) and \(\operatorname{Bs}(|D|)\) for the base ideal and locus of \(|\mathcal{O}_X(D)|\).



Definition 6 (Base-Point-Free Linear Series)  

A linear series \(|V|\) is free (or base-point-free) if its base ideal is trivial: \(\mathfrak{b}(|V|) = \mathcal{O}_X\) (equivalently, \(\operatorname{Bs}(|V|) = \emptyset\)).
A divisor \(D\) or a line bundle \(L\) is free if its complete linear series is base-point-free.
A line bundle \(L\) is free if and only if \(L\) is generated by its global sections.



Proposition 2 (Maps to Projective Space)  

If \(\dim_k V \ge 1\) and \(B = \operatorname{Bs}(|V|)\), then \(|V|\) defines a morphism: \[
\phi_{|V|}: X \setminus B \longrightarrow \mathbb{P} V = \operatorname{Proj}(\operatorname{Sym} V).
\]
If \(W \subseteq V\) is a linear subspace, we have a commutative naturality diagram: \[
\begin{CD}
X \setminus \operatorname{Bs}(|V|) @>{\phi_{|V|}}>> \mathbb{P} V \setminus \mathbb{P}(V/W) \\
@VVV @VV{\pi}V \\
X \setminus \operatorname{Bs}(|W|) @>{\phi_{|W|}}>> \mathbb{P} W
\end{CD}
\] where \(\pi\) is the linear projection with center \(\mathbb{P}(V/W)\).



Definition 7 (Intersection Number (Snapper’s Formulation))  

Let \(X\) be a proper variety over \(k\). Let \(Y \hookrightarrow X\) be an irreducible subvariety of dimension \(m = \dim Y\). For any line bundles \(L_1, \dots, L_m \in \operatorname{Pic}(X)\), the intersection number is defined by: \[
(L_1 \cdots L_m \cdot Y) := \sum_{I \subseteq \{1, \dots, m\}} (-1)^{|I|} \chi\left(X, \bigotimes_{i \in I} L_i^\vee \otimes_{\mathcal{O}_X} i_* \mathcal{O}_Y\right) = \sum_{I \subseteq \{1, \dots, m\}} (-1)^{|I|} \chi\left(Y, \bigotimes_{i \in I} L_i^\vee|_Y\right).
\]
If \(Y = X\) with \(\dim X = n\), we write \((L_1 \cdots L_n)\) instead of \((L_1 \cdots L_n \cdot X)\). Then: \[
(L_1 \cdots L_m \cdot Y) = (L_1|_Y \cdots L_m|_Y).
\]
For a general subscheme \(Y \subseteq X\) of pure dimension \(m\), associated with the cycle \([Y] = \sum_j \operatorname{length}_{\mathcal{O}_{Y, \eta_j}}(\mathcal{O}_{Y, \eta_j}) [Y_j]\), the intersection number is defined by linearity: \[
(L_1 \cdots L_m \cdot Y) := \sum_j \operatorname{length}(\mathcal{O}_{Y, \eta_j}) (L_1 \cdots L_m \cdot Y_j).
\]
If \(L_i \cong \mathcal{O}_X(D_i)\), we also write \((D_1 \cdots D_m \cdot Y)\) for \((L_1 \cdots L_m \cdot Y)\).




Convention: From now on, unless otherwise stated, every scheme is assumed to be separated, proper, and of finite type over an algebraically closed field \(k = \bar{k}\) with \(\operatorname{char}(k) = 0\). A variety is defined as an irreducible and reduced scheme.



Proposition 3 (Basic Properties of Intersection Numbers)  

Let \(X\) be a proper curve and \(L \in \operatorname{Pic}(X)\). Then \((L \cdot X) = \deg L\). If \(X\) is a proper variety and \(C \subseteq X\) is a curve, \((L \cdot C) = \deg(L|_C)\).
Let \(D \in \operatorname{Div}(X)\) be an effective Cartier divisor. If \(Y \subseteq X\) is an irreducible subvariety of dimension \(n = \dim Y\) such that \(D\) intersects \(Y\) properly (\(Y \not\subseteq \operatorname{Supp} D\)), then \(D|_Y\) is of pure dimension \(n - 1\) and: \[
(L_1 \cdots L_{n-1} \cdot \mathcal{O}_X(D) \cdot Y) = (L_1 \cdots L_{n-1} \cdot D|_Y).
\]
The intersection product is \(\mathbb{Z}\)-multilinear and symmetric: \[
\operatorname{Pic}(X)^m \times A_m(X) \longrightarrow \mathbb{Z}, \quad (L_1, \dots, L_m, [Y]) \longmapsto (L_1 \cdots L_m \cdot [Y]).
\] In particular, if \(Y_1 \sim_{\mathrm{rat}} Y_2\) are rationally equivalent cycles, then: \[
(L_1 \cdots L_m \cdot Y_1) = (L_1 \cdots L_m \cdot Y_2).
\]



Definition 8 (Numerical Equivalence)  

Two line bundles \(L_1, L_2 \in \operatorname{Pic}(X)\) are numerically equivalent (denoted \(L_1 \equiv_{\mathrm{num}} L_2\)) if for every irreducible curve \(C \subseteq X\), \[
(L_1 \cdot C) = (L_2 \cdot C).
\] Two Cartier divisors \(D_1, D_2\) are numerically equivalent (denoted \(D_1 \equiv_{\mathrm{num}} D_2\)) if \(\mathcal{O}_X(D_1) \equiv_{\mathrm{num}} \mathcal{O}_X(D_2)\).
The quotient group: \[
N^1(X) := \operatorname{Pic}(X) / \equiv_{\mathrm{num}}
\] is called the Néron-Severi group of \(X\) (modulo numerical equivalence).



Proposition 4 (The Néron-Severi Group and Picard Number)  

\(N^1(X)\) is torsion-free.
\(N^1(X)\) is a finitely generated free abelian group.
The rank \(\rho(X) := \operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb{Z}} N^1(X)\) is called the Picard number of \(X\).



Lemma 1 (Numerical Invariance of Intersection) If \(L_1 \equiv_{\mathrm{num}} L_1', \dots, L_k \equiv_{\mathrm{num}} L_k'\), then for any subvariety \(V \subseteq X\) of pure dimension \(k\), \[
(L_1 \cdots L_k \cdot [V]) = (L_1' \cdots L_k' \cdot [V]).
\]


Theorem 1 (Asymptotic Riemann-Roch I)  

Let \(X\) be an irreducible proper variety of dimension \(n = \dim X\), and \(D \in \operatorname{Div}(X)\). As \(m \to \infty\), \[
\chi(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) = \frac{(D^n)}{n!} m^n + O(m^{n-1}).
\] More generally, for any coherent sheaf \(\mathcal{F} \in \operatorname{Coh}(X)\), \[
\chi(X, \mathcal{F} \otimes_{\mathcal{O}_X} \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) = \operatorname{rank}(\mathcal{F}) \cdot \frac{(D^n)}{n!} m^n + O(m^{n-1}).
\]
If \(D\) is ample, then by Serre vanishing \(H^i(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) = 0\) for all \(i > 0\) and \(m \gg 0\), hence: \[
h^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) = \frac{(D^n)}{n!} m^n + O(m^{n-1}),
\] and for any \(\mathcal{F} \in \operatorname{Coh}(X)\), \[
h^0(X, \mathcal{F} \otimes_{\mathcal{O}_X} \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) = \operatorname{rank}(\mathcal{F}) \cdot \frac{(D^n)}{n!} m^n + O(m^{n-1}).
\]



Proposition 5 (Amplitude Checked on Curves and Reduction)  

Let \(f: Y \to X\) be a finite morphism of proper schemes. If \(L \in \operatorname{Pic}(X)\) is ample, then \(f^* L \in \operatorname{Pic}(Y)\) is ample.
A line bundle \(L \in \operatorname{Pic}(X)\) is ample if and only if \(L|_{X_{\mathrm{red}}}\) is ample, if and only if \(L|_{X_{i, \mathrm{red}}}\) is ample for every irreducible component \(X_i\) of \(X\).
Let \(L\) be a globally generated line bundle on a proper scheme \(X\). Then \(L\) is ample if and only if \((L \cdot C) > 0\) for every irreducible curve \(C \subseteq X\).



Proof. Proof of (3). Consider the following three assertions: - (a) \(L\) is ample; - (b) The morphism \(\phi = \phi_{|L|}: X \to \mathbb{P} H^0(X, L)\) is finite; - (c) \((L \cdot C) > 0\) for all irreducible curves \(C \subseteq X\).
We show \((b) \implies (a) \implies (c) \implies (b)\):

\((b) \implies (a)\): Since \(\phi\) is finite and \(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}(1)\) is ample, \(L \cong \phi^* \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}(1)\) is ample by (1).
\((a) \implies (c)\): If \(L\) is ample, its restriction to any curve \(C \subseteq X\) is ample, hence \((L \cdot C) = \deg(L|_C) > 0\).
\((c) \implies (b)\): Suppose \(\phi\) is not finite. Since \(\phi\) is a proper morphism, it cannot be quasi-finite. Hence there exists a point \(p \in \phi(X)\) such that \(\dim \phi^{-1}(p) \ge 1\). Choose an irreducible curve \(Z \subseteq \phi^{-1}(p) \subseteq X\). Endow \(Z\) with the reduced structure.
The restriction \(\phi|_Z: Z \to \mathbb{P}^N\) has set-theoretic image \(\{p\}\). Because \(Z\) is reduced, the scheme-theoretic image \(\operatorname{Im}(\phi|_Z)\) is reduced, meaning \(\operatorname{Im}(\phi|_Z) = \operatorname{Spec} k(p) \hookrightarrow \mathbb{P}^N\). Thus the pullback bundle: \[
L|_Z = (\phi|_Z)^* \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^N}(1) \cong \mathcal{O}_Z
\] is trivial. Consequently, \((L \cdot Z) = \deg(\mathcal{O}_Z) = 0\), contradicting assumption (c). Thus \(\phi\) is finite, completing the proof.



Proposition 6 (Asymptotic Riemann-Roch II) Let \(X\) be an irreducible projective variety of dimension \(n\), and let \(D \in \operatorname{Div}(X)\) be an ample Cartier divisor. Then: \[
h^0(X, \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) = \frac{(D^n)}{n!} m^n + O(m^{n-1}).
\] For any coherent sheaf \(\mathcal{F} \in \operatorname{Coh}(X)\), \[
h^0(X, \mathcal{F} \otimes_{\mathcal{O}_X} \mathcal{O}_X(mD)) = \operatorname{rank}(\mathcal{F}) \cdot \frac{(D^n)}{n!} m^n + O(m^{n-1}).
\]


Proposition 7 (Intersection with Complete Intersections in \(\mathbb{P}^N\)) Let \(X = \mathbb{P}^N\), and let \(Y \subseteq X\) be an irreducible subvariety of dimension \(n\). If \(H_1, \dots, H_n\) are effective hypersurfaces of degrees \(d_1, \dots, d_n\) in \(\mathbb{P}^N\), then: \[
(\mathcal{O}_X(H_1) \cdots \mathcal{O}_X(H_n) \cdot Y) = d_1 \cdots d_n \deg(Y).
\]


Proposition 8 (Projection Formula for Intersections) Let \(\pi: X_1 \to X_2\) be a morphism of integral proper schemes of the same dimension \(n\). For any line bundles \(L_1, \dots, L_n \in \operatorname{Pic}(X_2)\), \[
(\pi^* L_1 \cdots \pi^* L_n) = \deg(X_1 / X_2) \cdot (L_1 \cdots L_n).
\]


Theorem 2 (Cartier Class Group and Picard Group) If \(X\) is a reduced Noetherian scheme, then: \[
\operatorname{CaCl}(X) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \operatorname{Pic}(X).
\]


Proof. Proof idea. We show that \(H^1(X, \mathcal{K}_X^*) = 0\). Let \(X = \bigcup_{j=1}^m \overline{\{\eta_j\}}\) be the decomposition into irreducible components with generic points \(\eta_j\). Then: \[
\mathcal{K}_X^* = \bigoplus_{j=1}^m (i_{\eta_j})_* K_j^*,
\] which is a direct sum of pushforwards of constant sheaves from points, hence \(\mathcal{K}_X^*\) is flasque. Therefore \(H^1(X, \mathcal{K}_X^*) = 0\). Taking cohomology of the short exact sequence \(0 \to \mathcal{O}_X^* \to \mathcal{K}_X^* \to \mathcal{K}_X^* / \mathcal{O}_X^* \to 0\) yields: \[
H^0(X, \mathcal{K}_X^*) \xrightarrow{\;\operatorname{div}\;} H^0(X, \mathcal{K}_X^* / \mathcal{O}_X^*) \longrightarrow H^1(X, \mathcal{O}_X^*) \longrightarrow 0,
\] which implies: \[
\operatorname{coker}(\operatorname{div}) = \operatorname{Div}(X) / \operatorname{PDiv}(X) = \operatorname{CaCl}(X) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \operatorname{Pic}(X).
\]


Theorem 3 (Cartier Divisors vs. Weil Divisors) Let \(X\) be an irreducible variety that is regular in codimension 1. Then the cycle map induces injective homomorphisms: \[
\operatorname{Div}(X) \hookrightarrow \operatorname{WDiv}(X) \quad \text{and} \quad \operatorname{CaCl}(X) \hookrightarrow \operatorname{Cl}(X).
\] In particular, if \(X\) is smooth (or regular), these maps are isomorphisms.

title: Positivity in AG

Positivity is a central organizing principle in modern algebraic geometry, bridging algebraic topology, complex differential geometry (metric curvature), and birational geometry (the Minimal Model Program). This notebook follows the foundational text Positivity in Algebraic Geometry I by Robert Lazarsfeld, systematically developing the theory of ample, nef, and big divisors, convex cones in the Néron-Severi space, and asymptotic invariants of section rings.
The development progresses logically from classical intersection theory and asymptotic Riemann-Roch to convex cone geometry, asymptotic invariants, and birational decomposition theorems:

The following table summarizes the key properties, intersection-theoretic criteria, and asymptotic behaviors across the hierarchy of positivity:
